title: 16-year-old Dhinidhi Desinghu scripts history at Youth Olympics, becomes first Indian swimmer to win a medal
text: Dhinidhi Desinghu (Agency Photo) India's Dhinidhi Desinghu created history at the 2026 Youth Olympics in Dakar, Senegal, by becoming the first Indian female swimmer to win a medal at the competition. The 16-year-old secured bronze in the women's 100m freestyle, clocking 56.27 seconds. Croatia's Ana Bobanovic won gold in 55.89 seconds, while New Zealand's Alyssa Lawson took silver in 56.13 seconds. Watch Kynan Chenai: The 38-Year-Old Gun Barrel, Asian Games Gold and the LA 2028 Dream | TOISA Spotlight The medal adds another milestone to Desinghu's growing swimming career. She had earlier become the first Indian female swimmer to reach a Youth Olympics final after finishing third-fastest overall in the heats with a time of 56.80 seconds. A promising swimmer with another medal opportunity Her coach, Nihar Ameen, praised her hard work and recent performances, highlighting that she had broken the national record three times this year. "She has been working really hard. This year, she has broken the national record three times. She is in form. She has another shot at a medal in the 200m freestyle event. In fact, she has a better chance of winning another medal there," he said. Join conversation View All Comments â Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful Â· TOI community guidelines Ameen also spoke about her mental strength and experience, having already competed at the 2024 Paris Olympics. "Dhinidhi is mentally very tough. She has already competed at the 2024 Paris Olympics. We are very hopeful that she will win another medal at this Youth Olympics." Desinghu was the youngest member of India's contingent at the Paris Olympics. She is now looking to add another medal in the 200m freestyle at Dakar. Khushbu Darjada wins in judo There was more good news for India in judo, as 15-year-old Khushbu Rajakbhai Darjada won her women's 63kg round-of-16 bout against Guinea's Mamaissata Camara. Khushbu secured a 1-0 victory through a yuko, a minor scoring point awarded for an effective technique. Her opponent also received a minor penalty, known as a Shido, for a rule infringement. title: Irelandâs two-time Olympian Ciara Mageean dies aged 34 after cancer battle, weeks after getting married
text: Irelandâs two-time Olympian Ciara Mageean dies aged 34 after cancer battle/ Image: Instagram Ciara Mageean spent years establishing herself among Europe's leading middle-distance runners, culminating in the 1500 metres title at the 2024 European Championships in Rome. The two-time Olympian, who had represented Ireland on the biggest stages in athletics, died on Sunday morning, November 1, after being diagnosed with stage four bowel cancer in May 2025. She was 34. Mageean dies surrounded by her loved ones Mageean died at 6.30am on Sunday, November 1, surrounded by her family and loved ones, according to a statement published on her social media accounts. The Irish athlete had announced last year that she had been diagnosed with bowel cancer, with the illness later identified as stage four. The statement read: âAt 6:30am this morning, Ciara lost her battle with cancer surrounded by her loved ones. A beloved daughter, sister, wife, friend and inspiration to so many, she will be deeply missed.â It concluded with the Irish-language tribute: âAr dheis DÃ© go raibh a hanamâ, meaning âmay her soul rest in peaceâ. Mageean, who was from Portaferry in County Down, Northern Ireland, had married last month. Her death prompted tributes from Athletics Ireland, which described her as a much-loved and inspirational figure whose courage, warmth and spirit would leave a lasting legacy. An initial statement from the governing body said: âAthletics Ireland is deeply saddened to learn of the passing of Ciara Mageean. âCiara was a much-loved and inspirational figure who touched the lives of so many. Her courage, warmth and spirit will leave a lasting legacy. âThe thoughts and heartfelt condolences of everyone at Athletics Ireland are with Ciaraâs family, friends and loved ones at this incredibly difficult time. âMay she rest in peace.â From European bronze to the 1500m title in Rome Mageean's greatest achievement came at the 2024 European Athletics Championships in Rome, where she won the women's 1500 metres gold medal to become European champion. It was the first major title of her career, following years of competing at the highest level of international middle-distance running. Her European success had been built over several championships. She won bronze in the 1500m at the 2016 European Championships, then improved to silver at the 2022 edition before finally claiming gold two years later. The three medals marked a progression across eight years, with the Rome victory completing a long pursuit of a major senior championship title. Mageean also reached the final of the 1500m at the 2023 World Athletics Championships, finishing fourth. She had come close to a global podium but ended the competition just outside the medal positions. At the Commonwealth Games, she represented Northern Ireland and won silver in the 1500m at Birmingham 2022. The result added another major championship medal to a career that had brought success across European and Commonwealth competition. Two Olympic appearances and the Paris disappointment Mageean represented Ireland at the Rio 2016 and Tokyo 2020 Olympic Games, becoming a two-time Olympian during a career that took her to the sport's biggest international competitions. Join conversation View All Comments â Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful Â· TOI community guidelines She had been expected to compete at a third consecutive Olympics in Paris in 2024, but an Achilles injury forced her to withdraw from the Games. The setback came in the same year as her European Championship triumph in Rome, leaving her with the distinction of becoming a continental champion but unable to compete at the Olympics that summer. Her career had included both the demands of repeated championship campaigns and the injuries that disrupted her preparations. Despite missing Paris, her European gold, two further European podium finishes, Commonwealth silver and two Olympic appearances established her as one of Ireland's leading middle-distance athletes. Mageean's death at 34 brings to an end a career in which she represented Ireland and Northern Ireland at major international championships, culminating in the European title she won in Rome in 2024. title: Dhinidhi Desinghu scripts history with first-ever Indian swimming medal at Youth Olympics
text: Dhinidhi Desinghu (File photo) BENGALURU: Indian swimming has a new milestone to celebrate, and Bengaluru talent Dhinidhi Desinghu is at the heart of it. The 16-year-old became the first swimmer from the country to win a medal at the Youth Olympic Games, claiming bronze in the women's 100m freestyle in Dakar, Senegal, on Monday. While Dhinidhi had set her sights on gold and a sub-55-second finish, her podium finish was a historic achievement for Indian swimming. Croatia's Ana Bobanovic took gold in 55.89 seconds, while New Zealand's Alyssa Lawson claimed silver in 56.13 seconds. The performance had been building momentum from the heats. Dhinidhi clocked 56.80 seconds to finish third-fastest overall and become the first Indian female swimmer to qualify for a Youth Olympics final. She carried that form into the final. âI'm very happy but also at a loss for words. In the heats, my timing went below 57. I've never had a time below 57 in the event, and I knew something special would happen," she told TOI. Going into the final, there was a mix of nerves and confidence. The conditions, too, worked in her favour. "Generally, when I swim outdoors, and it's hot and humid, I swim better, because the conditions are similar to what it is back home," she said. The result, however, was initially not quite what she had hoped for. "When I touched the pad and saw the timing, I wasn't very happy. I wanted to win gold and I wanted my time to break 55, but didnât achieve either. But slowly it sank in â I am India's first swimmer to win a medal at the Youth Olympics and that does mean something special," added the teenager, who trains under Nihar Ameen. The win's significance went beyond the medal itself. Dhinidi believes her podium finish is a breakthrough for women's swimming in the country. "I think what makes it more special is that it's a woman who has given India its first medal in swimming in the competition. It will mean a lot for women's swimming because we're not at the same level as the men. This will make it a memorable chapter in women's swimming in our country and help in the growth of our sport," she said. Join conversation View All Comments â Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful Â· TOI community guidelines She is the third Indian to reach a final at the competition, after two-time Olympian Srihari Nataraj, who made the final in 2018, and Tirthank Pegu, who is competing in the ongoing edition. But milestones are nothing new to her. Dhinidhi was just 14 when she made her Olympic debut at Paris 2024, becoming the youngest member of the Indian contingent. She had also represented India at the 2022 Asian Games in Hangzhou and the 2024 World Aquatics Championships in Doha. For now, the triumph is still sinking in. âIt (medal) will take some time to sink in. After Paris, it took a couple of years to sink in that I was an Olympian. So, it is safe to say this will take a long time to sink in," she signed off. Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

title: Hockey is in blood of Punjab, says Mann as Champions Trophy kicks off in Jalandhar
text: Punjab CM Bhagwant Mann shakes hands with players of the Indian men's hockey team on the field during the inauguration of the Hero Asian Champions Trophy 2026 at the Surjeet Hockey Stadium in Burlton Park in Jalandhar on Tuesday Jalandhar : Punjab chief minister Bhagwant Mann on Tuesday inaugurated the ninth Asian Champions Trophy hockey tournament at the Olympian Surjit Singh Hockey Stadium in Jalandhar, marking the first time the state has hosted the international event. Six nations are competing in the tournament. Jalandhar will host all the league matches, while Mohali will stage the semi-finals and final. Welcoming the teams and felicitating their captains, Mann said Punjab was ready to reclaim its place on the global hockey stage. He expressed hope that the tournament would strengthen the stateâs bid to host the 2030 Hockey World Cup. âPunjab and hockey share an inseparable bond. The stateâs contribution to Indian hockey is not merely a matter of statistics but a legacy built on passion, sacrifice, discipline and an unbreakable sporting spirit,â he said, adding, âHockey is in the blood of Punjab, and every generation of our players has carried this legacy forward with immense pride.â Highlighting Punjabâs contribution to the sport, Mann said, âFrom the 1928 Amsterdam Olympics to the 2024 Paris Olympics, Punjab has produced 77 hockey Olympians, with 48 players from the state winning Olympic medals. Punjabi players have also captained the Indian hockey team at the Olympics on 10 occasions, reflecting Punjabâs enduring leadership in the sport.â Paying tribute to legendary hockey players, Mann recalled the contributions of Balbir Singh Sr, Udham Singh, Pritipal Singh, Ajit Pal Singh, Surjit Singh and Pargat Singh, saying their achievements continued to inspire generations of young athletes. The CM said Indiaâs bronze-medal victories in menâs hockey at the Tokyo Olympics in 2021 and the Paris Olympics in 2024 had revived national pride in the sport after a gap of 52 years between consecutive Olympic medal-winning campaigns. âPunjabâs strong representation in both teams is evidence of the stateâs continuing importance to Indian hockey. The current Indian hockey team, led by Harmanpreet Singh , has eight players from Punjab,â Mann said. The opening day drew former Olympians, international athletes and thousands of local spectators, including young players from regional sports academies. âHosting events like this helps the youth stay connected to our sporting legacy,â said Ajit Singh, a 24-year-old local hockey player. Fifteen children from the Khelo India academy cheered as the Indian menâs team opened its campaign with a 13-0 win over Bangladesh. Sehajpreet Kaur, from Kukad Pind, said she took up hockey because of Harmanpreet Singh and Hardik Singh. âI will watch them play live. It is a feeling I canât describe,â she said. Arsh Sandhu, a student from Suranasi, arrived with his friends wearing India jerseys. Vinod Sharma, who walked 2km from the main gate to reach the stands, said, âThis is a big thing for Jalandhar. title: Skye Blakely opens up on âsacrificesâ after injury setbacks kept her out of two Olympic Games
text: Skye Blakely opens up on âsacrificesâ after injury setbacks kept her out of two Olympic Games Skye Blakelyâs first world all-around title came after two Olympic dreams were cut short by injury. The 21-year-old American won gold at the 2026 World Artistic Gymnastics Championships in Rotterdam on October 23, scoring 55.733 across four events. She also helped the United States win team silver and later added bronze medals on vault and uneven bars. But the result meant more than four medals. After missing the Tokyo and Paris Olympic teams, Blakely says the sacrifices behind her return helped her believe she could reach the top and compete again at the highest level. Skye Blakely explains the sacrifices behind her gymnastics career and comeback Blakely knows that chasing a place among the world's best comes with choices that other college students may not have to make. While her friends enjoy campus life and social activities, much of her time goes into training, competitions, recovery and studies. She admitted that she sometimes feels left out, but she is willing to accept it. âIâm not scared to sacrifice things to achieve my biggest dreams,â Blakely told the Associated Press. She explained that once she sets her mind on something, she finds the drive to work towards it, even when the process becomes difficult. Her career has already tested that determination twice. In 2021, she tore a ligament in her left elbow during vault warm-ups at the U.S. Olympic Trials. The injury ended her hopes of making the Tokyo team when she was just 16. Three years later, she had another chance. Blakely finished second behind Simone Biles at the 2024 U.S. Championships and looked set to compete for a place on the Paris team. However, she ruptured her right Achilles tendon during floor exercise training just two days before the Olympic Trials. Once again, she had to watch the Olympics from home. The recovery took time. Instead of rushing back into the all-around, Blakely worked on rebuilding her strength and routines. She continued competing for the University of Florida while taking a careful approach to her return. By the 2026 U.S. Championships, she was competing in the all-around again, although she was still working to bring back the difficulty in her routines. Skye Blakely wins Rotterdam gold and looks towards the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics Blakely's return to the world all-around final was not even certain when she arrived in Rotterdam. She knew she would compete on vault, uneven bars and balance beam, but did not learn until the night before team qualification that she would also perform on floor. During the final, she scored 14.200 on vault, 14.400 on uneven bars and another 14.200 on balance beam. Before her last event, she reminded herself why she had kept going. âDo it for the girl in 2021 and the girl in 2024 who couldnât do everything, just fight for her,â she told herself. She finished with 12.933 on floor, taking her total to 55.733. Russia's Liudmila Roshchina won silver with 55.199, while China's Ke Qinqin took bronze with 55.032. Join conversation View All Comments â Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful Â· TOI community guidelines Blakely later said her faith and belief in herself helped her control her nerves. Her four medals also made her the first gymnast to compete in NCAA gymnastics and win the world all-around title in the same calendar year. Her plans do not stop with the world title. Blakely intends to stay at the University of Florida for at least the upcoming season and hopes to help the Gators win an NCAA national championship. Florida finished third at the 2026 NCAA Championships. The 2028 Los Angeles Olympics are another goal. Suni Lee, Jade Carey, Jordan Chiles and Hezly Rivera are among the gymnasts who could compete for places on the five-member U.S. team. Simone Biles has also not ruled out another Olympic appearance. For Blakely, Rotterdam has given her a reason to trust her ability again. As she told the Associated Press, the win reminded her that she can handle difficult situations and move forward with confidence. Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

title: âInjury much better nowâ: Neeraj Chopra on the path to recovery; to resume training and rehabilitation in next few weeks
text: Neeraj Chopra (PTI Photo) New Delhi: Olympic and world champion javelin thrower Neeraj Chopra said his recovery from injury is on the right path and training, rehab process will begun in the next couple of weeks. The 2020 Tokyo Olympics gold medallist has kept next year as his target after sustaining an injury, with his focus on delivering strong performances ahead of LA 2028. Chopra, who won gold at the Tokyo 2020 Olympics and silver at the Paris 2024 Olympics in men's javelin throw, has been one of India's leading figures in recent years. However, Chopra missed the recent 2026 Asian Games in Aichi-Nagoya after he suffered an ankle ligament injury during a training session, which also ruled him out for the rest of the season. "My injury is much better now. I faced some issues initially in the first month and a half, but it has improved significantly. I consulted Dr. Dinshaw Pardiwala and he has advised that I can now resume training and begin proper rehabilitation. My plan is to start both in the next couple of weeks," Neeraj told SAI Media. The two-time Olympic medallist clarified that he followed complete rest as advised by his medical team. "For my injury, the doctors had advised rest, and that is exactly what I followed. With regard to competitions, TOPS (Target Olympic Podium Scheme) and SAI (Sports Authority of India) have been supporting me for years. I have been part of the TOPS Core Group for many years now, and whenever I need any support, they are there," he added. Join conversation View All Comments â Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful Â· TOI community guidelines In Neeraj and Kishore Jena's absence, Yashvir Singh won a silver medal and Rohit Yadav a bronze in javelin throw at the 2026 Asian Games. Neeraj also welcomed the Union Cabinet's approval of the Khelo India Sports Goods Manufacturing Scheme on October 28, calling it a major step for Indian sport. "The Khelo India Sports Goods Manufacturing Scheme, which was approved by the Union Cabinet, is an amazing step. Athletes face a lot of issues in procuring certain equipment in India or have to import sporting equipment from abroad. With schemes like these, as equipment will be manufactured in India, it will become much easier for them to source it," he noted. He then went on to extend his best wishes to the Indian contingent for the upcoming Youth Olympic Games and added, "I wish all the best to the athletes heading to the Youth Olympics. Enjoy the experience and don't take too much pressure or get nervous. Whatever pressure you face at the Youth Olympics is good for you as it teaches you a lot. Use this opportunity to observe others and channel the pressure to your advantage, and I am sure you will do your best. " Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

title: Sabrina Ionescuâs off-court lifestyle: How the New York Liberty starâs WNBA success, Nike endorsements, business investments and personal interests are shaping her future beyond basketball
text: How Sabrina Ionescu turned rejection into an NCAA record and WNBA championship(Getty Images) Ionescuâs success is about a lot more than what she has accomplished for the New York Liberty. Sheâs a WNBA champion and Olympic gold medalist for Team USA at Paris 2024, and has become a leading figure in womenâs basketball, grabbing headlines for her leadership, signature footwear and burgeoning commercial portfolio. Her activities outside the court suggest a larger ambition to leave a lasting impression in sports and business, and Ionescuâs career is a case study in how athletic success can lead to opportunities beyond the court. All from global brand partnerships to investments in womenâs soccer and emerging basketball leagues. How Sabrina Ionescu built her business portfolio beyond WNBA Sabrina Ionescuâs commercial portfolio has grown along with her New York Liberty accomplishments. The No. 1 overall pick in the 2020 WNBA Draft, she has evolved into one of the leagueâs best guards, helping lead New York to its first WNBA title in 2024, and she captured an Olympic gold medal with Team USA at Paris 2024 to cement her place in the sport. Celebrity Net Worth estimates Ionescu to have a net worth of $10 million in September 2026. But this is an estimate and not a confirmed accounting of her finances. She makes money from professional basketball, endorsements and business interests, with off-court earnings making up a large portion of her financial profile. What drives Sabrina Ionescuâs endorsement and brand success Nike stays at the heart of Ionescuâs reputation. She was the first womenâs basketball player to have a unisex signature footwear and apparel collection with the company in 2023. The Sabrina line has continued to grow; Nike announced the Sabrina 4 collection in April 2026 and launched it in July. Her presence in both womenâs and menâs basketball has helped make her a recognizable name in performance footwear. Her broader endorsement portfolio has included partnerships with AT&T, BodyArmor, Fanatics, State Farm, Xbox and others. These partnerships allow her basketball audience to engage with companies and Ionescu to create a public profile outside of her performances on the court; in 2025, Forbes estimated her total earnings at $10.5 million, a sign of the growing weight of commercial opportunities in her overall financial picture. How Sabrina Ionescu balances basketball and business interests Ionescu has also studied investments in sports and technology. She became an investor and commercial advisor to Bay FC, a National Womenâs Soccer League club based in the San Francisco Bay Area, in March 2025. She is involved in contributing to commercial strategy and helping the clubâs athletes develop their own endorsement portfolios. The move is more of an interest in helping the growth of womenâs sports in general than just basketball. Her investments have also included Buzzer Media and Nex, and her work with Kevin Durantâs Boardroom and Thirty Five Ventures has broadened her exposure to sports media and business. Those interests could provide opportunities beyond her playing career, although the value of any individual investments and any future returns have not been publicly established. Outside of business, Ionescu is married to NFL player Hroniss Grasu, whom she married in March 2024. She has remained connected to her family roots, the University of Oregon and the communities that molded her. She also has a public profile through youth-sports initiatives with the SI20 Foundation, which aims to increase opportunities for young people through athletics. title: High performance shooting centre opens in Navi Mumbai
text: shooting centre Navi Mumbai: Lakshya Shooting Club and Axis Bank inaugurated a high-performance shooting centre at CBD Belapur, the first of its kind in the MMR, to support Indian athletes preparing for international competitions, including the Olympic Games. The para-inclusive centre will provide training, coaching, sports science, nutrition, medicine and athlete-development support under one roof. This was conceptualised by Olympian shooter and Dronacharya awardee Suma Shirur, who dreamt of opening such a facility in the city to tap young talents. The six-storey centre has two dedicated 10-metre shooting ranges, strength and conditioning facilities, biomechanics assessment, physiotherapy, sports psychology and nutrition support, recovery areas and residential facilities. It will offer Elite Residency, Day Scholar and Development programmes, providing separate pathways for athletes at different stages. The centre will focus primarily on elite shooters preparing for international competitions, while Lakshyaâs wider network will continue identifying and nurturing emerging talent. Lakshya Shooting Club was established in 2006 by Indian Olympian and former national shooting coach Suma Shirur. Its athletes have competed at national and international events, including the Olympic and Paralympic Games, Asian Games, Commonwealth Games and World Championships. They include three-time Paralympic medallist Avani Lekhara , who won gold medals at Tokyo 2020 and Paris 2024, and Parth Mane, the 2024 junior world champion and a team silver medallist at the Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games 2026. Axis Bank group head Vijay Mulbagal said the partnership sought to provide aspiring and elite athletes with access to infrastructure, coaching and technical support. Shirur, Lakshyaâs founder and high-performance director, said the centre would support every aspect of athletesâ performance as they prepared for global competition. The green-certified building was constructed to meet sustainability standards for energy and resource efficiency. title: For those on night shift, sleep isnât optional
text: Chandigarh: For doctors, nurses and other healthcare workers battling irregular shifts, a good nightâs sleep can often be the first casualty. But poor sleep is not just about feeling tired the next day. PGI experts say recognising sleep disorders and managing shift-work fatigue are important for the well-being and clinical efficiency of healthcare professionals. From knowing when to have that cup of coffee to tweaking mobile screen settings and taking a strategically timed nap, practical ways to improve sleep took centre stage at a seminar on sleep health organised by the Continuing Nursing Education Cell at PGIMER Tuesday. Around 90 nursing officers, doctors, faculty members and other healthcare professionals attended the seminar, which focused on sleep hygiene, challenges posed by shift work and the long-term consequences of untreated sleep disorders. Dr Navneet Dhaliwal, joint medical superintendent, PGIMER, stressed the importance of sleep health literacy for both the personal well-being and clinical efficiency of healthcare staff. Putting the spotlight on a condition often dismissed as mere snoring, Prof Sandeep Bansal of PGIMERâs ENT department spoke about obstructive sleep apnoea (OSA) and its consequences beyond snoring. He outlined signs and symptoms that could help identify the condition, simple assessment scales for early risk evaluation and underlying anatomical causes. Bansal, who is also president of the Indian Association of Surgeons for Sleep Apnoea, highlighted weight management as an important preventive measure and discussed treatment options for adults as well as children. The shift-workerâs sleep dilemma was taken up by Dr Monika Sharma, former sleep adviser to the Indian Olympic contingent for the Paris 2024 Olympics. She discussed lifestyle changes, cognitive techniques and relaxation strategies that healthcare professionals can use to combat shift-work fatigue and improve sleep quality. Her advice also touched upon everyday habits that can disrupt sleep. She explained the role of caffeine and its timing, ways to optimise mobile-screen settings to reduce blue-light interference with the body clock, and the effective use of strategic naps. The seminar, titled âSleep Health Literacy: Knowledge | Awareness | Better Healthâ, was held at PGIMERâs APC Auditorium. title: From crying at the sight of a swimming pool to the Paris Olympics: How Bengaluruâs 14-year-old Dhinidhi Desinghu overcame her fear of water to become Indiaâs youngest athlete at the 2024 Games
text: At six, Dhinidhi Desinghu struggled with something many swimmers eventually learn to love: being in the water. Getting her feet into a swimming pool and putting her head underwater felt frightening, and her parents had to enter the pool themselves to help her feel comfortable. Eight years later, that same Bengaluru girl stood on the Olympic stage in Paris, representing India in the womenâs 200-metre freestyle. Dhinidhiâs journey is not simply a story of a young athlete reaching a major sporting event. It is about how a childhood fear gradually gave way to confidence, how a demanding routine became part of everyday life, and how a teenager learned to compete among some of the worldâs most accomplished swimmers. Her selection for Paris 2024 made her the youngest member of Indiaâs Olympic contingent at the age of 14. From a frightened beginner to a national-level swimmer In an interview with The Indian Express ahead of the Paris Olympics, Dhinidhi recalled how difficult her early swimming lessons had been. She did not want to enter the water, and her parents had to support her patiently as she worked through the fear. Her mother, Jesitha, also described how anxiety affected Dhinidhi at swimming competitions. Despite showing promise in the pool, the young swimmer sometimes became so nervous before races that she would feel unwell. Rather than forcing her to push through every moment of fear, her family continued to support her as she gradually became more comfortable. A turning point came at a state-level meet in Mangaluru. According to her motherâs account, Dhinidhi was initially reluctant to compete after the family had travelled for the event. They agreed to visit the pool first, leaving open the possibility of returning without racing. After looking around, Dhinidhi decided she could take part and went on to win gold. That experience helped change her relationship with competition. Instead of allowing anxiety to dictate her choices, she began building confidence through participation and practice. Her progress soon became visible in the results. Dhinidhi joined Dolphin Aquatics in Bengaluru, where she trained under coach B. M. Madhu Kumar. In August 2023, at just 13, she set a national record in the Group II girlsâ 100-metre freestyle at the Sub-Junior and Junior National Aquatic Championships, clocking 57.67 seconds and breaking the previous mark of 59.12 seconds. She also collected medals at major domestic competitions. At the 2023 National Games in Goa, she won seven gold medals, according to World Aquatics. These performances helped establish her as one of Indiaâs promising young swimmers well before her Olympic debut. A routine built around school, training and ambitious goals Reaching the highest level of sport requires more than talent. For Dhinidhi, it meant organising much of her day around training while continuing her education. A report by myKhel described a routine that began before sunrise. Dhinidhi would wake at around 4 am, reach the pool before 5 am and train until approximately 7.30 am before heading to school. After classes, she returned to the pool for another training session in the afternoon, often spending several additional hours working on her swimming. The schedule left little room for an ordinary school-day routine. While other teenagers might spend their evenings relaxing with friends, Dhinidhi had to balance homework, meals, recovery and preparation for the next dayâs session. She also kept track of her progress in a diary. As reported by *The Indian Express*, she recorded training sessions, target timings and national records so that she could measure how far she had come and what she wanted to achieve next. Writing down her goals gave her a practical way to connect everyday effort with longer-term ambitions. That discipline helped her gain experience beyond domestic competitions. She competed at the 2022 Asian Games in Hangzhou and the 2024 World Aquatics Championships in Doha before travelling to Paris. The Olympic Games were therefore a major milestone, but not her first encounter with international competition. Taking the Olympic stage at 14 Dhinidhi qualified for Paris 2024 through a universality selection, a mechanism that allows eligible countries with limited representation in swimming to enter athletes under specific criteria. She competed in the womenâs 200-metre freestyle on July 28, 2024. She finished her heat in 2 minutes 6.96 seconds and placed 23rd overall among 31 swimmers, according to World Aquatics. Her time was not enough to advance to the next round, but the result must be understood in the context of her age and the level of competition she faced. After the race, Dhinidhi described the experience as an extraordinary opportunity. She said she was happy with how she had followed her coachâs instructions and felt that it was one of the better morning swims she had produced, even though it was not a personal best. The Olympics did not instantly turn her into a medal winner, nor did it mark the end of her development. Instead, it gave her experience of competing in one of sportâs most demanding environments and an opportunity to learn from athletes at the highest level. Dhinidhiâs story is a reminder that progress does not always begin with confidence. Sometimes it starts with a child who is afraid to put her head underwater, parents who help her take one small step, and a willingness to try again. By the time she reached Paris, the fear that once kept her away from the pool had become part of a much longer journey, one shaped by practice, patience and the courage to keep moving forward. title: âI donât think perfection exists, but Iâm searching for itâ: Kynan Chenaiâs unfinished Olympic pursuit | TOISA Spotlight
text: Kynan Chenai âGoosebumps!â That is the first word Kynan Chenai uses when asked what comes to mind when he thinks back to the Asian Games mixed-team trap final. He and Neeru Dhanda had won gold for India, but Chenai says there was little room to think about the medal while he was shooting. His attention was on the target, the gun mount, and the moment he needed to press the trigger. âAt that point, nothing else mattered. It didn't matter if someone missed a target or if someone else broke theirs. All that mattered was hitting my target.â The emotion came later. âSo, sitting here with you and thinking about it now, the one word that comes to mind is goosebumps.â Watch Kynan Chenai: The 38-Year-Old Gun Barrel, Asian Games Gold and the LA 2028 Dream | TOISA Spotlight Chenai had finished 16th in qualification in the individual event. In the mixed team, held a day later, he combined with Neeru Dhanda to qualify for the final and then shot 19 of 20 in the final. The change in performance was not lost on him. âAt the Asian Games, I'm glad my experience and ability allowed me to flip the switch between the individual competition and the mixed-team event,â he says. âI was able to back myself and get that energy back after the individual event, which had taken place just a day earlier.â âI'm glad I was able to flip that switch. However, it comes down to my experience and my ability to grit my teeth and grind through difficult situations.â Gold medallist India's Neeru Dhanda, left, and Kynan Chenai pose for photographers during the medal ceremony after the trap mixed team shooting event at the 20th Asian Games, in Nagoya, Japan. (PTI Photo/Atul Yadav) The final also required Chenai to work alongside Dhanda, who had come off a demanding Asian Games campaign and was exhausted after shooting in the rain. He says the two had their own routines and that he trusted her to know what she was doing. He told her he would help if she needed anything; otherwise, they would focus on their targets and assess the result afterwards. Dhanda told him at one point, âMy battery is down.â Chenai's reply was characteristically brief: âThen go and recharge it!â He laughs about their banter and says he was impressed by how she found the energy to keep going. âEventually, I was very impressed by how she managed to gather some energy and hold everything together to a certain extent. I'm glad I was able to do the same, and it worked out very well for the country.â India's Neeru Dhanda, left, and Kynan Chenai celebrate after winning the gold medal (Photo by Atul Yadav) The 38-year-old barrel behind the gold There was another detail behind the performance: the barrel on his gun belonged to his father, Darius Chenai, former national trap champion, who introduced Kynan to the sport when he was 10. The barrel was 38 years old. Chenai had been using a high-rib barrel for four or five years but was not getting the consistency he wanted. The decision to change it came after discussions with his team. His Perazzi gun allows different components to be fitted to the same action, so he could use another barrel without changing the entire gun. He did not have a regular barrel at home; his father's gun was the only one with one available. âI asked him, and he said, âYeah, take it, use it.â He wasn't using it at the time.â The older barrel worked well enough to be part of an Asian Games gold-medal performance. His father has since been teasing him about how many shells he is putting through it and warning him to be careful with something already so old. âBut at the end of the day, it's all fun and jokes with him. He's quite proud that I've been able to use something of his and achieve some success with it.â The first person who taught him to shoot Kynan with father Darius (Photo from Instagram) Darius was also the person who first took Chenai to the range and put a gun in his hands. A two-time national champion in trap shooting, he taught his son the basics of shooting and, just as importantly, how to handle a firearm safely. Chenai says his father explained that a gun had to be respected, cleaned and put away properly. Some of the techniques he learnt then remain part of his shooting today. âI've had many different role models throughout my career. I could give you a list of names, but Dad is one of them. He's the first one, the OG.â He also names Manjir Singh, Manojit Singh Sandhu and Ranjan Sodhi as influences. More recently, David Kostelecki, his coach and a two-time Olympic medallist, has become an important source of advice. âI've been trying to learn from him how to win an Olympic medal. I keep picking his brain.â Chenai grew up in Hyderabad and spent 10 years at Hebron School in Ooty. He describes himself as a child more interested in sport than studies, keen to be involved in whatever was happening around him. Prithviraj Tondaiman, an accomplished Indian trap shooter who competed at the Paris 2024 Olympics and was part of India's gold-medal-winning men's trap team at the 2022 Asian Games in Hangzhou, was a young shooter at the range when Chenai was growing up. Tondaiman has often told him that he wanted to do everything: put the microphone on the range, load clay targets into the machine, check that it worked, shoot and then pick up the empty cartridges. âI was one of those kids who wanted to be involved in everything,â Chenai says. âI was into hockey, swimming, shooting and football. I loved everything.â Eventually, he had to settle on one sport. âBut eventually, as life goes on, you realise that you don't have enough time to do everything. You have to pick one thing, and I'm glad I picked this one.â Kynan Chenai with Manvjit Singh Sandhu and Prithviraj Tondaiman (Photo from Instagram) Rio, the missed Olympics and the road to LA The Olympics became the main target in his twenties. Chenai was 25 when he made his debut at Rio 2016, but he now looks back at that version of himself as a shooter who wanted to reach the Games without fully understanding what it took to win a medal there. âIn my twenties, the one goal was to go to the Olympics. That was the main thing I wanted to achieve. However, I didn't know how to win an Olympic medal. I was a kid running on fumes. I was just shooting my way through whatever I could, relying on sheer grit and, as they say, sheer dumb luck.â Rio gave him the experience of competing at the Olympics and, in his words, a clearer sense of what he needed to do differently next time. Chenai finished 19th in the men's trap qualification with a score of 114. âThat was a great experience for me because I learnt what to do and what not to do for my next Olympics. It was as simple as that.â He missed Tokyo and then Paris, both disappointments for a shooter who still wants another Olympic opportunity. But Chenai says he has learnt to move on rather than let the absence consume the next phase of his career. âI still have the goal of going to the Olympics. Yes, as you said, I missed the last two, which was disappointing, but it wasn't earth-shattering. I had already been to the Olympics in Rio.â However, the disappointment does not vanish while the Games are under way. He watches other athletes compete and thinks about being there himself. âWhen the Olympic fever is at its peak, you're watching the Games on TV and seeing people do great things. You want to be part of it too, right? When you're not there, it hurts.â His own measure of time is the closing ceremony. âBut after the closing ceremony, you move on and carry on.â Kynan at Rio Olympics (Instagram Photo) Getting to Los Angeles, one competition at a time Los Angeles 2028 is the next Olympic target, but Chenai is not looking to plan every step two years in advance. He wants to win another World Cup medal, too, and says his focus has shifted towards the competition immediately in front of him. Asked how he is approaching the final stretch towards LA, he answers without dressing it up: âThere's no thinking behind it. There's just winning.â The first task is to win a quota place for India. He says that can be done at a World Cup, World Championship or Asian Championship, after which an athlete must qualify through trials in India under the federation's selection policy. âWithout a quota place, we can't go. So, it comes back to what I was telling you earlier: give 100 per cent in one competition and see what happens. After that, we move on to the next one.â For Chenai, preparation means knowing when not to keep shooting. He says athletes can exhaust themselves mentally if they train hard right up to the competition. A shooter might put in 200 shells a day for 10 days, only to arrive at the event tired of repeating the same routine. âYou're going to make a mistake, almost certainly, because you've been training with 200 shells a day for the last 10 days. You'll come back the next day, and your mind will say, âOh man, we've got to do this again?ââ His team follows a regimented tapering process to make sure he is mentally fresh when it counts. The rest of life has to be kept under control, too. Kynan at Asian Games 2026 Podium (Photo by Instagram) âYou also work very hard to make sure everything in your life settles down around the time of your competition. After the competition, things can become hectic again. But during that period, your life has to be very mellow. There should be no drama, nothing.â He describes it as work that happens away from the trigger. Balancing life beyond the shooting range He has also had to make room for life outside the range. Chenai got married seven months before and his businesses take up time as well. âI'm 35 now, so, as my family says, it's high time!â he says. âShooting is my one love, of course, it takes up a lot of our time and effort.â âHowever, life has changed between my twenties and my thirties. I have to give time to other things in life as well. I have to make time for my family, my businesses and whatever else there is outside shooting.â Kynan is married to Ria Rajeshwari Kumari, Indian Olympian trap shooter and silver medallist at 2022 Asian Games (Photo from Instagram) He says the balance has changed his appreciation for the hours he gets at the range: âWhen I'm on the range, my appreciation for the game is greater because I love it so much and value the time I get to do what I need to do.â Chenai has been part of Indian shooting long enough to see changes in the support available to athletes. He credits National Rifle Association of India president Raninder Singh with helping put systems in place through which shooters can train at NCOEs, receive support under the Target Olympic Podium Scheme and access ammunition regularly. âHe's put standard operating procedures in place that allow athletes to be part of NCOE and TOPS, receive ammunition and practise their targets every day. Not every month, but every day.â In his view, the ability to train consistently for around 250 days a year helps shooters develop the muscle memory needed to compete internationally. He says India's shotgun shooters have made progress, while rifle and pistol shooters remain capable of competing with the best despite a disappointing Asian Games. âOkay, they didn't have a good Asian Games. So what? In my opinion, they are still the best in the world. Indian rifle and pistol shooters are among the top performers. Shotgun is coming along, and you've seen that here.â Raninder Singh, Former NRAI President (Photo from agencies) He is also quick to point out that each discipline comes with different demands. Shotgun takes place outdoors, where rain and sun can affect competition; indoor shooters deal with conditions such as temperature and lighting. âI don't know all the logistics involved, but I can tell you that every sport has its own difficulties, and we are genuine contenders at the world level.â Join conversation View All Comments â Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful Â· TOI community guidelines Still searching for perfection Chenai does not claim to have worked everything out. He says the years since Hangzhou have made him more mature in how he responds to competition, and that handling pressure remains a learning process. âI'm not saying I'm perfect or that I've figured everything out, because that's not possible. Nobody does that. I say this all the time: I don't think perfection exists, but I'm searching for it.â Asked what success means to him now, he does not reduce it to a medal count or an Olympic appearance. âIt's about being the best version of myself, yes. And I can also tell you that if I'm consistent, I'm successful.â Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

title: Olympic champion Athing Mu-Nikolayev expecting first child as fans await answers on her athletics comeback
text: Olympic champion Athing Mu-Nikolayev expecting first child as fans await answers on her athletics comeback Olympic 800m champion Athing Mu-Nikolayev has announced that she is expecting her first child with husband Yegor Nikolayev. The American runner shared the news on Instagram on October 15, 2026, after more than a year away from competition. Her last race was the USATF Outdoor Championships on August 1, 2025, where she finished fourth in her 800m semifinal in 1:59.79. The happy news comes after a difficult period in her career. However, Mu has yet to reveal her baby's due date or confirm her plans for a return to racing. Athing Mu-Nikolayev Shares Pregnancy News After a Difficult Period in Athletics Mu-Nikolayev shared several photos with her husband as they prepared to welcome their first child. In the Instagram post, she wrote, âBaby on board ð«¶ð¿âï¸ Canât wait to meet our little Sunshine!â One picture showed the couple standing in an open field while Mu held ultrasound photos. Other pictures showed her baby bump. Olympic 100m champion Noah Lyles congratulated the couple in the comments. Athletes Hunter Woodhall and Masai Russell also shared their best wishes. Mu married fellow athlete Yegor Nikolayev on March 8, 2025. Although the announcement brings happy news about her personal life, it does not confirm why she has stayed away from competition throughout 2026. Her last two seasons were difficult after an injury disrupted her training and she failed to qualify for the Paris 2024 Olympics. Mu tore her hamstring about six weeks before the 2024 US Olympic Trials. She returned for the 800m final in Eugene, Oregon, but fell around 200 metres into the race after getting tangled with other runners. She finished ninth in 2:19.69 and missed the chance to defend the Olympic gold she won at Tokyo 2020, held in 2021. Her return in 2025 also proved difficult. She finished last in the 800m at the Prefontaine Classic in July, clocking 2:03.44. At the USATF Outdoor Championships in August, she improved to 1:59.79 but failed to reach the final. According to LetsRun.com , her former coach Bobby Kersee said she was still dealing with physical and mental challenges after the injury. He also explained that she had not fully recovered, saying, âShe still had nagging pains here and there. There were still some off-balances or whatever. She wasnât 100% herself.â Mu and Kersee ended their coaching relationship in 2025 after around three years together. Kersee remained confident in her ability, telling LetsRun.com , âIâm sure theyâll seek out good coaching and once sheâs healthy, then sheâs going to be very difficult to beat. Sheâs that talented.â Join conversation View All Comments â Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful Â· TOI community guidelines Can Athing Mu-Nikolayev Return for the LA28 Olympics ? Mu has not announced when her baby is due or whether she plans to compete again. The photos have led to speculation that the baby could arrive in early 2027, but no date has been confirmed. The Los Angeles Olympics will take place from July 14 to 30, 2028. If the baby arrives in early 2027, Mu could have around 16 to 18 months before the Games. That would give her time to consider a return, although pregnancy, recovery and training needs will all matter. Mu won Olympic gold in the women's 800m at Tokyo 2020. Missing Paris 2024 was a major setback, but LA28 could give her another chance to compete on the Olympic stage. For now, there is no confirmed comeback plan. Mu's pregnancy announcement marks an important new chapter in her life, while her return to athletics remains an open question. title: An Idaho horse-racing track that fell silent in 2015 has reopened as a $42 million, 50-acre public park with restored wetlands, more than three miles of trails and a skate park built by Olympic venue designers
text: (Image credit: Facebook/Expo Idaho) The transformation of abandoned spaces into public green spaces can offer a new life to landscapes that had once served a different purpose. In Garden City, Idaho, a former horse-racing track that fell silent in 2015 has now been reopened on the 23rd of October as a nearly 50 acre public park built on the former Les Bois horse racing track along the Bois River Greenbelt, bringing about restored wetlands, nature trails and recreational spaces along the Boise River. Known as the Park at Expo Idaho, the $42 million development funded through the American Rescue Plan Act gives the community a new outdoor destination with its olympic class skate park and playgrounds while bringing the site's natural landscape back into focus. The park occupies the former site of Les Bois Park, a horse-racing venue that became inactive after horse- racing wagering ended in 2015. Following this closure, Ada County began exploring how the land could be put to a different use. Its location along the Boise River floodplain, with a direct connection to the Boise River Greenbelt together became a great opportunity to create a public space that is an exemplar of recreation and restoration. (Image credit: Expo Idaho) How the park is bringing wetlands back to life One of the defining features of the new park is its restored wetland landscape, which provides a natural contrast to the recreational spaces surrounding it. The Lowlands area includes wetland habitats, stream channels, native vegetation and a boardwalk that allows visitors to explore the landscape while remaining on designated paths. Wetlands play an important role in the environment, helping provide habitats for wildlife, retain water and trap sediment. The restored waterways also create spaces where fish can move and spawn, while native vegetation offers food and shelter for birds and other animals. The design had to account for the Boise River's flood capacity, with planners working alongside the US Army Corps of Engineers to balance wetland restoration with the river's natural flow. The restoration has already begun attracting wildlife. During a visit before the park's opening, project staff reported seeing fish in the streams, along with frogs, salamanders and a variety of birds. Kestrels and kingfishers were among the species observed around the wetlands, offering an early indication of how the restored habitat is being used by wildlife. The planting effort has involved more than a million plants and starter plugs, alongside trees and shrubs that will gradually establish themselves across the landscape. The park may take several years to reach its full growth, but the return of wildlife suggests that the ecological benefits are already beginning to emerge. An olympic-designed skate park and nature playground Alongside its natural spaces, the Park at Expo Idaho has been designed to accommodate a wide range of outdoor activities. One of its major attractions is the All-Wheel Skate Garden, designed by California Skateparks, the company behind the skateboarding venue used at the 2024 Paris Olympics. (Image credit: Facebook/Expo Idaho) The facility includes features for different experience levels and is intended for skateboards, bikes, scooters and roller skates. There is also a dedicated roller derby rink which is another recreational option, giving local sports communities a space to practise and play.Other facilities include gathering areas, a food truck plaza and spaces for events and live music. More than 3 miles of trails wind through the park's ridges, valleys and restored wetlands, while the connection to the Boise River Greenbelt makes it easier for visitors to explore the wider riverfront area. The park also retains reminders of its former identity. Elements inspired by the horse-racing venue have been incorporated into parts of the design wonderfully, allowing visitors to experience the site's history alongside its renewed purpose. By bringing together wetland restoration, native planting and recreational facilities, the Park at Expo Idaho offers more than a new place for outdoor activities.

title: How do you beat Novak Djokovic? Jan-Lennard Struff reveals the only way
text: Jan-Lennard Struff Jan-Lennard Struff finally found a way to beat Novak Djokovic after eight unsuccessful attempts. The German produced one of the biggest wins of his career at the Swiss Indoors Basel on Thursday, defeating the 24-time Grand Slam champion in a three-set battle. The 36-year-old won 6-7(4), 7-5, 7-6(5) after two hours and 36 minutes. It was his first victory against Djokovic in nine meetings. What's the only way to stop Novak Djokovic? Struff shares his winning formula Jan-Lennard Struff knew he had to change his approach against the Serbian. Instead of playing cautiously, he decided to take risks and attack whenever he got the opportunity. Speaking after the match, the German explained what he believed was the only way to beat the former world No. 1. "I knew I needed to go for it. There was only one way to play it. So, I was very, very happy." Struff said. ID@undefined Caption not available. Struff's aggressive approach worked perfectly. He produced 27 aces during the match and saved all six break points he faced. His final ace sealed the victory. Djokovic, meanwhile, failed to convert any of his break-point opportunities. Struff knew he would have to produce his best tennis to have a chance against the Serbian. His previous meetings had not gone well, with Djokovic winning all eight. "The last serve went in the corner like many balls today. I knew I had to play my best tennis to have a chance. The last eight times he beat me very, very easily. So, very, very happy and pleased with the performance." he added. The victory was particularly special for Struff because he had struggled against Djokovic throughout his career. How Djokovic dominated their previous meetings Jan-Lennard Struff and Novak Djokovic first played against each other in Doha in 2017. The Serbian won that match in straight sets. They met again at the 2019 French Open, where Djokovic registered a comfortable 6-3, 6-2, 6-2 victory. At the 2020 Australian Open, Struff managed to win a set but eventually lost in four sets. Djokovic continued his winning run in their next meetings at Cincinnati, the US Open, the Tokyo Olympics and the Davis Cup. Their previous match before Basel took place at the 2025 US Open. Djokovic won 6-3, 6-3, 6-2 in the fourth round. However, Struff finally ended that losing run in Basel. Jan-Lennard Struff's biggest career achievements Although Jan-Lennard Struff has never been a regular member of the world's top 10, he has enjoyed some important moments in his career. In 2023, he reached the Madrid Masters final as a lucky loser. However, he could not win the title after losing to Carlos Alcaraz. Join conversation View All Comments â Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful Â· TOI community guidelines He also reached the final in Stuttgart that year but lost to Frances Tiafoe. Struff finally won his first ATP title in April 2024. Playing in front of his home fans in Munich, the German defeated Taylor Fritz 7-5, 6-3 to lift the trophy. He was 33 at the time and became one of the oldest players to win their first ATP title. After that memorable victory, Struff spoke about how much the moment meant to him. "I waited so long. I'm 33 years old and played so long on Tour. It's just an amazing feeling to do it here in Germany." Struff said at the time. title: No Sharath Kamal, no Nikhat Zareen: Major shake-up in IOA Athletesâ Commission
text: Sharath Kamal New Delhi: The Indian Olympic Associationâs (IOA) Athletesâ Commission is set for a change of guard, with former vice-chairperson Sharath Kamal and two-time World champion boxer Nikhat Zareen missing from the electoral list for the Nov 3 elections. The development also marks the end of Mary Kom âs tenure as chairperson, with neither of the two outgoing office-bearers in contention for the new commission. The elections for the 2026-30 term will precede the IOA Executive Council (EC) polls on Dec 5. The commissionâs chairperson and vice-chairperson have voting rights in the EC, making their positions significant in the Olympic bodyâs decision-making structure. Sharathâs absence stems from a technical issue with his nomination, sources familiar with the matter told TOI. The former India table tennis captain had submitted his application to contest as a Sportsperson of Merit, with the form routed through the ad-hoc committee currently administering the Table Tennis Federation of India (TTFI). Watch Tilak Varma on batting at No. 5 and 6: âI want to finish games for the countryâ The application, however, was rejected by the Returning Officer (RO) after it reportedly reached the electoral authority without the signature of the competent official in the ad-hoc committee. The election rules provide for rejection, without further notice, of incomplete or unsigned nomination forms. Sharath, who served as vice-chairperson in the outgoing commission, will consequently miss the race. His absence is particularly striking, given that he recently served as deputy chef-de-mission (CDM) at the Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games. The nomination process has also affected boxing. The names of Nikhat and Narendra Berwal, who recently won bronze at the Asian Games, were reportedly forwarded for consideration but were not accepted because the IOA does not recognise the Boxing Federation of India (BFI) as a member national sports federation. The BFI is currently not recognised by either the IOA or the sports ministry amid governance concerns and internal disputes. The TTFI, meanwhile, was suspended by the ministry over governance failures and administrative lapses. Mary Komâs name was not forwarded by the BFI. Sources said her reduced involvement in Indian boxing, business interests and television commitments were among the factors. The IOA was also reportedly unhappy after she initially accepted, then declined, the chef-de-mission (CDM) role for the Paris Olympics 2024. Join conversation View All Comments â Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful Â· TOI community guidelines The new commission will have 10 elected members, comprising five men and five women. Six must have competed at one of the last three Olympic editions, while the remaining four must have won medals at specified major competitions, including the Asian Games, CWG, World Championships or National Games. While the RO is empowered to scrutinise nominations, the exclusions raise questions about ensuring athletes are not disadvantaged by administrative disputes involving their federations. title: 'Still some time for the Olympics': Neeraj Chopra shares update on injury, reveals comeback plans
text: Neeraj Chopra Two-time Olympic medallist Neeraj Chopra is targeting a strong return to competition in 2027 after an ankle ligament injury forced him to miss the 2026 Asian Games in Japan and end his season early. The Indian javelin star said he is focused on recovering and improving his performance as he looks ahead to the 2028 Olympics. Speaking to reporters at the launch of the 2026 Audi Q3 in Mumbai, Chopra stressed that there is still time before the next Olympics and that his immediate priority is to return to competition at his best. Watch Bombay Sport Exchange: Jonty Rhodes on why Indian parents must rethink sport Chopra, who won gold at the Tokyo 2020 Olympics and silver at Paris 2024, said his attention is firmly on recovering from the injury and preparing for next season. title: Sir Andy Murrayâs investments in sports businesses: How the former Wimbledon champion built a diverse portfolio across sportswear, padel tennis, startups and hospitality beyond his playing career
text: Andy Murray of Britain poses with the trophy after defeating Novak Djokovic of Serbia in the menâs singles final match at the All England Lawn Tennis Championships in Wimbledon, London, July 7, 2013. (AP Photo/Kirsty Wigglesworth, File) Sir Andy Murrayâs achievements on court include three Grand Slam titles, two Olympic singles gold medals and a rise to world No. 1. But his ambitions extended beyond tennis long before his retirement at the 2024 Paris Olympics. He began investing in businesses across sportswear, technology and hospitality while still competing at the highest level. His portfolio includes a partnership with British sportswear brand Castore, investments connected to the growing sport of padel, and ownership interests in hospitality and other businesses. Although reports have put different figures on his overall wealth, the value of a business or investment portfolio should not be confused with Murrayâs personal net worth or the money he has earned from individual ventures. How has Sir Andy Murray built his business portfolio? Murray began considering life after professional tennis years before he played his final match. In a 2015 partnership announcement with equity crowdfunding platform Seedrs, he explained that investing in innovative British startups appealed to him. The collaboration also reflected his interest in businesses connected to sport, health and wearable technology. That early interest developed into a portfolio spanning several industries. Rather than relying exclusively on prize money and sponsorships, Murray explored opportunities where he could support companies, contribute his sporting profile or participate in businesses with long-term growth potential. There is no single publicly verified figure that establishes the current value of all his investments. Reports have placed his wealth at different levels, but private company stakes, property interests, business liabilities and changing valuations make precise calculations difficult. According to Celebrity Net Worth, any net worth figure should be treated as an estimate rather than an audited statement of his finances. Sir Andy Murrayâs investments in sportswear and startups One of Murrayâs best-known business relationships is with Castore, the British performance sportswear company founded by brothers Tom and Phil Beahon. Murray became an early investor and worked with the brand on AMC, a tennis apparel collection reflecting his experience as a professional player. The partnership connected his sporting identity with a British business seeking to establish itself in performance clothing. His startup interests have also included companies operating outside traditional sports. Seedrs gave him a route to explore early-stage businesses, while reports have linked his portfolio to ventures in areas such as employee benefits, financial technology, digital advertising and health services. Companies mentioned in coverage of his investments include Perkbox, WeSwap, Landbay, Adludio and ZoomDoc. The extent and current status of individual holdings are not necessarily public. The broader strategy is diversification: early-stage businesses can offer opportunities for growth, but they can also fail or lose value. A reported investment does not establish that Murray still owns a stake, nor does it confirm how much profit he has made. His portfolio is best understood as a range of business interests rather than a guaranteed stream of returns. Sir Andy Murray expands into padel and sport Murrayâs sporting background has also influenced his investments in activities beyond professional tennis. Padel, a racket sport combining elements of tennis and squash, has attracted growing attention internationally. Game4Padelâs business model has been associated with installing courts at partner venues and generating revenue through court bookings. For Murray, the opportunity sits at the intersection of sport and business: participation can grow when facilities become more accessible, while operators gain a chance to build a sustainable commercial model. He has also been linked to the Hexagon Cup, a team-based padel competition, through Team AD/vantage. The involvement gives him another connection to the development of padel as a spectator and participation sport. His interest in sports-related businesses has reportedly extended to other ventures, including TMRW Sports and sports hydration brand Halo Hydration. However, the scale and current status of each investment should be distinguished from confirmed operating results. Why sports investments suit Murrayâs experience Elite sport has given Murray direct experience of training, equipment, performance demands and the commercial relationship between athletes and brands. That background may help him assess whether a product or sports business addresses a genuine need. His involvement can also provide visibility, although an athleteâs name alone does not guarantee commercial success. Padel and performance apparel also offer opportunities that do not depend on Murray returning to competitive tennis. Facilities, products and sporting events can continue to develop beyond an individual athleteâs playing career, making them potential long-term business interests. As with startup investments, their financial outcomes depend on demand, execution and the wider market. Sir Andy Murray expands into luxury Scottish hospitality Murrayâs hospitality venture is among the most personal parts of his business portfolio. In 2013, he bought Cromlix, a luxury country house hotel near Dunblane, Scotland, for a reported Â£2 million. The property has a family connection: it hosted a celebration for his grandparents and was also the venue for his brother Jamie Murrayâs wedding. Under Murray and his wife Kimâs ownership, Cromlix has been developed as a high-end destination with an emphasis on hospitality, dining and the surrounding Scottish countryside. The hotel received a Michelin Key and was named Scotlandâs best hotel at the AA Hospitality Awards in 2024, according to published reports. Those recognitions have helped establish its reputation, although awards do not automatically translate into profits. Cromlix has also demonstrated the risks of owning a hospitality business. Media coverage reported operating losses and further investment in renovations and planned improvements. Hotel performance can be affected by staffing costs, maintenance, food and beverage operations, occupancy and wider travel demand. The propertyâs purchase price and reputation therefore cannot, on their own, establish its current market value or profitability. Join conversation View All Comments â Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful Â· TOI community guidelines What Murrayâs business portfolio means after retirement Murrayâs move into business was not simply a response to retirement. His early involvement with Seedrs shows that he was considering opportunities beyond tennis while still playing professionally. Castore, Game4Padel and Cromlix illustrate three different approaches: supporting a sportswear brand, backing a developing sport and operating a hospitality property. Murrayâs post-tennis career is therefore best viewed as an evolving mix of investments and operating businesses rather than a single financial success story. His experience in professional sport has helped him identify opportunities in performance clothing and emerging sports, while Cromlix gives him a foothold in hospitality. title: 9 UP athletes shine at Asian Paralymic Games; CM congratulates
text: Chief minister Yogi Adityanath Lucknow: With Suvarna Raj winning the gold in the discus throw and Swati Chaudhary clinching silver in the W1 archery event on Thursday, nine athletes from UP have made their mark at the ongoing Asian Paralympic Games in Nagoya, Japan. Besides them, two other medal winners, including the stateâs sports secretary, Karnataka-born Suhas LY, and Meerut-born Simran Sharma , who is now settled in Delhi, also finished on the podium. Chief minister Yogi Adityanath congratulated the athletes who won medals on Thursday. On his X account, he wrote, âSuvarnaâs golden achievement, earned through tireless hard work and unwavering resolve, will give wings to the dreams of countless daughters.â Calling Swatiâs victory historic, the CM posted, âSwatiâs success would inspire countless young people across India to pursue their dreams and turn them into reality,â adding that everyone was proud of her. For Suhas LY, who secured bronze in the menâs singles badminton event, Yogi said that his achievement was an inspiration for turning dreams into reality through determination and tireless hard work. UPâs medal winners at the ongoing Games include Ajeet Singh and Pradeep Kumar in javelin throw, Ayush Verma in javelin throw and shot put, Prachi Pandey in table tennis, Ram Ratan Singh in discus throw, Preeti Pal in athletics, Praveen Kumar in high jump, Suvarna Raj in discus throw and Swati Chaudhary in archery. Two other athletes whom UP counts among its achievers are IAS officer Suhas LY in badminton and Simran Sharma in athletics. Sharma was born in Meerut and began her training in Modinagar. An official said that five sports colleges were operational in Lucknow, Gorakhpur, Saifai, Fatehpur and Saharanpur which offer training in 14 sports, along with free accommodation, meals and education. The Major Dhyan Chand Sports University coming up in Meerut will further strengthen the stateâs sports infrastructure, he said. The govt is also giving cash rewards to athletes, and those who win individual gold, silver and bronze medals at the Olympics are entitled to Rs 6 crore, Rs 4 crore and Rs 2 crore, respectively, the official added. title: Stephen Curryâs rise to NBAâs highest-paid player was about more than three-pointers, as his career choices and endorsement strategy helped build a $203.6 million fortune
text: Stephen Curry. Image via: Kelley L Cox-Imagn Images Stephen Curry has agreed to a two-year, $116 million extension with the Golden State Warriors, running through the 2028-29 season. The final year is a player option, a route to a 20th season with the same franchise. Curry was eligible for up to $136 million, so the new deal sits about $20 million below the ceiling. Even with the discount, Curry still tops the 2026-27 salary list at $62.6 million. The numbers point to a career built on more than his three-pointers. A run of contracts, a shoe-brand split and a new apparel deal explain how Curry got here. How did Stephen Curry become the NBAâs highest-paid player? Stephen Curry (Image via Instagram / @stephencurry30) Stephen Curry sits first on the 2026-27 contract list at $62.6 million, ahead of Nikola Jokic at $59 million and Jayson Tatum at $58.5 million. Three contracts and one shaky ankle explain most of the climb. Golden State drafted Curry seventh in 2009. Ankle trouble followed, and by 2012 the Warriors had to decide how much to trust the ankle. They offered a four-year, $44 million extension. It became one of the better bargains in league history. Curry won back-to-back MVP awards and the first two of four titles while playing under it. The large numbers arrived next. In July 2017, Curry signed a five-year, $201.2 million deal, the first in NBA history above $200 million. The contract also made Curry the leagueâs highest-paid player. In August 2021, a four-year, $215 million extension made Curry the first player with two contracts over $200 million. Yearly pay on that one rose from $48.1 million in 2022-23 to $59.6 million in 2025-26. A one-year, $62.6 million extension signed in August 2024 then covered 2026-27. The September deal works differently. Curry was eligible for $136 million and signed for $116 million. Pay drops to $55.7 million in 2027-28 and $60.2 million in 2028-29, with the second year a player option. Golden State general manager Mike Dunleavy said there has never been âa better face to a franchise in professional sports history.â The $62.6 million guard gave the team breathing room too. A smaller number cuts the Warriorsâ future payroll commitment, and it fits a long-held plan to finish a career in one uniform. The agreement arrives after a year in which a right knee injury held Curry to 43 games, though he still averaged 26.6 points. How much has Curry earned from contracts and endorsements? Through the 2025-26 season, Curry had collected $470.1 million in NBA salary. Add $62.6 million for 2026-27 and the $116 million extension, and the projected total reaches $648.7 million, provided the final-year option is picked up. Endorsements, investments and other off-court income sit outside that figure. Shoes carry the other big number. Curry began in Nike gear, then signed with Under Armour in 2013. The partnership grew into Curry Brand in 2020, with Curry serving as its president. A 2023 extension was supposed to run past the end of Curryâs playing days. Instead, the relationship ended in November 2025 and Curry Brand went independent. Under Armour kept releasing previously developed Curry products through 2026 while the brand looked at new partners. In June 2026, Curry signed a 10-year agreement with Chinese sportswear company Li-Ning worth more than $400 million, an average of more than $40 million a year. The deal covers signature shoes, basketball apparel, lifestyle products, and golf, with plans for Curry Brand stores in China and the United States. Curry can also sign other athletes under the brand. What else is in Curryâs business portfolio? Beyond sneakers, Curry has endorsement ties with Fanatics, Google, JPMorgan Chase, Panini, Rakuten and 2K Sports. The wider business interests sit under a company called Thirty Ink, covering media, branding, investments and philanthropy. Unanimous Media, co-founded with Erick Peyton in 2018, develops film, television, documentary, publishing and podcast projects with a lean toward sports, family and faith. Curry starred in the 2024 Peacock comedy âMr. Throwbackâ and published the photo book âShot Readyâ in 2025. Other ventures include Gentlemanâs Cut bourbon and Underrated, a platform that gives overlooked young athletes basketball and golf programs with competition, development and exposure. Estimates put Curryâs net worth at $350 million. What are Curryâs biggest career accomplishments? Curry is a four-time champion, winning in 2015, 2017, 2018 and 2022, and the 2022 Finals MVP. Curry has two MVP awards, and the 2016 vote is the only unanimous one in league history. In 2015-16, Curry averaged 30.1 points, made 402 three-pointers and led Golden State to an NBA-record 73 wins. The same season produced a 50-40-90 shooting year at more than 30 points a game, something no other player has done. The list keeps going. Curry has 12 All-Star selections, 11 All-NBA nods, and two scoring titles, in 2016 and 2021. Eight seasons ended with Curry leading the league in made threes. In March 2025, Curry became the first player to hit 4,000 career threes. Internationally, Curry owns gold from the 2010 and 2014 FIBA World Cups and the 2024 Paris Olympics, where late threes helped beat France in the final. Join conversation View All Comments â Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful Â· TOI community guidelines Inside the Warriorsâ record book, Curry holds the most All-Star selections (12) and the most All-NBA selections (11) in franchise history. As for Curryâs NBA career, he is one of the greatest to play the sport, with several stunning records and titles to his name. Many argue that Steph should be in the Greatest of All Time (GOAT) debate alongside Chicago Bulls legend Michael Jordan and, of course, LeBron James. Certainly, he deserves the place. Recently, the NBAâs official social media handle posted a short video asking league-wide stars for their opinion on one great NBA skill one would steal. Many called it Curryâs shooting, and some wanted his ball-handling as well. Regardless, Curry is a forged player; he developed into one of the greatest in the game.
