title: I want to build on what I have achieved this year: Dhiraj Bommadevara
text: Pics: Sanjana Pulugurtha Dhiraj Bommadevara has had a year to remember. He won two gold medals at the Archery World Cup Stage 3 in Antalya, clinched the menâs individual recurve title at the Archery World Cup Final in Mexico and returned from the Asian Games with two silver medals. ââI still have a lot of room for improvement, but this yearâs achievements have really motivated me, and Iâm going to push myself even harder,â says the 25-year-old archer from Vijayawada. In a candid chat with Hyderabad Times, Dhiraj reflects on his breakthrough year, the sacrifices that shaped his journey, the lessons he has learnt from setbacks and his ambitions for Indian archery. Dhiraj and Kumkum Anil Mohod with their recurve mixed team silver at the Asian Games. Dhiraj also won silver in the menâs team event âI wanted gold, but Iâm happy with two silver medalsâ Reflecting on his performance at the recently concluded Asian Games in Japan, Dhiraj says, âCompared to the last Asian Games, where I won one silver medal, this time I came back with two silvers. Even though I wanted the gold, itâs okay, I have two medals.â He adds, âI have a lot of room for improvement, and I can push myself forward during my upcoming training days. The Asian Games medals are a motivation for that next step. â Young Dheeraj in 2006 âI took the positives from Paris Olympics and pushed myself furtherâ For Dhiraj, finishing fourth in the mixed team event at the Paris 2024 Olympics was a significant moment in his career, despite missing out on a medal. âFinishing fourth was still a positive result, as no Indian archer had ever achieved that position before. I took a lot of positives from that,â he says. However, the hard work did not immediately translate into results in 2025. âGoing into 2025, I did everything I needed to do behind the scenes. I really put in the hard work and did everything. But 2025 didnât bring me many results,â he adds. Despite not getting the results he had hoped for, Dhiraj continued to trust the process and remain consistent with his training. His perseverance has paid off, making 2026 a landmark year in his career. âWhen things werenât working out, I didnât give up on them. Thatâs why I think this year has been very special for me,â he says. âIndian archery is only moving forwardâ While Indian archery continues its pursuit of an Olympic medal, Dhiraj believes the teamâs progress over the years offers reason for optimism. He says the focus should be on measuring progress against past performances. âIf we compare Indian archery today with where it was in the past, weâre only moving forward,â he says. Pointing to recent milestones, Dhiraj highlights the teamâs achievements at the Asian Games. âIt was the first time an Indian woman won an individual gold medal in recurve archery. It was also the first time we won silver in the mixed event. During the qualification round at the Asian Games, I broke the previous record held by South Koreaâs Lee Woo Seok,â he says. âOf course, we havenât won that Olympic medal, but with every win and every learning experience, weâre moving towards that medal,â he adds. âSharing a team with international archers helps us improveâ Dhiraj also values the opportunity to learn from fellow archers. Competing in the franchise-based archery league in Hyderabad, he says, allows Indian archers, both established and emerging, to gain insights into the mindset and match-day approach of international competitors. âWhen a foreign archer is part of our team, we understand how they think during a match and approach different situations. We also learn how they analyse their performances, win or lose. These insights have helped us at several championships, where we went on to win titles,â he says. Following the conclusion of the tournament in Hyderabad, Dhiraj will return to the Army Sports Institute in Pune, where he trains, to focus on the next phase of his preparation. âThe next three months are all about preparation. We have some national tournaments and Iâll focus on my preparation for the next World Championships cycle,â he says. During the Asian Games in Japan âThere was a time I almost gave up archeryâ Behind Dhirajâs rise is a story of sacrifice and perseverance. Nearly a decade ago, his mother, Revathi, sold her jewellery to buy him a second-hand bow as the family struggled to afford his equipment. At 16, he came close to giving up archery amid financial difficulties. âIâm happy that I was able to go through all of it,â he says, adding, âIn 2017, when I was 16, my family had run out of everything. But somehow, both my parents stood by me, and my sponsors have helped me a lot. â - Biswajit Talukdar You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. title: âOnly Modi can tourâ: Mann slams Paris denial after Japan
text: Punjab CM Bhagwant Mann CHANDIGARH: Punjab chief minister Bhagwant Mann on Thursday criticised the Centre for denying him political clearance to visit Paris, where he has been invited to attend a food festival featuring a Markfed exhibition stall. Replying to a question, Mann told media in New Delhi, âWhat do we do? There is a food festival being held in Paris, and we received an invitation from the French govt, with Markfed putting up a stall. Earlier, I was also scheduled to travel to Japan for three days to watch the semi-finals and finals of the hockey matches. Since we are hosting the Menâs Hockey Asian Champions Trophy starting Oct 27, we also wanted to extend a formal invitation to them in person. â Hitting out at the Narendra Modi-led Centre, Mann added, âThey simply refuse to give me permission (to travel abroad). It seems as though only PM Modi can tour the worldâvisiting even the most obscure places like Papua Guinea, âManglesia,â or âChanglesia.â We have now moved the high court, and I hope to receive approval tomorrow. Our goal in traveling is strictly to benefit Punjab, attracting investors so we can create employment opportunities for our youth. â The food festival in question refers to SIAL Paris, touted as the worldâs largest and most influential food innovation exhibition and trade fair held biennially at Paris Nord Villepinte exhibition centre. This is not an isolated incident, as CM Mann and his members have repeatedly been denied political clearance by the ministry of external affairs (MEA) for foreign visits. In Aug 2024, the Centre blocked Mannâs proposed trip to Paris to attend the Olympics and cheer on the Indian menâs hockey team, citing diplomatic and administrative reasons. Prior to this, Mann and then-industries minister Sanjeev Arora were denied approval for a planned investment outreach tour to the UK and Israel ahead of Progressive Punjab Investorsâ Summit. More recently, MEA refused him clearance to travel to Japan for the Asian Games hockey semi-finals on security grounds. In Sept 2022, Punjab minister Aman Arora was refused approval for an official knowledge-sharing tour to Germany, Belgium, and the Netherlands. Also, assembly speaker Kultar Singh Sandhwan was denied clearance to attend a legislative speakersâ conference in the US in Aug 2024. Minister Harbhajan Singh was blocked from representing Punjabâs governance model at a conference in Boston in Aug last year. Aam Aadmi Party (AAP) leadership has termed these rejections politically motivated, alleging partisan political discrimination by the Centre toward Punjab. In contrast, neighbouring Haryanaâs chief minister Nayab Singh Saini has consistently been granted prompt political clearances for his international delegations and investment tours. Recently, Saini led a high-level state delegation on a three-day official visit to Singapore from Oct 4 to Oct 6 to pitch investment, urban infrastructure, and trade partnerships. Shortly after, on Oct 14, he embarked on another four-day official tour to Sweden to engage with international trade ministers and global investors. title: Clayton Young defies doctorâs four-week rest advice to run Chicago Marathon personal best with hamstring tear
text: Clayton Young defies doctorâs four-week rest advice to run Chicago Marathon personal best with hamstring tear American runner Clayton Young finished the 2026 Chicago Marathon in 2:05:23 despite a 12-centimeter tear in his hamstring tendon. The October 11 race gave him a personal best and made him the top American man, but reaching the starting line was far from certain. His first doctor had advised him to rest for four weeks. Now, Young has shared how his faith and his wife, Ashley, helped him through those difficult weeks. He also has his sights set on the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics. Clayton Young Reveals How a Hamstring Tear Put His Chicago Marathon Plans at Risk In an October 15 conversation with CITIUS MAG host Chris Chavez, Young explained that he wanted to give himself every chance to race. He had also hoped to challenge the American marathon record of 2:04:43, set by his training partner Conner Mantz in 2025. When Chavez asked if he believed the record was possible, Young replied, âYeah. Yeah, I mean, or at least I believe that I would do everything I could until I was told not to.â The injury became a concern after the Great North Run in England on September 13. With around 250 metres left in the half-marathon, Young felt his hamstring tighten and had to slow down. He finished seventh in 1:02:04, but the pain did not go away. After cutting a speed workout short, Young underwent an MRI on September 17. The scan showed a 12-centimeter tear in an upper hamstring tendon near the pelvis. His first doctor recommended a platelet-rich plasma injection and four weeks without running. Following that advice would have ended his hopes of competing in Chicago. Young then sought further medical advice and worked with his coach, Ed Eyestone, to adjust his training. He completed a 22-mile run and returned to faster sessions while keeping a close eye on the injury. His hamstring was still not fully healed when he reached the starting line. The physical challenge was only part of the story. Young said the experience also changed how he viewed his faith. He and Ashley leaned on prayer and support from people around them while trying to decide what to do next. âThese last four weeks from a faith standpoint have neverâ¦ I want to be respectful of everybody in their faith. But Iâm going to look back on these last four weeks with more faith building experience than Iâve ever seen,â Young said. He added that the couple kept finding reasons to move forward even when running seemed like the wrong choice. âWhen everything said, donât run this race, it was so interesting to see how so many of the answers that we were receiving were just like, keep moving forward, take the next step, and trust in God and the plan that he has for you, even though it doesnât make sense,â he said. Ashley remained by his side throughout the difficult period. Young said the experience brought them closer and strengthened their faith. âYeah, Ashley and I grew stronger together. Our faith grew stronger together. And yeah, Iâm going to look back at this as a miracle,â he said. Young later confirmed that his hamstring had not fully recovered. âMy hamstring held up. No, it wasnât made perfect, but we got through this,â he said. Clayton Young Targets LA 2028 Olympics After Chicago Marathon Personal Best Young finished seventh overall in Chicago with a time of 2:05:23. According to USA Track & Field, the result made him the second-fastest American man ever on a course eligible for records. It also improved his previous best on such a course, which was 2:08:00 at the 2023 Chicago Marathon. His next major goal is the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics. In an interview with Menâs Health earlier this year, Young said, âMy biggest goals right now are to do everything I can to prepare for the LA 2028 Olympic Games.â Join conversation View All Comments â Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful Â· TOI community guidelines Young already has Olympic experience. He finished second at the 2024 U.S. Olympic Marathon Trials before placing ninth in the marathon at the Paris Games. He now has another personal best to build on as he works toward a return to the Olympic stage. For now, his hamstring recovery will be important as he plans his next races. Young has shown what he can do in Chicago, but his focus remains on getting ready for the challenges ahead and earning another chance to represent the United States in 2028. title: Hezly Riveraâs World Championships debut hit by ankle scare as 2028 Olympics ambitions come into focus
text: Hezly Riveraâs World Championships debut hit by ankle scare as 2028 Olympics ambitions come into focus Hezly Rivera is dealing with pain in her left ankle just days before her first World Artistic Gymnastics Championships in Rotterdam, Netherlands. The 18-year-old American gymnast changed parts of her podium training on October 15, skipping vault and limiting her floor and balance beam routines. Rivera confirmed the pain in comments shared by Gymnastics Now. The concern comes one year after an ankle injury forced her to miss the 2025 World Championships selection camp. Despite the setback, Rivera remains positive as she prepares for the competition. Hezly Rivera explains her ankle pain during World Championships training Rivera wore tape around her left ankle during podium training on October 15. She skipped vault, did not complete her tumbling passes on floor and changed her balance beam dismount. Speaking to reporters, Rivera explained her decision to take things carefully. âI am having some pain in my left ankle, so I just wanted to modify my training so I can properly heal,â she said, according to International Gymnast Magazine. When asked about the cause of the pain, Rivera chose not to share details. She also made it clear that she was staying positive despite the difficult start to her World Championships experience. âI feel like Iâm in a good mental state,â Rivera said. âObviously, this isnât how I wanted my world championships to go or the first podium training or whatever, but Iâm still being very grateful and keeping a positive attitude.â Rivera also spoke about enjoying time with her teammates. She praised Skye Blakelyâs leadership and said she was happy to compete alongside Claire Pease, her daily training partner. Although her training did not go as planned, she remained thankful for the chance to compete at Worlds for the first time. The ankle concern is especially important because Rivera missed the 2025 World Championships selection camp after rolling her ankle. She had won the U.S. all-around title that year and was expected to compete for a place on the American team heading to Jakarta, Indonesia. However, after speaking with her doctor and coaches, Rivera decided to withdraw from the selection camp and focus on recovery. Gymnastics Now reported her decision on September 27, 2025. A year later, she has reached the World Championships, but the latest ankle pain raises questions about how much she can do in Rotterdam. Rivera said she is taking things step by step as she works out what she can safely manage across the four events. Hezly Rivera keeps her focus on the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics Rivera has already experienced the biggest stage in gymnastics. At just 16, she made her Olympic debut at Paris 2024 as the youngest member of the U.S. women's team. She joined Simone Biles, Sunisa Lee, Jordan Chiles and Jade Carey as Team USA won Olympic gold. Rivera competed on uneven bars and balance beam during the qualification round. She did not compete in the team final, but she still earned an Olympic gold medal as part of the team. Now, her attention is also on the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics. Rivera wants to keep improving at the World Championships before returning to the Olympic stage. She has spoken about her goal of becoming one of the best gymnasts in the world and winning more major titles. title: From husband and wife to business partners: How Neeraj Chopra and Himani Mor are building a sports business to create a lasting legacy
text: Neeraj Chopra and his wife Himani Mor (PTI Photo) Neeraj Chopra has spent years perfecting the art of throwing a javelin beyond 90 metres. Now, India's golden boy is pursuing a different kind of ambition â building a sports business that can outlast his competitive career. And he is doing it alongside his wife, Himani Mor, who is not merely his life partner but the managing director of his new venture, Vel Sports. Launched in January 2026, Vel Sports marked a significant turning point for the Olympic and world champion, who ended his decade-long association with JSW Sports to establish his own athlete management firm. For Chopra, the move was about creating a trusted team that would allow him to concentrate on competition while laying the foundations for his legacy. Watch Harita Bhadra Exclusive | 2 Asian Games Medals, Now the 22.45s World Championships Chase For Mor, a former international-level tennis player with an academic background in sports management, the appointment was an opportunity to turn her own experiences as an athlete into a business philosophy: one that puts athletes' needs before commercial demands. Together, they want Vel Sports and the Neeraj Chopra Foundation to contribute to a stronger sporting ecosystem in India, helping athletes succeed both on and off the field. Their partnership is built around a shared understanding of elite sport, but also on a clear distinction between their professional responsibilities and personal relationship. From a sporting connection to marriage and business The story of Chopra and Mor began well before they became one of Indian sport's most recognisable couples. Both hail from Haryana â Chopra from Panipat and Mor from Sonipat â and their families had known each other for years. Their connection dates back to 2016, before Chopra became an Olympic champion. âWe have known each other since 2016, before he won the junior World Championship,â Mor told The Indian Express, recalling their early association through the Sports Authority of India's training centre in Sonipat. Sport was a natural meeting point. Mor came from a family with a strong sporting background. Her cousins competed in wrestling and boxing, while her parents played kabaddi. Her father captained the Indian team at the first circle kabaddi World Cup in Pakistan in 1983. âThere was a common interest. You talk to each other, get to know each other, and that's how our relationship started. Our families were aware. That's how we got married,â she said. Mor describes their marriage as a fusion of an arranged and a love marriage. They tied the knot in a private ceremony in Solan in January 2025. Their relationship subsequently evolved into a professional partnership, with Chopra launching Vel Sports in January 2026 and appointing Mor as managing director. He brought the experience of competing at the highest level and navigating commercial partnerships, while she brought an athlete's perspective combined with formal training in sports management. Neeraj Chopra and Himani Mor (Photo @Neeraj_chopra1 on X) Why Neeraj Chopra wanted his own sports business Chopra's decision to establish Vel Sports came after a decade with JSW Sports, which supported his rise from a promising javelin thrower to an Olympic gold medallist at Tokyo 2020, a world champion in 2023 and an Olympic silver medallist at Paris 2024. His departure from JSW Sports was described by both sides as a respectful conclusion to a successful association. Chopra acknowledged the role the organisation had played in his career, while the company expressed pride in their shared achievements. But the next phase of his journey demanded a different approach. âAnother reason for starting Vel Sports is because Neeraj wanted his own trusted team to take care of everything. He wants to focus on the sport,â Mor explained. Chopra remains an active athlete, but his ambitions extend beyond medals and records. He wants to create an organisation that can continue contributing to Indian sport after his competitive career ends. âHe might have another six years as an athlete. At this stage, throwing ninety metres is just a number. But he wants to create a legacy,â Mor said, while speaking to The Indian Express. âHe is now looking at breaking records and not just about winning a gold. He wants the next generation to have the mindset that they can win at the highest levels of sport and stay at the top.â That vision is central to Vel Sports. Rather than treating athlete management simply as a business of securing sponsorships and endorsements, the company intends to build a system in which commercial opportunities complement sporting ambitions. The athlete-first philosophy behind Vel Sports For elite athletes, commercial commitments can be both an opportunity and a challenge. Brand campaigns, appearances and promotional obligations can generate income and build a public profile, but they must be balanced against training, recovery and competition schedules. Mor believes the people managing those commitments need to understand what an athlete's daily life involves. âWe want to keep athletes and their priorities at the forefront,â she said. âWe want to create an ecosystem that works around athletes' schedules, allows them to balance their training while also maintaining their professional commitments. Being athletes ourselves, we understand what it takes to perform at the highest levels and what approach is best for an athlete. Because one missed session can cost them a lot.â The objective is to ensure that athletes and brands benefit without compromising sporting performance. Chopra has expressed a similar view, drawing on the lessons of his own career. At the beginning, he said, he did not have enough knowledge about competition planning or working with brands. Vel Sports is intended to help athletes navigate those areas with greater support. The model is not entirely new internationally. Athletes such as LeBron James, Lewis Hamilton and Coco Gauff have pursued business ventures while continuing their sporting careers. In India, Sunil Gavaskar co-founded Professional Management Group during his playing days in the 1980s. Chopra's move places him within that tradition, with the added ambition of building an athlete-focused business in a country where sporting careers can be shaped as much by access to resources and professional guidance as by talent. Beyond Vel Sports: Building a legacy for Indian sport Join conversation View All Comments â Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful Â· TOI community guidelines The couple's ambitions extend beyond athlete representation. The Neeraj Chopra Foundation aims to support emerging athletes and contribute to India's wider sporting ecosystem. One initiative is the Indian School of Coaching Excellence, launched in collaboration with badminton coach Pullela Gopichand's Badminton Gurukul and AISTS INDIA in August 2026. It aims to improve coach education through multidisciplinary programmes covering sports science, physical literacy, technology and athlete development. The underlying belief is that India's future sporting success depends not only on identifying talented athletes but also on giving them access to knowledgeable coaches and effective support systems. The foundation has also joined the Indian Olympic Association in a Clean Sport anti-doping awareness initiative. Chopra's experience as an athlete who has competed at the highest level gives him a platform to promote clean sport. For the couple, these projects represent different parts of the same vision: better management for established athletes, more support for emerging talent and stronger systems around the people responsible for developing champions. title: Centre grounds Punjab CM Bhagwant Mann foreign travel again; govt moves HC
text: Mann and his cabinet members have repeatedly been denied political clearance by the ministry of external affairs (MEA) for foreign visits CHANDIGARH: The Centre has yet again denied political clearance to Punjab chief minister Bhagwant Mann to travel abroad. And this time, Punjab govt has moved Punjab and Haryana high court. On Thursday, Justice Tribhuvan Dahiya directed Union govt to file a response to Punjab govtâs petition by Oct 16 on why it denied Mann clearance to travel to France from Oct 15 to 21. The Punjab CM has been invited to a Paris food festival, featuring a Markfed exhibition stall, but his travel plans were grounded by the Centreâs denial. âWhat do we do?â an exasperated Mann told mediapersons in New Delhi on Thursday. âWe received an invitation from French govt, and Markfed has put up a stall in Parisâ¦ but they (Centre) simply refuse to give me permission (to travel abroad). It seems only PM Modi can tour the world â visiting the most obscure places like Papua Guinea, âManglesia,â or âChanglesiaâ,â the Punjab CM said. He was earlier denied permission for a three-day trip to Japan, too, he said. âI wanted to watch the Asiad hockey semi-finals and finals. Since we are hosting the menâs Hockey Asian Champions Trophy from Oct 27, we wanted to extend a formal invitation to them in person but couldnât go,â Mann said. âWe have now moved high court, and hope to receive approval tomorrow. Our goal in traveling is strictly to benefit Punjab. We want to attract investors and create employment opportunities for our youth,â the CM said. Punjab govtâs petition challenges Centreâs decision as âarbitrary, without authority of law and violative of the federal structure of the Constitutionâ, and wants it quashed. According to the petition, Punjab govt had filed an application for the visit of a state delegation, led by the CM, to France for promotion of trade. It approached MEA through letters on Sept 3 and Sept 8 and submitted an online application on Sept 9. On Oct 12, Punjab govt found its application had been denied. The petition says no reason was assigned for the denial and neither was Punjab govt given an opportunity to clarify any concerns. It points out that Markfedâs participation in SIAL Paris 2026 had been confirmed under the APEDA India Pavilion and that the visit was intended to promote Punjabâs agricultural and processed food products in international markets. Punjab govt has sought a direction to the respondents to grant political clearance for the visit and asked for complete records relating to the application and the decision taken on it. This is not an isolated incident. Mann and his cabinet members have repeatedly been denied political clearance by the ministry of external affairs (MEA) for foreign visits. In Aug 2024, the Centre blocked Mannâs proposed trip to Paris to attend the Olympics and cheer on the Indian menâs hockey team, citing diplomatic and administrative reasons. Prior to that, Mann and then industries minister Sanjeev Arora were denied approval for an investment outreach tour to the UK and Israel ahead of Progressive Punjab Investorsâ Summit. More recently, MEA refused him clearance to travel to Japan for the Asian Games on security grounds. In Sept 2022, cabinet minister Aman Arora was refused approval for an official knowledge-sharing tour to Germany, Belgium, and the Netherlands. Also, assembly Speaker Kultar Singh Sandhwan was denied clearance to attend a legislative speakersâ conference in the United States in Aug 2024. And minister Harbhajan Singh was blocked from representing Punjabâs governance model at a conference in Boston in Aug last year. The Aam Aadmi Party (AAP) leadership has termed these rejections politically motivated, alleging partisan political discrimination by the Centre toward Punjab. In contrast, neighbouring Haryanaâs chief minister Nayab Singh Saini has consistently been granted prompt political clearances for his international delegations and investment tours. Recently, Saini led a state delegation to Singapore to pitch investment, urban infrastructure, and trade partnerships. Shortly after that, on Oct 14, he went on another four-day tour to Sweden to engage with international trade ministers and global investors. title: Simone Biles reveals how her embarrassing skin condition journey inspired Arcutis Biotherapeutics awareness campaign
text: Simone Biles reveals how her embarrassing skin condition journey inspired Arcutis Biotherapeutics awareness campaign (Image via Instagram: Jonathan Owens and Simone Biles) Talk about a warrior - on the spring floor as well as outside of it. Olympic gold medal winning-gymnast Simone Biles recently opened up about a personal health struggle that left her feeling self-conscious. But she thoughtfully turned her embarrassing experience with an inflammatory skin condition into an awareness campaign for Arcutis Biotherapeutics. Indianapolis Colts safety Jonathan Owensâ wife has partnered with the biopharmaceutical company for its âSkin to Believe Inâ campaign. The initiative encourages people living with eczema and seborrheic dermatitis to seek medical help and explore treatment options. The campaign was announced on September 29; it draws attention to skin conditions that cause persistent itching, flaking, and visible changes. According to Arcutis Biotherapeutics, nearly 36 million Americans suffer from inflammatory skin conditions like seborrheic dermatitis and the most common form of eczema - atopic dermatitis. Simone Biles, wife of Jonathan Owens, reveals eczema struggle In a Healthline interview, Simone Biles revealed that she mistook itching and flaking on her scalp for dandruff. She was even worried about the symptoms being contagious. Beyond her scalp troubles, she also noticed recurring dry patches on her arms. These skin symptoms became frustrating, particularly during her gymnastic training. She would catch herself scratching on the uneven bars or balance beam while waiting her turn to come. She would scratch until she bled. She felt uncomfortable about how the flakes showed up on camera during photoshoots. She would try to conceal them with oils. The Olympic gold medalist had spent years experimenting with over-the-counter products. She tried several shampoos, creams, and oils. But nothing relieved her skin condition. Embarrassment and demanding training schedules delayed her from seeking professional help for her skin ailment. Biles finally revealed her skin sorrows on social media during the 2024 Paris Olympics. Immediately thereafter, she sought skin help from a dermatologist. She finally found a name for her condition. She was diagnosed with seborrheic dermatitis on her scalp, while she had eczema [atopic dermatitis] on her arms. Zoryve treatment helps manage skin symptoms After she found a name for her unknown skin condition, Simone Biles finally embraced relief with Zoryve [roflumilast]. Arcutis Biotherapeutics developed this prescription topical medication - the 0.3% foam formulation relieved her seborrheic dermatitis on her scalp, while the 0.15% cream helped her eczema on her arms. She praised the treatment, saying it easily fit into her busy routine. She found the medication non-greasy, easy-to-use, and stressed that itâs not a steroid, pill, injection, or shampoo. The timely treatment reduced Bilesâ itching and flaking problem. The eczema patches on her arms also became clear. Caution note: individual effects can vary, so patients should consult a healthcare professional before starting treatment to determine appropriate options. Arcutis campaign aims to break skin condition stigma Simone Biles collaborated with Arcutis Biotherapeutics for its âSkin to Believe inâ campaign. The world-renowned gymnast hopes to help others overcome the embarrassment and misconceptions that come with visible skin conditions. Through her partnership, the Olympic gold medalist hopes people come forward and speak openly with healthcare providers about their skin troubles, instead of quietly enduring the symptoms or relying on home remedies. âIâve learned that we canât fix every problem on our own and itâs okay to seek help,â Biles said in the campaign announcement. This initiative clearly shows how her personal experience inspired Arcutis Biotherapeuticsâ awareness campaign. Arcutis and Simone Biles connection explained Arcutis CEO Frank Watanabe said that Bilesâ first encounter with Zoryve came organically and started on social media. The decorated gymnast shared her skin problems in a TikTok post during the 2024 Paris Olympics, the CEO said in an interview. Dermatologists recognized her itchy, flaky scalp symptoms as seborrheic dermatitis and encouraged her to explore available treatment options. They encouraged her to check out some of the FDA-approved products available for the condition. Thatâs how she got started on Zoryve and connected with Arcutis. âSheâs a very enthusiastic supporter of the product. Working with her is great,â Watanabe said via Fierce Pharma. Arcutis has worked with other public figures to raise awareness of inflammatory skin conditions - professional golfer Max Homa and actress Tori Spelling, along with her daughter Stella McDermott, in its âFree to Be Meâ patient awareness campaign for inflammatory skin conditions. Personalized care is essential because weather conditions and individual triggers can also flare symptoms. Beyond treatment, Jonathan Owensâ wife told Healthline that managing stress is a crucial part of health. She spends time with her girlfriends, gets her nails done, enjoys a massage, and takes a bath at night to unwind herself. She also said that stepping away from her demanding gymnastics career helped her relieve her stress. âHonestly, without training every single day, I donât feel as stressed.â Biles said. â[Everyone] can find different ways to alleviate their stress. title: Back from Asiad gold, hockey captain eyes LA Olympics glory
text: India hockey team captain Harmanpreet Singh Barnala : Fresh from leading India to a second consecutive Asian Games gold, hockey captain Harmanpreet Singh has set his sights on the ultimate prize â gold at the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics. With 21 months to prepare, he said the team would focus on fitness, tightening its defence and studying the strategies of European sides. Harmanpreet, who also captained India to bronze at the 2024 Paris Olympics, said the squad would work on its shortcomings from the Asian Games and prepare to take on the worldâs best. âWe would like to win laurels at that prestigious tournament. We aim to win gold and put India back on the world hockey map in a big way,â he told TOI during a visit to Barnala on Friday. Defence will be a key focus, he said, adding that every player must be able to thwart opposition attacks when India does not have possession. The team will also work on converting penalty corners and improving its field goals, with forwards expected to create more opportunities from passes.Harmanpreet also has a personal milestone in sight. With 240 career goals, he is closing in on hockey legend Balbir Singh Srâs tally of 246. Before surpassing the Indian great, he aims to overtake Australiaâs Jamie Dwyer, who scored 243 goals, and South Africaâs Greg Nicol, who scored 245. âBalbir Singh Sr is an icon for me and many others. Scoring more goals than him, even after playing more matches, would be a dream come true,â he said. The Asian Champions Trophy, scheduled to be held in Punjab from Oct 27 to Nov 5, will offer him an opportunity to close the gap. Harmanpreet hopes to score more than six goals in the tournament as a tribute to Balbir Singh Sr. The captain also sees the home tournament as a chance to draw more youngsters towards sport and away from drugs. For now, however, the bigger target remains clear: Olympic gold in Los Angeles in 2028. title: Andy Murrayâs wife Kim Sears and their four children: How family life has evolved since the former tennis champion retired from professional tennis and embraced fatherhood
text: Andy Murray and Kim Sears' combined net worth: Inside their journey from Grand Slam wins to business growth and family focus (Image Via Getty Images) Andy Murrayâs life changed dramatically when he retired from pro tennis at the 2024 Paris Olympics. The former British champion has adapted to a different lifestyle with wife Kim Sears and their four children following years of international travel, rigorous training schedules and big tournaments. Recent interviews have also shown how much he is enjoying the extra time at home after spending a good portion of his playing career away from his family. The couple have daughters, Sophia, Edie and Lola, and son, Teddy. Murrayâs connection to tennis is still strong through his experience and continuing interest in the sport, but retirement has created more time for normal parenting and family activities. They also own Cromlix, the Scottish country-house hotel, which means the couple have a business interest in common beyond the tennis circuit. Watch Andy Murray's Family! [Parents, Wife, Children] How Andy Murray enjoys family life after tennis retirement For Murray, retirement has been about showing up for the moments that were difficult to be present for consistently in his playing career. Professional tennis demanded long periods of travel between tournaments, training facilities and recovery sessions. Sometimes his family joined him on the tour, but inevitably the schedule curtailed the amount of unstructured time he could spend with his children. Murray said in a July 2026 interview that he liked retirement and having more time with his children. He admitted heâd been away a lot of his career and had missed his family often. The change has meant he can enjoy many of the routines that many parents take for granted, rather than family time dictated by an international competition calendar. The adjustment also demonstrates how the priorities of the couple have changed over time. Murray and Sears had children while he was still playing at the top level. Their eldest daughter Sophia was born in 2016, then Edie in 2017, Teddy in 2019 and their youngest daughter Lola in 2021. The children grew up during different stages of Murray's career, including times of injury, recovery and his eventual retirement. Family life now provides a different pace from the pressure of professional competition. Murray will be able to spend more time with his children and nurture their interests as they grow up. He has previously spoken of the importance of being a good father, making it clear that fatherhood is a priority separate from his sporting achievements. The change doesn't mean that tennis has disappeared from his life. Instead, it has changed its role in his daily routine. Murrayâs schedule was shaped by years of matches and training, and he has had more freedom to pursue other interests, spend time with his family and consider opportunities related to the sport without the same pressure of competing on tour. Kim Searsâ background, artistic career and marriage to Andy Murray Kim Sears has been in Murrayâs life since they were teenagers. The pair first met at the US Open in 2005 when Sears was still at school, and Murray was on the way up in the professional game. Their relationship developed with his career, and the rigors of international competition were brought into their home. They tied the knot on 11 April 2015 at Scotlandâs Dunblane Cathedral. Sears has tennis in his blood, too. Her father, Nigel Sears, is a former professional player and well-respected coach. Raised in the sport, she understands the demands it puts on you, though she has developed her own interests outside her husbandâs career. Art is one of those hobbies. Sears is known for her portraiture and animal paintings, and she has maintained a fairly private public profile despite Murrayâs international fame. Her creative work has also informed her involvement with Cromlix, shaping the interiors, artwork and overall atmosphere of the hotel. The couple bought a Victorian country house, Cromlix, near Dunblane in 2013. The property has a personal significance for Murray's family and a linkage to the local community. The couple have since turned the estate into a hospitality business, with Sears playing a key role in its creative direction since taking ownership. The hotel has therefore become a common project that unites family ties, design and business. From this, their partnership has grown beyond the public persona of a tennis champion and his wife. Sears has been there for Murray through the highs and lows of his playing career, but she has also continued to develop her own artistic interests and played an active role in the couple's business. Parenting is still a big part of lifeâs daily routine, but retirement has brought them a new avenue to share their time and responsibilities. How Andy Murray balances fatherhood and life beyond tennis Murrayâs own approach to fatherhood has been influenced by his experience of raising children through a demanding professional career. The couple have largely kept their children away from too much public exposure, allowing them to grow up away from the constant attention that comes with their fatherâs sporting achievements. The family has still given glimpses of life together now and then. Previously, the comedian has talked about the ups and downs of being a parent, from taking part in activities his daughters pick to the realities of keeping children amused. He also discussed the strange opportunity of spending long periods of time at home during the COVID-19 lockdown, while admitting that lending a hand with childrenâs education could be a challenge. The obligations of professional life against domestic life are different now that he is no longer playing. Murray no longer has to structure his whole year around tournaments, travel and physiotherapy. This flexibility allows him to be more involved in his kidsâ routines and to enjoy family experiences without needing to be away from home for extended periods. The familyâs link to Cromlix means their private and professional lives are also intertwined. The hotel is more than just a business; it is part of the coupleâs family history and relationship with Scotland. Their children visit the property, and the estate offers the family a connection between their current life and Murrayâs roots in Dunblane. In an interview in June 2026, the couple talked about their family visits to Cromlix and what the property means to them personally. Murrayâs life outside tennis is still being built, and his continuing relationship to the sport means retirement isnât a total departure from the world that defined much of his adult life. But the emphasis has shifted. His family, his interests away from the court and the coupleâs work at Cromlix now have more space to sit alongside his tennis legacy. In their case, retirement isnât so much about filling the void of major tennis triumphs as about clearing the decks for another kind of achievement: showing up for family life after years molded by the pro tour. Although Murray remains connected to tennis through his experience and ongoing interest in the sport, retirement has allowed him to place greater emphasis on fatherhood, family routines and the coupleâs hospitality business. Their next chapter reflects a shift from the demands of elite competition towards family experiences and shared projects. title: From personal battles to sporting glory: Punjabâs athletes at Para Asian Games 2026
text: Table Tennis player Shubham Wadhwa Shubham Wadhwa : From a Bedridden Life to the Table Tennis Table, a Dream to Win for India In 2016, a bike accident changed Shubham Wadhwaâs life in ways he could not have imagined. A spinal cord injury left the Ludhiana-born athlete paralysed below the chest and confined to bed for nearly three years. A national-level table tennis player during his school days, Wadhwa had stepped away from the sport to pursue modelling. The accident brought that chapter to an abrupt end, forcing him to rebuild his life from scratch. âFor three years, I was bedridden. Friends kept reminding me of table tennis. When I finally returned to the table in 2019-20, it gave me a new life,â he told TOI. With his familyâs support, Wadhwa began finding his footing again. A scholarship opportunity at Lovely Professional University (LPU) in 2018 opened another door, allowing him to pursue Computer Science Engineering. It was also where he discovered a renewed purpose in table tennis, this time as a para-athlete competing in the menâs Class 3 category. âAfter the accident, I had to start from zero. Table tennis gave me direction again,â he told TOI. What followed was a journey of rebuilding, having to constantly push himself each day. Now a 10-time national gold medallist, Wadhwa has carried his game onto the international stage. In 2026, he won a gold and two bronze medals at the ITTF World Para Future in Gold Coast, followed by silver in mixed doubles and bronze in menâs singles at the ITTF World Para Elite in Taipei City. Away from the table, he has also revisited wheelchair modelling, an interest he developed during his university years. At the Asian Para Games 2026 in Japan, Wadhwa is making his debut, competing in singles, doubles and mixed doubles. âFor me, spending three years bedridden, now the goal is to win a medal for India.â From fighting her own battles to lifting Indiaâs hopes: Jaspreet Kaur For Jaspreet Kaur, 32, from Bathinda, the road to international para-powerlifting began with a warning that forced her to rethink her life. Having contracted polio at the age of three, she went on to complete an MTech and work as a software engineer. But long hours at a desk saw her weight climb to nearly 80kg, putting increasing strain on her body. Determined to reclaim her health, she left her job, joined a gym and discovered a sport that would change her direction. âI discovered para-sports while trying to lose weight,â she recalls. In 2021, learning about powerlifter Rajinder Singh Rahelu deepened her interest in the sport. What began as an effort to regain her health soon became a pursuit of excellence. After shedding nearly 40kg in 18 months, Jaspreet turned her focus to powerlifting, training in Gandhinagar, Gujarat, in the 45kg category. Her progress has since translated into medals and records. She won gold at the Khelo India Para Games 2025, setting a national record with a lift of 101kg, and claimed bronze at the Asia-Oceania Open Championships in Bangkok in 2026. She also won silver at the Brazil Open Para-Powerlifting Championship and represented India at the 2026 Commonwealth Games. The journey, however, has not been measured only in kilograms lifted. Travelling alone, particularly by train, once meant dealing with physical difficulties, stares and social stigma. âEarlier, travelling alone, especially by train, was physically tough. The stares and social stigma hurt, but sports has lifted my confidence, it has built my confidenceâ she told TOI. Her decision to leave UPSC preparation initially worried her parents, but their concern has since turned to pride. â Itâs a journey I have consciously chosen every day,â she told TOI. Now for her second Asian Para Games outing, Jaspreet says her preparation has been good. She is eyeing a medal, hoping to deliver her personal best and make India proud. Once stopped from pursuing sports to making her mark: Seema Rani For 40-year-old Seema Rani, the road to para-powerlifting began with a life that had already demanded more of her than most. A fever when she was three, followed by an injection that affected both her legs, left her with a 79 percent disability and dependent on a wheelchair. Growing up in Haripur Khalsa, she had spent most of her life within the familiar boundaries of home, in a joint family where stepping out on her own was not something she had known. Her father a labourer and mother a housewife. When Seema first expressed an interest in sport, her family was reluctant to let her pursue it. âFor someone who had rarely left home, the prospect of training and competing meant challenging not just physical limitations, but years of hesitation and uncertainty,â she told TOI. When Parmjeet Kumar , a para-powerlifter from her village, was welcomed back with the entire village celebrating his historic medal at the World Championship, that is what ignited a spark in her. In 2019 she began practising but it was only in 2022 when she was selected to train at the SAI centre in Gandhinagar, under the guidance of coach Rajinder Singh Rahelu, that she began her formal career. In 2025, Womenâs elite 61 kg category, Seema had made a national record in Khelo India Para Games, lifting 97kgs. Now, Seema is looking ahead, determined to improve with every competition. Her ambition is to keep pushing her limits and work towards the biggest stage in sport. She told TOI, â I believe in my preparation and all I want to do is perform better than ever.â Parmjeet Kumar: From a Village Gym to the World Stage, Chasing a Paralympic Dream For Parmjeet Kumar, 34, the journey to international para-powerlifting began with curiosity. Growing up in Haripur Khalsa in Punjab , he had little access to sporting facilities. But in 2004, a gym set up in a local haveli caught his attention. He would watch with interest, unaware that the weights inside would one day become his livelihood and his identity. Born with a disability after an injection administered during a fever when he was two, Parmjeet has both legs affected. His introduction to powerlifting was far from easy. The first time he tried lifting a 20kg bar, he struggled to raise it, with balance posing another challenge. Today, he has lifted 177kg at the Asia-Oceanic Championship in Bangkok, where he won silver in April. His journey has been shaped by years of discipline and the guidance of coach Rajinder Singh Rahelu, under whom he trained for nearly a decade. From Gandhinagar to Delhiâs Jawaharlal Nehru Stadium, Parmjeet has spent years building his strength. âInspiration is for a short time. Discipline is what is most needed. Motivation does not last long, but routine does,â he told TOI, is the philosophy he lives by. In 2021 Parmjeet made history after lifting 158 kgs securing bronze, becoming the first Indian to clinch a medal in the World Para Powerlifting Championships. After finishing fourth at the 2023 Asian Para Games, Parmjeet has continued to push forward. He competed at the Paris Paralympics in 2024 but suffered a hand injury. He recently represented India at the CWG 2026. Parmjeet is determined to give his best. His goal is simple, âimprove on my previous performance and change the colour of his medalâ, he told TOI. Mohd Yasser : 3rd Asian games outing, Chasing Olympic Dream For Mohd Yasser, 32, the journey from the fields of Malerkotla to the international athletics arena has been shaped by family support and the determination to keep going, even when setbacks derailed his ambitions. Yasser, who hails from Malerkotla in Punjab, suffered an impairment in his left hand at the age of eight. Growing up in a farming family, he had the unwavering support of his parents, who stood by him as he found his footing in sport. Athletics entered his life during his college days, when he participated in a meet in Malerkotla. It was there that coach Harminderpal Singh Ghuman spotted him, opening the door to a career he had not initially envisioned. The shot-putter gradually made his mark on the international stage. At the 2018 Asian Para Games in Jakarta, Yasser won bronze in the F46 category, establishing himself as a competitor to watch. He added another milestone at the World Para Athletics Grand Prix in Dubai in 2021, winning gold with a throw of 14.58m. But the journey has not been without its disappointments. At the 2023 Asian Para Games, an injury prevented him from delivering the performance he had hoped for. He went on to represent India at the Paris Paralympics, gaining further experience on the sportâs biggest stage. Now preparing for his third Asian Para Games outing, Yasser is focused on making the opportunity count. With his parents continuing to support him, he hopes to deliver his best performance and take another step towards his Olympic dream. title: 2036 Olympics: How South Korea, Qatar, Munich, South Africa, TÃ¼rkiye, Hungary compare with Ahmedabad's bid
text: India are one of the seven cities/countries bidding to host the 2036 Summer Olympics and Paralympics. (PTI) NEW DELHI: The International Olympic Committee (IOC) has confirmed seven interested parties for the 2036 Summer Olympics: India, Germany, Qatar, South Korea, South Africa, TÃ¼rkiye and Hungary. With the process currently at the dialogue stage, the bids will be shortlisted in March 2027, preferred hosts will be identified in December 2028, and the host will be announced in mid-2029. Germany's candidate is Munich; South Korea's project is associated with Jeonju and Jeonbuk, as well as Seoul; Qatar's is centred on Doha; and South Africa is considering a multi-city or nationwide model. Hungary has designated Budapest as its central venue, while TÃ¼rkiye is planning to host the 2036 Summer Olympics in Istanbul and India in Ahmedabad. Watch Asian Games gold medallist Sujeet Kalkal on fatherâs influence and how he turned final around South Korea South Korea is no stranger to hosting the Olympics. Seoul hosted the 1988 Summer Olympics, a landmark event in the country's emergence on the international stage. PyeongChang hosted the 2018 Winter Olympics, giving the country experience of hosting both the Summer and Winter Games. What is South Korea's 2036 project? Seoul, South Korea has hosted the Olympics before in 1988. (Reuters) The domestic selection process produced a significant change in direction. The Korean Sport & Olympic Committee selected Jeonbuk (North Jeolla Province), with Jeonju as its focal city, as the country's domestic candidate. The wider discussion has also involved Seoul, which has its own infrastructure and Olympic legacy. Jeonbuk has been pushing an Olympic plan that uses venues across the province and other Korean cities, while Seoul's supporters have argued that its existing facilities and transport infrastructure make it a more credible option. The regional approach could distribute the benefits of the Games beyond the capital. It also raises a practical question: how will the country present a single, coherent proposal to the IOC when different domestic stakeholders have championed different hosting models? What should Ahmedabad learn from South Korea? South Korea's advantage is its proven experience in delivering the Olympics. Ahmedabad, by contrast, is building its case around the 2030 Commonwealth Games and the possibility of using the Olympics to transform India's sporting ecosystem. The comparison, therefore, is not simply about how many stadiums each city has. It is about whether Ahmedabad can offer the IOC an equally convincing account of how the venues will work, how athletes will move between them, and what will remain after the Games. Qatar Qatar showcased its abilities by hosting the 2022 FIFA World Cup. (Reuters) Qatar is selling accumulated investment and operational readiness. Rather than making the Olympics the starting point for a major infrastructure build-out, it wants to demonstrate that much of the necessary infrastructure is already in place. Doha previously sought to host the Summer Olympics in 2016 and 2020 but failed to reach the final stage of either selection process. The 2016 project was rejected at the applicant stage, while the 2020 campaign did not make the final group of candidate cities. Since then, Qatar has substantially expanded its major-event credentials. Its record includes: - The 2022 FIFA World Cup. - The 2023 AFC Asian Cup. - The 2024 World Aquatics Championships. - The 2030 Asian Games, which Qatar is scheduled to host. This record gives Qatar something that a first-time Olympic host cannot easily replicate: experience in managing a major-event ecosystem, including stadiums, accommodation, transport, broadcasting and international sporting operations. What is Qatar's 2036 project? A view of the Khalifa International Stadium in Qatar. Qatar's pitch is centred on Doha and the wider metropolitan area, with Lusail and Al Rayyan among the locations relevant to its existing sports infrastructure. The Qatar Olympic Committee has said that approximately 95% of the required sports infrastructure is already available. The final project will still need to establish the suitability of venues, their capacity, operating arrangements and any gaps that must be addressed. Its approach is tied to Qatar National Vision 2030, with an emphasis on sustainability, inclusion, legacy and limiting unnecessary construction. The country is also looking to build on the facilities and experience developed for the 2022 World Cup. One important complication is the calendar. Doha's summer temperatures could make a conventional July-August Olympics difficult. Qatar's 2022 World Cup was moved to November and December because of the heat, and a Summer Olympics in Qatar would face a comparable question about competition conditions and scheduling. What should Ahmedabad learn from Qatar? How the 2036 Olympics host selection process will work. (Image: IOC) Qatar sets the benchmark for infrastructure readiness and delivery experience. Its challenge is not whether it can build major sports facilities, but whether it can make the case for a Summer Olympics that meets athletes' needs, accounts for the climate and delivers an enduring public legacy. Ahmedabad can counter with a different argument: hosting would accelerate the development of a sports ecosystem in a country with a vast population and a large potential athlete base. However, the Indian proposal will need to be precise about which facilities already exist, which are planned and how each investment will be used after 2036. Qatar's experience also offers a warning for India: successfully delivering one mega-event does not, by itself, settle questions about long-term legacy, sustainability or international scrutiny. Munich, Germany Munich had hosted the 1972 Summer Olympics. The 2036 Games will mark 100 years since Berlin hosted the controversial 'Nazi Games'. (AP) Munich, which hosted the 1972 Games, wants to show that a modern Olympics need not be a giant construction project. Its proposition centres on existing venues, short distances, a familiar Olympic setting and the conversion of Games infrastructure into long-term public assets. The year 2036 has particular significance: it would fall exactly 100 years after the Berlin Games, which the Nazi regime exploited for propaganda. This gives Germany an opportunity to frame the event around democratic values and a very different modern identity, but it also makes the anniversary politically sensitive. Germany's domestic selection process was competitive. Munich defeated Cologne-Rhine-Ruhr in the German Olympic Sports Confederation's selection, winning by 90 votes to 51. Hamburg's earlier plans had been rejected in a referendum, while Berlin withdrew its proposal. Munich was eventually selected as Germany's candidate for the 2036, 2040 or 2044 Games. What is Munich's 2036 project? Munich enjoys the support of its locals in its 2036 Olympics bid. (AP) The German Olympic Sports Confederation's official concept, Munich for Germany, has several distinguishing features: - Existing facilities: The Olympic Park, which hosted events in 1972, is the centrepiece. - Short distances: Munich wants to keep a large proportion of competition venues within a compact geographical area. - A recognisable city setting: Locations such as the English Garden, Nymphenburg Palace and Odeonsplatz feature in the wider vision. - Post-Games housing: The Olympic and Paralympic Village is intended to become a climate-neutral, accessible neighbourhood for more than 10,000 people. - Sustainability: The bid promotes the circular use of resources and a legacy that extends beyond the event itself. The DOSB says approximately half of all competitions would take place in the Olympic Park. The concept is intended to reduce the need for new construction and make use of Munich's existing sporting infrastructure. Munich's domestic public mandate is also notable: 66.4% of residents voted in favour of hosting the Olympic and Paralympic Games in a referendum. What should Ahmedabad learn from Munich? Munich's strongest argument is that it may not need to build as much as its rivals. That is a direct challenge to Ahmedabad's model. India's plans involve a major programme of urban development and sports infrastructure around the city. Munich, by contrast, is presenting existing venues and legacy reuse as competitive advantages. For Ahmedabad, the lesson is to explain not just how much infrastructure will be developed, but also how much can be reused, how much it will cost to maintain and what the city will gain in return. A compelling Olympic proposal must be an urban development plan as well as a sports master plan. South Africa South Africa had hosted the 2010 FIFA World Cup. (AP) South Africa wants to bring the Summer Olympics to Africa for the first time. Its case combines the symbolic significance of being the first African host with the country's existing experience of delivering major international sporting events. South Africa has never hosted an Olympic Games. Its major-event record includes the 1995 Rugby World Cup and the 2010 FIFA World Cup. The latter is especially relevant because it demonstrated the country's ability to stage a global event across multiple venues and cities. It also offers an example of how a major tournament can be used to develop or upgrade infrastructure. The country has explored hosting the Olympics for several years, with the government approving its entry into the IOC's Continuous Dialogue process for a potential 2036 or 2040 Games. What is South Africa's 2036 project? South Africa are hoping to become the first African nation to host the Olympics. (Getty Images) The proposal initially outlined by South African Olympic leadership is a multi-city model involving Cape Town, Johannesburg and Durban. The logic is to distribute venues and responsibilities across existing urban centres rather than force the entire event into one city. It draws inspiration from the use of multiple locations at Paris 2024 and aims to make greater use of existing facilities. The three cities offer different strengths: - Cape Town: A globally recognisable setting and a proposed centre of the national project. - Johannesburg: Major-event experience and established sporting infrastructure, including FNB Stadium. - Durban: Existing major sports facilities, including Moses Mabhida Stadium. The final configuration remains subject to development. South African officials have also indicated that a preferred host city would need to be selected as the project progresses. What should Ahmedabad learn from South Africa? South Africa and India are both trying to make a larger historical argument through the Olympics. For South Africa, success would mean hosting the first Summer Olympics on African soil. For India, it would mean hosting the country's first Olympic Games and taking a major step towards its ambition of becoming a global sporting power. Both can argue that hosting would expand participation and create a wider sporting legacy. Both also need to show that their national ambitions are backed by credible funding, reliable governance and realistic plans for coordinating the host locations. The key distinction is that South Africa's project is explicitly designed to spread the Games across multiple cities. India's proposal is centred on Ahmedabad, even though the benefits of hosting would be national. TÃ¼rkiye Turkiye has made five unsuccessful attempts at winning the bid to host the Olympics. (Getty Images) Istanbul is trying to turn repeated Olympic disappointment into a stronger, more mature proposal, using existing infrastructure and upcoming international events to demonstrate readiness. Istanbul has made five previous unsuccessful attempts to host the Summer Olympics: 2000, 2004, 2008, 2012 and 2020. The 2020 campaign is especially relevant because Istanbul reached the final vote, finishing behind Tokyo. The city therefore has experience of an Olympic campaign at the highest level but has yet to convince the IOC to award it the Games. TÃ¼rkiye's current bid process has been underway for several years. The Turkish National Olympic Committee (TMOK) says it formally backed Istanbul's candidacy in April 2024 and entered the IOC's Continuous Dialogue process. What is TÃ¼rkiye's 2036 project? Istanbul's proposal combines existing venues and infrastructure with a wider national effort to demonstrate its ability to organise major competitions. The city's Olympic authorities, the Ministry of Youth and Sports, Istanbul Metropolitan Municipality and the Turkish Paralympic Committee have been involved in presenting the project's vision to the IOC. Their work has addressed the expected impact of the Games, the legacy plan and the relationship between the Olympic project and Istanbul's urban development objectives. The most important practical milestone is the 2027 European Games, which TÃ¼rkiye intends to use as a rehearsal for its Olympic ambition. Tokyo had edged Turkiye in winning the bid to host the 2020 Games. (Getty Images) TMOK has described the event as a live rehearsal and a test of confidence. The intention is to demonstrate venue readiness, transport and logistics, operational capacity and the ability to work with international sporting bodies before the IOC makes its decision on the 2036 Games. TÃ¼rkiye's government has also pointed to its experience of hosting major sporting competitions, ongoing investment in swimming facilities and the availability of an Olympic Village. Those claims will need to be assessed alongside the complete competition-venue plan and the wider logistics of the proposed Games. What should Ahmedabad learn from TÃ¼rkiye? Istanbul's advantage is that it has repeatedly pursued the Olympics and understands the demands of the bidding process. However, its history also demonstrates that persistence and a strong city identity do not guarantee success. The 2027 European Games offer a useful parallel with Ahmedabad's role in the 2030 Commonwealth Games. Both cities have a major multisport event that can serve as evidence of their ability to host something larger. For Ahmedabad, the critical question will be whether the Commonwealth Games become a genuine test of operational readiness and long-term planning, rather than simply a milestone on the way to an Olympic bid. Hungary Hungary had initially bid to host the 2024 Olympics but it was later withdrawn. (AP) Hungary is exploring a bid to host the 2036 Olympic and Paralympic Games in Budapest, with a vision centred on existing and temporary venues rather than the construction of new permanent stadiums. The proposed model envisages at least 80% of events taking place in Hungary, with the possibility of sharing venues with neighbouring countries. Budapest has pursued Olympic hosting ambitions for the 1916, 1920, 1936 and 1960 Games, but none resulted in the city being awarded the event. Its most recent campaign was for the 2024 Olympics, but it was withdrawn in February 2017 after the Momentum Movement gathered approximately 266,000 signatures demanding a referendum on the proposal. Since then, Hungary has hosted several major international sporting events, including the 2017 and 2022 World Aquatics Championships and the 2023 World Athletics Championships. These events have strengthened the country's experience in organising international competitions, although an Olympic bid would still require broad political consensus and firm financial guarantees. What is Hungary's 2036 project? The proposed Games would draw on Hungary's existing sporting infrastructure, including PuskÃ¡s ArÃ©na, the National Athletics Centre, MVM Dome and Duna ArÃ©na. Where suitable facilities are unavailable, organisers could consider temporary venues or explore sharing facilities with other countries. Preliminary discussions have included possible venues in Vienna, Bratislava, KoÅ¡ice, Brno, Ljubljana, Zagreb, Belgrade and Cluj-Napoca, although no final agreements have been reached. What should Ahmedabad learn from Hungary? Budapest has pursued Olympic hosting ambitions for the 1916, 1920, 1936 and 1960 Games. (Getty Images) Hungary's proposition is about hosting the Olympics with less new permanent construction, while Ahmedabad's is about using the Olympics to accelerate sporting and urban development. - Venues: Hungary prioritises existing and temporary facilities, potentially supplemented by venues across Central Europe. Ahmedabad's plans centre on a proposed sports enclave and wider infrastructure development. - Legacy: Hungary emphasises avoiding underused stadiums and investing in infrastructure that Budapest already needs. Ahmedabad frames the Games as a catalyst for wider participation and India's sporting ambitions. - Experience: Hungary has recently staged major international championships. Ahmedabad's 2030 Commonwealth Games offer an opportunity to demonstrate its ability to deliver a multisport event. - Main obstacle: Hungary needs political agreement and a workable cross-border model. Ahmedabad needs to demonstrate that its infrastructure plans, funding, governance and operational capabilities can meet Olympic requirements. - The key contrast: Hungary asks whether the Olympics can be staged with minimal new permanent stadium construction. Ahmedabad asks whether the Olympics can justify and accelerate a major programme of development. What is Ahmedabad's plan for the 2036 Games? Ahmedabad will host the 2030 Commonwealth Games. (PTI) India's campaign is framed around the vision "Rising Together" and the idea that hosting the Games could transform the country's sporting ecosystem, rather than merely stage a fortnight of competition. The Indian Olympic Association (IOA) has described the ambition as an opportunity to increase participation, strengthen communities and create opportunities through sport. Join conversation View All Comments â Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful Â· TOI community guidelines IOA CEO Raghuram Iyer has also made the ambition explicit: India wants to become a sporting superpower, with the longer-term goal of entering the world's top five or top 10 sporting nations. India's own project - Sports City: Plans associated with the Commonwealth Games include 11 sports complexes and complementary facilities such as gyms, swimming pools and training spaces. - Municipal investment: Ahmedabad's draft municipal budget for 2026-27 earmarked â¹17,018 crore for development, including mobility, sustainability and urban development. - 2030 Commonwealth Games: These provide a nearer-term opportunity to test venue delivery and event operations. - 2038 Asian Games: India has also pursued Ahmedabad as a possible host, potentially creating a sequence of major multisport events leading towards the Olympic ambition. title: Matthew Richardsonâs âmisconductâ probe shocks girlfriend Emma Finucaneâs family: âNone of us knewâ
text: Matthew Richardsonâs âmisconductâ probe shocks girlfriend Emma Finucaneâs family: âNone of us knewâ British cyclist Matthew Richardson has spoken publicly after being removed from Great Britainâs squad for the 2026 UCI Track Cycling World Championships in Shanghai, China, amid an investigation into alleged misconduct. The 27-year-old Olympic medallist said he would fully co-operate with British Cycling and expressed disappointment at missing the competition, which begins on October 14. Meanwhile, the family of his girlfriend, fellow cyclist Emma Finucane, said they were shocked by his withdrawal. Richardson has declined to comment further while the investigation is ongoing, and the allegations against him have not been established. Matthew Richardson promises full co-operation with British Cycling investigation Richardson addressed the situation in a statement on Instagram on October 13, acknowledging the seriousness of the reports surrounding his withdrawal. He said: â I understand the seriousness of what has been raised in recent reports about my withdrawal from the 2026 UCI Track Cycling World Championships. âBritish Cycling has said it looks into matters like this through its established procedures. I will co-operate fully with its processes. I assure everyone that I will do so properly, and appropriately and with contrition for the feelings of anyone who might be affected. âOut of fairness to everyone involved, and on advice, like British Cycling, I will not be commenting further until any process is complete. I am deeply disappointed to miss the World Championships, and I wish the Great Britain team and every rider competing the very best.â British Cycling confirmed his removal from the squad but did not publicly explain the decision. The Times reported that the organisation was investigating Richardsonâs behaviour towards fellow riders, following a complaint from another cyclist. According to the report, concerns included alleged discriminatory behaviour towards athletes from minority backgrounds. These claims remain allegations, and the investigation has not reached a publicly reported conclusion. British Cycling also said: âBritish Cycling takes any allegations of harassment, bullying or discrimination extremely seriously. âWhere concerns are raised, they are investigated thoroughly through our established procedures. âOut of fairness to anyone involved in an investigation, we would not comment on any ongoing process.â Richardson had been selected for the menâs sprint squad alongside Harry Ledingham-Horn, Ed Lowe and Joe Truman. He was expected to compete in the individual sprint, team sprint and keirin events. Emma Finucaneâs family reacts as Matthew Richardson misses World Championships Richardsonâs withdrawal came as Finucane, 23, prepared to compete in Shanghai. Her brother, Sean Finucane, 21, spoke to the Daily Mail about the familyâs reaction to the news. He said: âWe are all pretty shocked and surprised - heâs a lovely guy. Heâs been here a lot and never shown any signs of that sort of behaviour. âMy parents flew out to Shanghai yesterday - none of us knew.â Join conversation View All Comments â Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful Â· TOI community guidelines Finucane, who won four gold medals at the 2026 Commonwealth Games in Glasgow, is scheduled to compete in the individual sprint, team sprint and keirin in China. Richardson was also hoping to return to international racing after a crash in Japan in July left him with a broken shoulder blade and a badly bruised hip. The injury forced him to miss the Commonwealth Games, where he had been expected to compete for medals. Earlier this year, Richardson won gold in the menâs sprint and keirin at the European Championships in Konya, Turkey, and took silver in the team sprint. Born in Maidstone, England, he moved to Australia at the age of nine and represented the country at the 2024 Paris Olympics, winning two silver medals and a bronze. He later switched to Great Britain. For now, Richardsonâs immediate focus is co-operating with British Cyclingâs investigation, while Finucane continues her campaign at the World Championships. title: Matthew Richardson âfastest everâ claim takes back seat as Team GB cyclist is pulled from World Championships
text: Matthew Richardson âfastest everâ claim takes back seat as Team GB cyclist is pulled from World Championships Matthew Richardson , the British track cycling star who once called himself the fastest cyclist in history, has been withdrawn from the 2026 UCI Track Cycling World Championships in Shanghai following allegations of misconduct. British Cycling confirmed the decision on October 12 but did not give a reason. According to a report by The Times , Richardson is under investigation over alleged discriminatory remarks and his behaviour towards teammates. The 27-year-old was expected to compete for medals in three events when the championships begin on October 14. The allegations have not been established as proven misconduct. Matthew Richardson faces investigation over alleged discriminatory remarks Richardsonâs removal from the Great Britain squad follows a complaint reportedly made by another rider. The Times reported that the investigation concerns alleged discriminatory remarks on social media about people from minority backgrounds. A rider who spoke to the newspaper also claimed Richardson did not change his behaviour even when interacting with athletes from minority backgrounds. British Cycling has confirmed that Richardson will not compete in Shanghai, although it has not publicly detailed the allegations or announced the outcome of an investigation. A spokesperson for the governing body said: âBritish Cycling can confirm that Matt Richardson has been withdrawn from the Great Britain Cycling Team squad for the upcoming 2026 Tissot UCI Track Cycling World Championships in Shanghai, China.â British Cycling also said: âBritish Cycling takes any allegations of harassment, bullying or discrimination extremely seriously. âWhere concerns are raised, they are investigated thoroughly through our established procedures. âOut of fairness to anyone involved in an investigation, we would not comment on any ongoing process.â Richardson is understood to be leaving the teamâs base in China. No public finding of misconduct has been announced, and the investigation remains ongoing. The situation also comes years after an independent review of British Cycling in 2017 found a âculture of fearâ within the organisation. That earlier review concerned the governing bodyâs wider working environment and does not establish the truth of the current allegations against Richardson. Matthew Richardsonâs Team GB career and Olympic success Richardson was born in Maidstone, Kent, and moved to Perth, Australia, with his family when he was nine. He represented Australia at the Paris 2024 Olympics, winning two silver medals and a bronze before switching to Great Britain shortly after the Games ended. The move made Richardson one of Britainâs leading track cycling names. In 2025, he broke the world record for the flying 200-metre time trial, recording 8.941 seconds at an event in Konya, Turkey. His speed helped build his reputation as one of the sportâs top sprinters. Richardson was expected to compete in the team sprint, individual sprint and keirin at the Shanghai championships, scheduled to run from October 14 to 18. His withdrawal is a setback for Britainâs medal hopes, particularly after he won two silver medals at the 2025 World Championships in Santiago, Chile.
