title: From Asian Games glory to tractor duty, hockey star Jarmanpreet Singhâs message to youth
text: Jarmanpreet Singh recently shared a 17-second video of himself driving a tractor and ploughing his fields. AMRITSAR: From winning medals for India on the international hockey stage to ploughing his familyâs fields in his native village, Olympian Jarmanpreet Singh has shown that sporting glory does not diminish oneâs responsibilities at home. The defender, who hails from Razadan village near Baba Bakala in Amritsar district, recently shared a 17-second video of himself driving a tractor and ploughing his fields, captioning it âNation duty â home dutyâ. After representing the country at major international tournaments, the Income Tax officer posted in Bengaluru said he had returned home to fulfil his responsibilities towards his parents, delivering a simple message to young people about the importance of family and giving time to those who stood by them. Jarmanpreetâs sporting achievements include gold medals at the 2022 Asian Games in Hangzhou, China, and the 2026 Asian Games in Japan, a silver medal at the 2022 Commonwealth Games in Birmingham and bronze at the 2024 Paris Olympics. His father retired from the Punjab Police. The video offered a glimpse of the hockey star away from the sporting arena, taking up an everyday agricultural task at home. For Jarmanpreet, the visit was not merely a break between tournaments but an opportunity to stand by his parents and share their responsibilities. He said children should understand that their duties towards their parents did not end when they moved away for jobs or achieved success in their respective fields. They should make time for their families rather than allow professional commitments to keep them constantly occupied, he said. âEvery child should fulfil their responsibilities towards their parents and spend enough time with the family,â was his message to the youth. His example also carries particular significance for young people who leave their villages to pursue education, careers or sporting ambitions. While professional success and financial independence are important, maintaining close family bonds and being available for parents should remain a priority. Jarmanpreet, who is employed with the Income Tax Department and represents India in hockey, will now return his focus to the sport as preparations begin for the next Asian Champions Trophy campaign being hosted by the Punjab government and 2028 Los Angeles Olympics. title: From Tokyo to Nagoya: Lovlina Borgohainâs long road to the top of the podium | Exclusive Interview
text: Lovlina Borgohain NEW DELHI: Lovlina Borgohain âs Asian Games gold was not just a medal upgrade from silver in the last edition. It was the latest marker in a 15-year career that has taken the Assam boxer through Olympic success, injuries, difficult phases and a mentally demanding Paris 2024 campaign. At the 2026 Asian Games in Aichi-Nagoya, Borgohain finally changed the colour of her Asian Games medal, defeating Chinaâs Bao Ziyi 5-0 in the womenâs 75kg final. The victory, on her 29th birthday, made her only the second Indian woman after MC Mary Kom to win boxing gold at the Asian Games -- 12 years after Komâs 2014 triumph. Watch âThis medal means a lotâ: Lovlina Borgohain on Asian Games gold & Olympic ambitions For Borgohain, however, the gold's significance went beyond the history books. âItâs still difficult to get out of this moment. I still have the gold medal in my hand," said a beaming Borgohain while lifting the gold medal next to her face. "Itâs a very special moment for me. I canât express how I feel,â she continued as she spoke to TimesofIndia.com upon returning from Japan. Borgohain had finished with silver at the 2022 Hangzhou Asian Games, losing to Chinaâs Li Qian in the final. Three years later, she returned to the continental stage determined to go one step further. I got a silver medal in the last Asian Games and this time I got a gold medal. This is why it is so special. And to do it on my birthday is extra special Lovlina Borgohain Her path to the gold in Nagoya was not straightforward. She began with a 5-0 quarter-final win over South Koreaâs Seong Su-yeon before edging Kazakhstanâs reigning 70kg world champion Natalya Bogdanova 3-2 in a closely fought semi-final. She then produced a 5-0 win over Ziyi in the final. The contrast with Hangzhou made the medal particularly meaningful. âEvery event is very important. We believe that the Asian Games medal is the highest after the Olympics. I think this medal is shining amidst all the medals. The colour has changed. This medal means a lot to me,â Borgohain said. New Delhi: Asian Games 2026 gold medallist boxer Lovlina Borgohain poses for photographers upon her arrival at the Indira Gandhi International (IGI) Airport, in New Delhi, early Sunday, Oct. 4, 2026. (PTI Photo) (PTI10_04_2026_000011B) âI got a silver medal in the last Asian Games and this time I got a gold medal. This is why it is so special. And to do it on my birthday is extra special.â The victory also continued a curious connection between Borgohain and Japan. Five years ago, Tokyo had brought her an Olympic bronze medal â the breakthrough that changed the trajectory of her career. âI was very excited because I was going to Japan again. I had won a medal in (the) 2020 Olympics in Japan, and my life changed because of that,â she said. âI had a positive mindset before leaving India. I wanted to make it the best tournament of my life. I knew that I could do it because Japan is lucky for me.â My perspective has not changed because of the medal. When I lose, my self-belief remains the same. Sometimes I am confident, and sometimes I am down. But I am the same person that I was before Lovlina Borgohain âEverything is a game of the mindâ The gold also offered a reminder of Borgohainâs ability to rebuild. Her career has not followed a straight line since the Tokyo Olympics. Injuries, changes in form and the disappointment of the Paris Olympics tested her, while the pressure that came with becoming an Olympic medallist added another layer to the challenge. Borgohain does not, however, see the Asian Games gold as something that has fundamentally changed her. âI donât think I am looking at myself differently because of this medal. I have won and lost a lot of medals. Peopleâs perspective changes because of the medal. But I am always the same in my own eyes,â she said. New Delhi: Asian Games 2026 gold medallist boxer Lovlina Borgohain poses for photographers upon her arrival at the Indira Gandhi International (IGI) Airport, in New Delhi, early Sunday, Oct. 4, 2026. (PTI Photo) (PTI10_04_2026_000007A) âMy perspective has not changed because of the medal. When I lose, my self-belief remains the same. Sometimes I am confident, and sometimes I am down. But I am the same person that I was before.â That mindset became particularly important after Paris 2024, when she failed to reach the medal rounds. Borgohain describes the period as one of the most difficult phases of her career. âI have a 15-year journey. Every time I go to a competition, my mindset is different. When we play, we reach the medal. It is not easy to recover from a tough period. The 2024 Paris Olympics wasnât an easy period for me mentally,â she said. âBut I think everything is a game of the mind. It depends on how we look at it. If we take tough things easy, it becomes easy. If we take easy things hard, it becomes hard. I think that helped me a lot to keep myself calm and relaxed.â It matters a lot for an athlete because of this medal I am qualifying for the World Championships. I am getting a good treat otherwise I would have to play the Nationals and follow the same process Lovlina Borgohain Borgohain qualifies for World Championships The Asian Games victory has also given Borgohain a more direct route towards the next stage of her career. The gold means she qualifies for the World Championships, rather than having to go through the national selection route. A strong performance there could also put her on the road to another Olympic qualification campaign. âIt matters a lot for an athlete because of this medal I am qualifying for the World Championships. I am getting a good treat otherwise I would have to play the Nationals and follow the same process,â she said. Nishio: India's Lovlina Borgohain, in blue, competes against China's Ziyi Bao during a women's 75kg boxing bout at the 20th Asian Games, in Nishio, Aichi, Japan. (PTI Photo/Arun Sharma) (PTI10_02_2026_000066A) *** Local Caption *** âSo that is a big advantage of the medal, and it boosts my confidence that I can do better. If I do well there, then I can qualify for the Olympics also.â For now, though, Borgohain is resisting the temptation to look too far ahead. âThere is a lot of planning. But not everything is the same. I am living in the present. I donât know what will happen tomorrow. I will try to live like this. It makes me feel good. I will try to live like this.â âYoung athletes have stronger mindsetâ Borgohainâs gold was part of a strong boxing campaign for India at the Asian Games. India finished the competition with six boxing medals, including three golds, with Parveen Hooda and Ankush Panghal also winning their respective finals. In the Asian Games, our Indian team came out on top. I think our athletes are very strong. Their mentality is very good. We used to think that we would not be able to do it. But now our young athletes have the mindset that âwe have to do it Lovlina Borgohain Some months back, Indian boxers had returned with 10 medals at the Glasgow Commonwealth Games, including seven golds. No country had won more golds in boxing at a single edition of the CWG. It was also India's largest haul in the sport in a CWG. For Borgohain, the improvement reflects a broader change in the mentality of Indian boxers. âWe had a very good performance. Both men and women did very well. Everyone knows the results of the Commonwealth Games. The results of the Commonwealth Games changed the results of Indian Boxing,â she said. Nishio: India's Lovlina Borgohain, in blue, after winning gold medal in the women's 75kg final boxing bout against China's Ziyi Bao at the 20th Asian Games, in Nishio, Aichi, Japan. (PTI Photo/Arun Sharma) (PTI10_02_2026_000058A) *** Local Caption *** âIn the Asian Games, our Indian team came out on top. I think our athletes are very strong. Their mentality is very good. We used to think that we would not be able to do it. But now our young athletes have the mindset that âwe have to do itâ.â Join conversation View All Comments â Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful Â· TOI community guidelines She also pointed to the support structure around the team, including government backing and the environment created by the coaching staff led by Santiago Nieva. âThe support of the government matters a lot. They donât let us down. We are getting good competition. The environment of our foreign coaches, led by Santiago (Nieva), is very positive. That is why we are getting good results.â For Borgohain, then, the Asian Games gold is both an ending and a beginning â the end of a 12-year wait since Mary Komâs historic gold and the completion of a personal journey from Hangzhou silver to Nagoya gold. But she is not treating it as a destination. The next target can wait. For now, she is content to live in the moment â with the gold medal still in her hand. title: India, Qatar among seven bidders as race to host 2036 Olympics takes shape
text: Commonwealth Games 2030 in Ahmedabad (AP Photo) India's ambition to host the 2036 Olympics has taken another major step forward, with the International Olympic Committee (IOC) on Tuesday confirming the country among seven bidders in the race to stage the Summer Games. Qatar, South Korea, Germany, Hungary, Turkey and South Africa are the other countries currently in discussions with the IOC, setting up what could become one of the most competitive Olympic hosting contests in years. The IOC is aiming to select the 2036 host in 2029 through a vote of its 100-plus members. The timeline represents a return to a more traditional contested process after the fast-track and largely closed-door approach used to award the 2032 Games to Brisbane. The IOC has also kept the possibility of discussions extending towards the 2040 and 2044 editions. Watch âThis medal means a lotâ: Lovlina Borgohain on Asian Games gold & Olympic ambitions Ahmedabad at centre of India's Olympic ambition India's proposal is centred on Ahmedabad, which is scheduled to host the 2030 Commonwealth Games and boasts the Narendra Modi Stadium, the world's largest cricket stadium. India has been openly pursuing the Olympics for several years, with the country's sporting administration presenting its ambitions during the Paris 2024 Games. Qatar, another prominent contender, has built substantial experience in hosting major international sporting events, including the 2022 FIFA World Cup and world championships across several Olympic sports. Its proposal is centred on Doha, although the possibility of involving other Gulf neighbours could emerge as the bid develops. A major issue for a Qatar Olympics would be the traditional July-August window. The Summer Games have been held during those months at every edition from Athens 2004 through Brisbane 2032, but Qatar's extreme summer temperatures could require a change to the established calendar. Seven bids, with more time for competition South Korea's proposal would be anchored by Seoul, which hosted the 1988 Olympics, while events could be spread across the country. Germany's bid is centred on Munich, which previously hosted the Summer Games in 1972. South Africa is proposing a national bid centred on Cape Town and is seeking to deliver the first African-hosted Summer Olympics of the modern era. Hungary and Turkey have put forward Budapest and Istanbul respectively as their proposed host cities. The IOC has set October 31 as the deadline for other national Olympic committees to express an interest in entering the 2036 race. It has also published a 30-page document outlining the framework and requirements for prospective bidders. The next major milestone will come in March, when the IOC executive board, chaired by president Kirsty Coventry, is expected to approve a shortlist of candidates that will proceed to develop detailed hosting projects. Her first major decision was to pause the previous fast-track process, giving IOC members a greater say in choosing the host. IOC members had expressed a desire for a genuine choice between multiple candidates rather than simply endorsing a preferred option put forward by the executive board. The eventual vote is now targeted for 2029, giving the shortlisted bidders roughly two and a half years to develop and promote their proposals. The IOC's membership includes sports administrators, current and former athletes, members of royal families, politicians, business leaders and personalities such as Oscar-winning actress Michelle Yeoh. Among those eligible to participate in the eventual vote are India's Nita Ambani and Qatar's Emir Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad Al Thani, adding another layer of interest to a contest that could ultimately stretch beyond the 2036 Games. title: 'The sport wasnât ready to let go of me': Lovlinaâs journey from Paris heartbreak to Asian Games gold
text: Asian Games Gold medallist India's Lovlina Borgohain (Image: REUTERS) NISHIO: For her 29th birthday, Lovlina Borgohain had already decided what she wanted to gift herself. Gold. On Friday, at the Nishio Gymnasium, she unboxed it herself. âItâs a special birthday for me. Iâm feeling very, very happy. I wanted to give myself a gold medal for my birthday, so I put my 100% into getting it,â she said, moments after beating Chinaâs Ziyi Bao 5-0 in the womenâs 75kg final. It was a gift that carried considerable weight given that its 265-gram medal would see Lovlinaâs maiden Asian Games title, making her only the second Indian woman after Mary Kom to fetch it. Lovlina, who had already fought several bouts in her mind, was reminded of the three inside the ring on Friday, she ticked that final box too. It was a dominant performance, but a fight in every sense. Lovlina ducked, punched, fell, picked herself up and kept coming, throwing everything at Bao before securing a unanimous 5-0 verdict. Watch Lovlina Borgohainâs golden birthday: Asian Games medal after comeback Not many had given the boxer from Baramukhia village in Assam a serious shot at gold. But then, Lovlina has never been much of a people pleaser. What made the victory sweeter was that it represented more than the medal, the validation of a change in mindset. After her quarterfinal exit at the Paris Olympics in 2024, Lovlina hit her lowest point. She publicly apologised for failing to win a medal, faced criticism and began to feel that her career was slipping away. Somewhere along the way, she changed the way she looked at boxing. The weight of expectations gave way to the simple joy of doing what she loved. âIt was that low which carried her all the way to gold. With the gold medal glittering around her neck, she told TOI, âFor 15 years, there were many ups and downs. I took boxing as a challenge. I had to win, then enjoy. When you work so hard and lose, you start feeling horrible that youâve given the game your everything and still havenât been able to get the medal you worked for,ââ she said. âThatâs the feeling I got after Paris. Thatâs when I thought I wouldnât be able to compete again and stayed away for months. But when I wanted to walk away from boxing, the sport wasnât ready to let go of me. title: EXCLUSIVE | 'Fear may never completely go away': Sujeet Kalkal on turning Olympic heartbreak into Asian Games gold
text: Sujeet Kalkal (Image credit: PTI) NEW DELHI: Two years ago, Sujeet Kalkal was stranded at Dubai International Airport, watching his Olympic dream slip away with every passing hour. On his way to Bishkek, Kyrgyzstan, for the Asian Olympic Qualifying Tournament, Kalkal was stuck in Dubai for three days after floods disrupted his travel plans. By the time a flight was arranged, it was too late. He could not reach Bishkek in time, and with it went his chance to qualify for the Paris Olympics. Watch âThis medal means a lotâ: Lovlina Borgohain on Asian Games gold & Olympic ambitions Two years later, the disappointment of Dubai has been replaced by an Asian Games gold. Kalkal, the world No. 2 in the men's 65kg category, fought back from 2-9 down against Tajikistan's Abdulmazhid Kudiev in the final to win 10-9, ending India's eight-year wait for a wrestling gold at the Games. The comeback was symbolic of what Kalkal's career has looked like since that Olympic setback. He has had to rebuild, compete through the disappointment and find a way back to the biggest stages. On Sunday, he did that with an Asian Games title. When the final whistle came, Kalkal folded his hands, looked up and thanked God. He then took a lap of the arena with the Indian tricolour draped around his shoulders, tears and a broad smile. For a wrestler who had once been denied even the chance to fight for an Olympic place, the moment carried a little more weight than an Asian Games gold. "This gold means a lot to me. Not just because it is an Asian Games gold, but because there is so much behind this medal. The last few years have had many ups and downs, and I missed a few opportunities, but I never lost belief in myself," Kalkal told TimesofIndia.com in an exclusive interview on his way back to Imlota village in Bhiwani, Haryana, where his parents were waiting to welcome him. Sujeet Kalkal (Image credit: PTI) The Dubai episode, he says, is now behind him. What remains is the lesson from it - and a much bigger target. "Paris was very difficult for me to miss, but that experience made me stronger instead of breaking me. LA 2028 is obviously a very big goal for me," Kalkal said. And he is clear about what he wants from that opportunity. "Olympics mein jaana hai toh sirf participate karne ke liye nahi jaana, bhaisaab. Gold ke liye jaana hai [âIf youâre going to the Olympics, donât go just to participate, brother. Go there to win gold]." India had not won a wrestling gold at the Asian Games since 2018. Kalkal's victory ended that wait and added another major title to a career that already includes an U23 World Championship crown, Asian Championships success and a Zagreb Open triumph. "India has won a wrestling gold at the Asian Games after eight years, so being a part of it is very special for me. This medal reminds me that if you keep working hard, your time will come," he said. The road to the Asian Games gold was not easy for Kalkal. He had a challenging draw, but handled each bout with confidence. After a comfortable opening victory, he made a statement in the quarterfinals by throwing Iran's Abbas Ebrahimzadehsavadkouhi from a standing position within the opening 20 seconds. The semifinal brought an even bigger test, but Kalkal overcame Olympic champion Kotaro Kiyooka to reach the gold medal bout. Then came the final against Tajikistan's Abdulmazhid Kudiev, and it looked like the toughest challenge of them all. Instead of allowing the deficit to affect him, Kalkal fought his way back into the contest. He produced eight points to turn a seven-point deficit into a 10-9 victory and seal the Asian Games title. "The simple plan was to wrestle my own way and not be impressed by my opponent's name. Whether he is an Olympic champion, a world champion or anyone else, everyone starts from zero on the mat. I just trusted my preparation and my strength. I knew that if I executed my best, I could beat anyone. Instead of thinking too much during the match, I just had to fight for every single point," he said. Sujeet Kalkal during his gold medal bout (Image credit: PTI) Kalkal also dedicated the gold to the country and remembered his father, who stood by him throughout his journey. "I dedicate this gold to the whole of India. Of course, my first call was to my father. He has supported me tremendously throughout this journey, and without his support, it would have been impossible for me to reach this point. His support will always remain with me," the Indian wrestler said. The final also reflected the mental change Kalkal says came from the disappointment of 2024. "Fear may never completely go away, but now I know how to fight with fear. When you go through tough situations in life, small things stop bothering you. What happened in Dubai, missing the Olympic qualifiers - every experience taught me something," the Indian wrestler said. Join conversation View All Comments â Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful Â· TOI community guidelines "Now I don't run away from pressure. I enjoy pressure because those are the moments when you realise how strong you actually are," Kalkal said. The Asian Games gold now joins an already impressive list of achievements for Kalkal, but he is not dwelling on the medals he has already won. The next target is Los Angeles. And this time, he wants to get there on his own terms. "Gold ke liye jaana hai." Poll Vote & Share your view Which factor do you think played the biggest role in Kalkal's comeback? title: Celebrating sports with asiad biryani and olympic drinks
text: Olympics, Asian Games and Their Unexpected Food Legacy Did Indiaâs last-minute medal surge at the Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games increase demand for âAsiad biryaniâ in Kerala? This is a specialty of hilly areas, like Idukki, in which meat, particularly marrow-rich bones, is cooked with tapioca for a hearty meal. One theory for the name is that it honours Shiny Abraham, part of Keralaâs golden generation of athletes, who comes from Idukki. Another is that the dish, also called ellum kapayam, is so loaded with energy-giving fat and complex carbohydrates that it is perfect for intense physical activity. Several sporting events have associated foods. Strawberries and cream at Wimbledon. Sandwiches made with spicy pimentos and cheese at the Augusta Masters golf tournament. Mint julep cocktails made from bourbon, syrup and mint at the Kentucky Derby horse races. The bottle of milk drunk by the winner of the Indianapolis 500 race. Vada pav at the cricket matches played on Mumbaiâs maidans. But these are all linked to specific venues. With events that move around, like the Olympics and Asian Games, it seems harder to form a lasting food connection. Food items can trend during the games, especially with most athletes posting on social media. A rich chocolate muffin was the unexpected hit of the 2024 Paris Olympics, while at this yearâs Milano-Cortina Winter Olympics, it was a chocolate lava cake. The Winter Olympics organisers this year also had one smart product with lasting potential â pasta shaped like the five interlinked rings of the Games. It came with a special recipe for making it, but plain pasta shaped in such a distinctive Olympic manner could be iconic at all the Games, not least because pasta is always one of the top foods eaten by athletes. But this also underlines the problem with creating really distinctive foods for sporting events. Athletes are primarily focussed on functional foods for their sports, rarely wanting to risk something unusual. Usain Bolt famously ate only chicken nuggets at the Beijing Olympics, and duly broke three world records. Many teams now travel with personal nutritionists who will choose what their athletes will eat. One of the few mentions of food at the first Asian Games, in Delhi in 1951, is that the Japanese team insisted on preparing their own food, avoiding what was provided by the Indian hosts. They topped the medal table, with 24 golds. India came second with 15 golds. The food at the second Asian Games in Delhi, in 1982, is better documented. Catering was handled by ITDCâs Ashoka Group, with their French executive chef, Roger Moncourt, credited with creating an international level operation. Moncourt had insisted on importing cooking equipment that could operate at the scale needed. A report in the Akashvani journal spoke admiringly about âa cutting machine which washes, dries and cuts vegetables in different sizes in minutes, and an automatic machine to butter bread slicesâ. This enabled the kitchen to produce Indian dishes like âneelgiri korma, Goan fish curry, Madras chicken curry, murgh anarkali, gobhi mussalum, Kashmiri pulao and Kerala fish curryâ, along with continental and Chinese options. But the Akashvani report also highlighted another problem with organising events in India â whether and how to serve alcohol. No alcohol was provided in the Games village, but two stadiums were provided with bars âwhere liquor will be served to journalists covering the gamesâ. The Times of India, in a report titled âNo flood of foreigners for Asiadâ, highlighted the problems in getting international attention for the Games, and Indiaâs reputation for making it hard to get a drink was clearly not helping. This will be an issue for Ahmedabadâs ambitions to host the Olympics. Here, the example of Helsinkiâs 1952 Olympics might help. Finland strongly restricted alcohol sale, but compromised by creating canned pre-mixed drinks, whose sale could be better controlled. One of these, a gin and grapefruit soda called Lonkero, was so popular that it is still sold today, a lasting liquor legacy of the Olympic Games. title: Mary Kom  to Lovlina: Two generations, one boxing legacy
text: Lovlina Borgohain Guwahati: Lovlina Borgohain has followed a path that bears striking parallels with the legendary Mangte Chungneijang Mary Kom . But the two Indian boxing icons have built their legacies across different eras, weight categories and career trajectories. Separated by 17 years and about 350 kilometres, Mary Kom and Lovlinaâs boxing careers trace a strikingly similar arc, from modest farming households in two of Indiaâs most remote corners to international debuts that both began with silver medals. Kom, now 41, has not competed in any events and is already past IBAâs 40âyear ceiling for elite amateur boxing. Lovlina turned 29 on Friday. Kom was born in Kangathei village in Moirang in Manipur âs Bishnupur district, to Mangte Tonpa Kom, a tenant farmer. Borgohain was born in Bara Mukhia village in Assam âs Golaghat district, to Tiken Borgohain, a small-scale businessman and farmer. The parallel sharpens once their careers begin. Kom made her international debut in 2001 at the first-ever AIBA Womenâs World Boxing Championship in Scranton, Pennsylvania, at just 18 years old, in the 48kg category, winning silver in her very first appearance on the world stage. Lovlinaâs international debut came in 2013 at the Nations Womenâs Junior Cup in Serbia in the 70kg category, where she too won silver, at age 17, almost the same age as Kom, with the same colour medal, on debut. Komâs debut was immediately at the senior World Championship level, but Lovlinaâs senior international bow came five years later, in 2018, at AIBA Womenâs World Boxing Championship in New Delhi, where she won bronze in the 64kg category in her maiden senior appearance. Mary Kom was Indiaâs trailblazer on the Olympic stage, winning bronze at the London 2012 Games in the 51 kg category. Nine years later, Lovlina became only the third Indian boxer to win an Olympic medal when she claimed bronze at Tokyo 2021 in the 69kg division. Mary Komâs international dominance stretched over a much longer period. Her six World Championships gold medals remain the defining statistic of her career, alongside Olympic bronze and multiple Asian titles. Lovlina was forced into the 75kg category after the 69kg division was dropped from the Paris Olympics programme. She adapted quickly, winning Asian Championships gold in 2022 and becoming world champion at 75kg in 2023. She also won Asian Games silver in Hangzhou in 2023 to secure her Paris quota. At Paris 2024, however, Lovlinaâs campaign ended in the quarter-finals after a defeat to Chinaâs Li Qian, who eventually won the gold medal. The two careers intersect at one significant milestone, both becoming Olympic medallists and world champions, making them the only Indian women boxers to combine those achievements. For Lovlina, it is not about comparison with Mary but more about extending a legacy. Mary opened the Olympic door for Indian womenâs boxing; Lovlina became the next generation to walk through it. title: Persistence shapes Lovlinaâs the road to Asiad gold
text: Guwahati: Persistence, not speed, is what shaped a 13-year journey from an international debut to an Asiad gold. Each title arrived after an earlier attempt that fell one rung short, a pattern that defines Lovlina Borgohain âs career more than any single result. Thirteen years after her international debut, Borgohain has joined Mary Kom as the second Indian woman boxer to win an Olympic medal and gold at the World and Asian Championships and Asian Games . After Bhogeswar Baruahâs feat in 1966, she is also the second Assamese athlete in six decades to win an individual Asian Games gold. From a junior silver at the Nations Womenâs Junior Cup in Serbia in 2013 to boxingâs biggest titles, Borgohainâs rise has been defined by repeated comebacks after falling one step short. She beat Chinaâs Bao Ziyi 5-0 in the womenâs 75kg final to turn her previous Asian Games silver into a gold and end a 12-year wait for Indian womenâs boxing since Mary Komâs victory. The Asian Games title was the one major international crown missing from her collection. Borgohain had already won World and Asian Championship gold, as well as an Olympic bronze. She finished with silver at the 2023 Asian Games in Hangzhou. The Paris Olympics in 2024 brought another setback. Borgohainâs route to the title was repeatedly interrupted by narrow reversals. Her boxing journey began in 2012, when coach Padum Boro spotted her at a Sports Authority of India trial at her school. She began training at the Netaji Subhas Regional Centre in Guwahati that year and won gold at the Indian Womenâs Junior National Championships. In 2017, she won bronze in the 69kg category at the Asian Championships in Vietnam, marking her senior international debut. The following year, she won a World Championship bronze after exiting the Commonwealth Games in Australia in the quarter-finals. Borgohain initially took up Muay Thai, following her twin sisters, Lima and Licha. An SAI scouting programme later redirected her to boxing, recognising in the teenage kickboxer the reflexes and build the sport required. title: Inspiring story on family: âMy road to success began the day my grandfather and his wife officially adopted my sister and meâ-  Simone Biles reflects on the people who shaped her journey
text: FILE - Simone Biles, of the United States, celebrates after winning the gold medal at the medal ceremony during the women's artistic gymnastics individual vault finals at Bercy Arena at the 2024 Summer Olympics, on Aug. 3, 2024, in Paris, France. (AP Photo/Francisco Seco, File) For Simone Biles, success did not begin with an Olympic gold medal, a world championship title or a difficult gymnastics routine. Long before she became one of the most famous gymnasts in the world, her life took a major turn when her grandparents stepped in and gave her and her younger sister, Adria, a stable home. Biles has often spoken about how important that moment was in her life, especially because she and her siblings had spent time in foster care after their biological mother struggled to care for them. Her maternal grandfather, Ron Biles, and his wife, Nellie, eventually adopted Simone and Adria and raised them in Spring, Texas. Her quote, âMy road to success began the day my grandfather and his wife officially adopted my sister and me,â says much more than it appears to at first. It is not simply about the legal moment when she became their daughter. For Biles, it represents the beginning of a safer childhood, a stronger support system and the chance to discover what she could become. Her story also shows that sometimes the people who change our lives are the ones who simply decide to stay, support us and give us the confidence to move forward. What happened before Simone Biles was adopted by her grandparents? Simone Biles was born in Columbus, Ohio, in 1997. Her early childhood was not easy. Her biological mother, Shanon Biles, struggled with drug and alcohol dependency, and Simone and her siblings spent time in foster care. During that period, her grandparents became an important source of comfort and stability. Biles has remembered being especially excited whenever her grandfather visited her while she was in foster care. Ron Biles and Nellie Biles eventually took Simone and her younger sister, Adria, into their home. Ron was Simoneâs maternal grandfather, while Nellie was his wife. The couple later legally adopted both girls, while another relative took care of Simoneâs older siblings. This was a major change for a young Simone. She was no longer moving through an uncertain situation and wondering where she would live. She had a home where she could grow up with people who were committed to her. The adoption also gave her something that would become extremely important as she grew older: a dependable support system. The story becomes even more meaningful when looking at how Biles viewed the relationship. She did not grow up thinking of Ron and Nellie as people who had simply rescued her. They became her parents in every way that mattered to her. Biles has previously explained that she considered being adopted normal because it was the life she knew. She did not spend her childhood feeling that something was missing. Why does Simone Biles describe her adoption as the beginning of her success? When Biles talks about her adoption as the beginning of her road to success, she is pointing to everything that happened after that turning point. Success did not arrive overnight. The adoption created the foundation from which she could build her life. One of the biggest changes was stability. A child needs more than talent to reach a high level in any sport. They need adults who can provide encouragement, transportation, time, money, emotional support and a safe place to return to after a difficult day. Biles found that support with Ron and Nellie. Nellie, in particular, became deeply involved in Bilesâ life and eventually became the mother figure she knew. Biles has spoken about how her parents supported her ambitions and made sure she had what she needed to compete. That support became especially important once gymnastics entered her life. Biles first encountered gymnastics during a daycare field trip when she was around six years old. She began copying the movements of older gymnasts, and coaches noticed that she had unusual natural ability. Her family then supported her as she started taking gymnastics more seriously. It is easy to look at Biles today and see the medals, records and extraordinary routines. Her quote asks people to look much further back. Before any of those achievements, there was a child who needed a safe place to grow. Her grandparents helped provide that place. How did Ron and Nellie Biles help Simone build her future? Ron and Nellie did more than give Simone and Adria a home. They became active parts of the girlsâ lives and supported their interests as they grew up. As Simoneâs gymnastics career developed, the family continued to stand behind her. Nellie has spoken about creating a strong support system around Simone, including family traditions such as weekly dinners and attending church together. The family also traveled to support Biles during major competitions, showing that her achievements were never treated as something she had to experience alone. Ron also played an important role in Bilesâ gymnastics journey. He and Nellie later opened the World Champions Centre in Spring, Texas, where Biles trained. The facility became another part of the environment that supported her development as an elite gymnast. But their influence was not only about gymnastics. The most important thing they gave Biles was the feeling that she belonged. That can be seen in a story from the time of the adoption. After the adoption papers were signed, Biles asked Nellie if she could call her âMom.â For a young child, that simple question carried enormous meaning. It showed that Biles was beginning to see Nellie not simply as her grandmotherâs wife, but as the person who would fill the role of her mother. Nellie has also described the emotional process of becoming a mother to children who were previously her grandchildren. She said there was a point when she realized she would do anything for them, and that was when she knew she was truly their mother. That bond helped shape the person Biles became. Her career required an extraordinary amount of discipline, but having people who believed in her gave her somewhere to find strength when things became difficult. What does Simone Bilesâ quote teach us about success and the people behind it? The most powerful part of Bilesâ quote is that she does not describe success as something she achieved completely by herself. Instead, she connects her journey to a decision made by other people when she was still a child. That is important because Bilesâ career is often described through her individual achievements. She became a multiple Olympic gold medalist, a world champion and one of the most decorated gymnasts in history. At the Paris 2024 Olympics, she added more medals to a career that had already made her one of the biggest names in gymnastics. Yet behind every routine was a larger story. There was the child who experienced foster care. There was the grandfather who wanted to make sure she and Adria were cared for. There was Nellie, who became her mother and helped create a loving home. There was a family that supported her when gymnastics changed from something she enjoyed into a demanding career. Bilesâ story also shows why success should not always be measured from the moment someone wins something. Sometimes the most important victory happens years before anyone is watching. For Biles, that turning point came when Ron and Nellie gave her a permanent home. It gave her the opportunity to grow, find gymnastics, develop her talent and eventually become the athlete the world knows today. Her words also carry a message for children who may be going through difficult situations. A difficult beginning does not necessarily decide how the rest of a personâs life will look. The right people, the right support and the right opportunities can change the direction of a life. That is what makes Bilesâ quote so meaningful. She is not saying that adoption alone made her successful. She is recognizing what that moment gave her: stability, love, encouragement and the chance to discover her own potential. Before Simone Biles became an Olympic champion, she was a young girl who needed someone to believe in her. Ron and Nellie Biles did exactly that, and the life that followed became far bigger than anyone could have imagined. title: Lovlina turns 29 with golden punch, ends Assamâs 60-yr wait by matching Baruah feat
text: Lovlina Borgohain after winning the gold medal Guwahati: Olympic medallist Lovlina Borgohain ended Assam âs six-decade wait for an individual Asian Games gold medal on Friday, defeating Chinaâs Bao Ziyi 5-0 in the womenâs 75kg boxing final at the Aichi-Nagoya Games. The victory, secured on her 29th birthday, made Lovlina only the second Assamese athlete to win individual gold at the Asian Games after Bhogeswar Baruah, who triumphed in the 800m at the 1966 Bangkok Games. Baruahâs winning time of 1:49.4 was a Games record and earned him the distinction of becoming Assamâs first Arjuna Award recipient. Assam did win an Asian Games gold in the intervening years, with sprinter Hima Das finishing first in the mixed 4x400m relay at Jakarta 2018. Lovlinaâs triumph, however, is the stateâs first individual Asian Games gold since Baruahâs historic victory. For Lovlina, the medal completes a remarkable comeback after her quarterfinal loss in Paris olympics in 2024. Lovlina is only the second woman Indian boxer after Mary Kom to combine an Olympic medal, a World Championships title, an Asian Championships title and an Asian Games gold. She is also the first Indian woman boxer to reach back-to-back Asian Games finals, converting her 2023 silver into gold in 2026. Her father, Tiken Borgohain, said the win was especially emotional because Lovlina had wanted to change the colour of the silver she won at the previous Games. âToday also happens to be her birthday. She had spoken about winning this gold,â he said, thanking those who had prayed for her success. CM Himanta Biswa Sarma , while congratulating Lovlina, said, âThere can be no bigger gift to oneself on a birthday than bagging the ultimate honour for the country. We are so proud of you, Lovlina! The nation is proud of you and celebrates this achievement. Assam awaits your glorious return.â Assam Police on its official X handle wrote: âOur very own DSP Lovlina Borgohain strikes GOLD!..Youâve made Assam Police, Assam and the entire Nation proud!.â Lovlina was appointed as a deputy superintendent of police in Assam Police in 2022 following her medal at Tokyo Olympics. title: Who is Katy Marchant? Olympic gold medallist retires at 33 ahead of LA28 Olympics to return to family farm with husband Rob
text: Katy Marchant (via Getty) Katy Marchant has announced her retirement from professional cycling at the age of 33. The Leeds-born track cyclist leaves the sport after a career filled with Olympic, World Championship and European success. Her biggest achievement came at the Paris 2024 Olympics, where she won gold as part of Great Britainâs womenâs team sprint squad. Marchant also won an Olympic bronze medal in the individual sprint at Rio 2016. After 13 years at the top level, the mother of two has decided not to continue chasing a place at the Los Angeles 2028 Olympics. Instead, she will spend more time with her husband Rob and their children on the family farm. Who is Katy Marchant? Katy Marchant was one of Britainâs leading track cyclists for more than a decade. She represented Team GB at three Olympic Games and collected medals across some of the biggest competitions in the sport. Her first Olympic medal came at Rio 2016. Marchant won bronze in the individual sprint and established herself as one of Britainâs leading track sprinters. Eight years later, she reached another major milestone at Paris 2024. Marchant helped Great Britain win gold in the womenâs team sprint. The victory completed one of the biggest goals of her career. Her successful 2024 campaign did not end with Olympic gold. Marchant also won gold medals at the World Championships and European Championships. However, her career was also marked by a serious crash in late 2024. She later battled back to professional cycling. Marchant continued competing after becoming a mother of two. She had given birth to her second son a year before this summerâs Commonwealth Games in Glasgow. At the 2026 Commonwealth Games, she won silver in the team sprint. But the event also gave her a feeling that her professional career could be coming to an end. Marchant said, âIâve done this for 13 years, I am 33, and I have achieved more than I could have dreamt of.â She also explained that retirement had become clear to her, âWhen I thought about retirement in the past, I said to myself: âYouâll know when you know. title: New beginnings, new heroes: Women lead India's charge as a new generation shines in Nagoya
text: Lovlina Borgohain and Neeru Dhanda (Image credit: X) As Neeru Dhanda led the Indian contingent out for one last time at the Mizuho Park Athletic Stadium on Sunday night, it was symbolic of how Indiaâs Asian Games campaign had unfolded over the past two weeks. The women had come to the fore - packing punches, vaulting to new heights, lifting weights, taking aim, towering over opponents with sixes, blazing the track, finding the fairway and hitting the back of the net. Indiaâs final tally of 85 medals, including 21 gold, may represent a drop from the 106 medals and 28 golds won in Hangzhou. But numbers alone cannot tell the story of these Games. Watch Lovlina Borgohainâs golden birthday: Asian Games medal after comeback There were path-breakers everywhere, athletes who pushed through glass ceilings that had stood for years. The aftermath will bring reviews, reflections, deliberations and reports. But before the analysis begins, it is only fair to celebrate those who made these Games count. For almost 12 days, the Indian gold rush had remained subdued. Then, just as the sun finally began showing up in Nagoya, the floodgates opened. Eleven gold medals came in the final two days, transforming what had threatened to become a disappointing campaign into a collection of stories about guts, resilience and glory. Dhanda, the 26-year-old from Sangatpura in Haryana, had set the tone by winning Indiaâs first individual gold of these Games in the womenâs trap event. The women went on to win 11 gold medals, apart from the three secured in mixed events. The contingent had 83 debutants, who accounted for 41 of Indiaâs 85 medals â a clear indication of a changing guard across several sports. But if one athlete were to be picked as the face of that change, it would be difficult to look beyond 17-year-old Kumkum Mohod. The Maharashtra archer won two gold medals and a silver, but her biggest achievement went beyond the medal tally. She ended South Koreaâs two-decade domination of the womenâs recurve events by becoming the first Indian to win individual recurve gold at the Asian Games. It did not take her long to make the biggest stage of her young career her own. Even her Korean opponent Oh Ye-jin, whom Kumkum beat for the individual gold, was left impressed. âFor a 17-year-old, she is very composed and has a very bright future,â Oh said. Another teenager, Prithika Pradeep, also emerged with two gold medals, adding to the sense that a new generation is beginning to announce itself. Pranavi Urs became the first Indian woman to win an Asian Games golf gold. Behind every medal was a story of humble beginnings, survival in sport, societal pressures overcome and personal tragedies endured. That made the successes more than just entries in a medal table. The comeback girls They were not newcomers to the big stage. They had competed at the biggest of them all â the Olympics. But Nagoya offered unfinished business. Lovlina Borgohain had contemplated walking away from boxing after a difficult phase post the 2024 Paris Olympics. Instead, she returned to punch her way to gold. Parveen Hooda, returning after a doping ban, produced her own golden comeback. The bronze she had won in Hangzhou and subsequently lost became gold in Nagoya. Mirabai Chanu did not win gold, but her silver in the 49kg category had the weight of a championâs achievement. It also completed her Asian Games medal collection. Golden standards The womenâs kabaddi team survived a tense battle against Iran. The womenâs hockey team ended a 44-year wait for Asian Games gold. And Harmanpreet Kaur and her team ensured that cricketâs gold returned to India. Yet, for all the celebration, there were glaring blanks. Manu Bhaker, one of Indiaâs biggest sporting heroes, returned without a medal. There were plenty of nearmisses and some disastrous outings. Indiaâs badminton return of a solitary bronze was another disappointment, particularly with a strong menâs doubles combination of Satwiksairaj Rankireddy and Chirag Shetty, PV Sindhu and Lakshya Sen in the squad. title: Simone Bilesâ LA 2028 comeback in doubt as Joscelyn Roberson tells her to âstay with your husbandâ
text: Simone Bilesâ LA 2028 comeback in doubt as Joscelyn Roberson tells her to âstay with your husbandâ Simone Biles is still undecided about competing at the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics, but a message from former US teammate Joscelyn Roberson has given her another reason to think about life away from gymnastics. Roberson reminded Biles that she does not have to return and can instead stay home with her husband, Jonathan Owens. Biles, 29, has not ruled out a fourth Olympic appearance, and she recently tested a difficult skill in the gym that made a comeback feel possible. But the decision also involves her family plans, the demands of training and what she wants from the next stage of her career. Simone Biles quotes Joscelyn Roberson on LA 2028 Olympic return Biles has competed at three Olympics, starting with Rio 2016 before Tokyo 2020 and Paris 2024. A return in Los Angeles would give her a chance to compete at a home Olympics and become the first American gymnast to appear at four Olympic Games. But Roberson, who was Bilesâ teammate and roommate, is not trying to convince her to return. Instead, she has been encouraging Biles to enjoy her life away from the sport. âHey babes, youâre good. Remember, you donât have to come back. Stay at your house and stay with your husband,â Biles quoted Roberson to The Associated Press. Biles has admitted that she is still trying to work out what she wants. In September, she told The Associated Press, âI feel like itâs kind of in the works which way Iâm leaning towards.â Her decision is also tied to her life with Owens and her plans to start a family. Biles said those personal matters have to be considered alongside the physical demands of preparing for another Olympics. âI am getting to the age of 30 where we start to talk about, âWhat does your reproduction cycle â¦ whatâs going on in there? What does that look like? How healthy is it?ââ she said. âAnd so I think these are major things that are on the table at my age that I have to take into consideration and weigh those options and what that looks like and when we want to start a family.â Simone Biles says recent gym attempt made decision harder There is also a part of Biles that still wants to know what she can do. She recently went into the gym with her sister Adria and attempted a double layout. She landed it and said she was surprised by how little fear she felt. And of course I was like, what the h**l? That wasnât that bad. Like, I wasnât as scared as I thought I was going to be. And that scared me more with the decision.â Biles also knows that a return could affect younger gymnasts competing for places on the 2028 US Olympic team. âI know some of the girls would be like, âOh no, Simoneâs coming back,ââ Biles said. Months later, the possibility is still open. âIâve experienced so much and Iâd done so much, so itâs like, I also have to be doing it for the right reasons,â Biles said. title: Elite World Cup referees for India friendlies
text: Ilgiz Tantashev is among Asiaâs most renowned referee Kolkata: The All India Football Federation (AIFF) has enlisted officials from Uzbekistan for Indiaâs friendlies against Brazil and Uruguay, with three of the four referees having officiated at the FIFA World Cup 2026. One of the officials, Ilgiz Tantashev, is among Asiaâs most renowned referee, having officiated at the 2024 Summer Olympics in Paris, FIFA Club World Cup, two AFC Asian Cups, three AFC U-23 Asian Cups, AFC Champions League Elite since 2015, and six iterations of the AFC Cup. The Uzbek referee, however, was in the eye of a storm after his handling of the fierce contest between France and Paraguay at the recent World Cup. Officiating his third group-stage match, Tantashev failed to book a single Paraguay player in their fiery defeat, promoting France to say their players were lucky to escape without any serious injuries after being targeted with aggressive challenges throughout the game. âWe asked Uzbekistan to send their referees because they officiated at the World Cup,â said a senior official. âThey are experienced, good enough to handle teams of Brazil and Uruguayâs stature.â Given his experience at the highest level, Tantashev is expected to take charge of the friendly against Brazil, while Rustam Lutfulin will be the fourth official. The roles will be reversed for the clash against Uruguay three days later. Andrey Tsapenko and Timur Gaynullin, both of whom were also at the World Cup, will be the assistant referees. Indiaâs Arunava Bhattacharya has been appointed as the match commissioner. The senior official has overseen conduct of over 50 international matches as Asian Football Confederation (AFC) match commissioner since 2019 and FIFA since 2023. title: Golden girl Poovamma seeks parity in recognition from state govt
text: MR Poovamma, who won a gold medal in the 4x400 relay at the 2026 Asian Games, being welcomed at Mangaluru International Airport on Friday Mangaluru: Asian Games gold medallist MR Poovamma on Thursday voiced her disappointment over the lack of recognition and support accorded to Karnataka athletes, saying there was a marked difference in the treatment of sportspersons from the state and those from elsewhere. Poovamma, who was felicitated at the City Centre Mall here for her latest international achievement, said the issue had left her with a sense of dissatisfaction despite the pride of winning another Asian Games medal. Acknowledging her concern, member of the Legislative Council Ivan DâSouza, who was present at Poovammaâs felicitation ceremony, said Karnatakaâs athletes should receive the same recognition as sportspersons from other states. âWe are incredibly proud of MR Poovamma, but it is disheartening to see a lack of support and recognition for our homegrown champions. Our local athletes must be treated on par with those from other states, and we will fight tirelessly for this,â he said. DâSouza assured that he would raise the issue with the state govt to ensure due recognition for Karnataka athletes. Poovamma was part of Indiaâs gold-winning womenâs 4x400m relay team at the ongoing Asian Games in Aichi-Nagoya, along with Kiran Pahal, Prachi Choudhary and Vithya Ramraj. The quartet clocked 3:29.69 to win gold. She also won silver in the mixed 4x400m relay with Manu T S, Vishal T K and Vithya Ramraj. Recalling her journey, Poovamma said Mangaluru had been where she learnt the value of hard work and perseverance. âWithout the unwavering support of my family, I could never have reached the Asian Games podium,â she said. She also credited a long-term endurance-focused training strategy for her international performances and spoke of the sacrifices made by her parents to ensure that her training continued. âMy parents sacrificed everything to ensure my training never stopped,â she said. A prominent name on the international athletics circuit, Poovamma has represented India at the 2008 Beijing, 2016 Rio and 2024 Paris Olympics, competing in the womenâs 4x400m relay. title: "I would bleed": Simone Biles breaks down over painful skin battle that left her âmiserableâ before the Olympics
text: Simone Biles (Getty Images) Simone Biles has opened up about a deeply personal health struggle that continued for years while she trained and competed at the highest level. The Olympic champion revealed that persistent itching and flaking eventually became so severe that she would scratch until her skin bled. What she initially believed was dandruff later led to diagnoses of seborrheic dermatitis and eczema. Now, Biles is using her experience to encourage people dealing with similar symptoms to stop dismissing them and seek professional dermatological care. Simone Biles reveals how her skin condition affected her Biles said her symptoms began several years ago while she was preparing for the 2024 Paris Olympics. She first noticed itching and flaking around her scalp and assumed dandruff was the cause. Instead of immediately seeing a dermatologist, Biles tried several over-the-counter products. They did not provide the relief she hoped for, and the problem eventually spread beyond her scalp. âI was itching and flaking. I would itch so hard and use a comb that I would bleed. I was just like, âI canât live like this. Iâm itching. Iâm miserable. I feel uncomfortable. I need to see someone who can give me relief,â â Biles tells PEOPLE ahead of the campaign launch on Tuesday, Sept. 29. The symptoms became especially difficult during her Olympic journey. With millions watching her compete, Biles worried that the visible flaking would be noticed on television. âI didnât go to the dermatologist immediately because Iâm so busy,â she says. âI was always in the gym, I was always traveling, so I didnât take that step, but it finally got so bad. At the Olympics, I was flaking everywhere, so I was afraid that someone would see it on the TV... thatâs why I finally went.â Biles was eventually diagnosed with seborrheic dermatitis affecting her face and scalp, along with eczema on her arms. She now manages the conditions with prescribed treatments. Simone Biles wants others to seek professional help Biles is sharing her experience through the Skin to Believe In campaign, launched in partnership with Arcutis Biotherapeutics. Her goal is to help people recognise that persistent skin symptoms may need more than home remedies. Dr. Angela J. Lamb, a board-certified dermatologist who joined Biles for the discussion, said delayed diagnosis can make these conditions harder to manage. She also noted that severe scratching can create additional risks. âI think Simoneâs story really mirrors what I see with patients,â Dr. Lamb says. âThe delay in diagnosis only makes things worse. Simone should not have been having her scalp bleeding. Luckily she didnât get any infections from that, but sometimes that can lead to infection.â Lamb also addressed a common misunderstanding surrounding these conditions. Seborrheic dermatitis and eczema are not contagious, meaning they cannot simply be passed from one person to another through everyday contact. âItâs not an infection. Itâs not contagious,â says Dr. Lamb. âSo sharing combs with folks or a bed or a pillow, itâs not like youâre going to transfer it... and same for eczema or atopic dermatitis, itâs not an infection.â For Biles, opening up about the experience is about making it easier for others to ask for help. âOnce we know that we canât fix every problem on our own, itâs okay to get help,â she tells PEOPLE. âOnce we raise awareness, then they can get that relief that they deserve. Thatâs really what itâs about, not silently suffering. There is help out there for you.â Join conversation View All Comments â Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful Â· TOI community guidelines She has one simple message for anyone struggling with ongoing symptoms. âWe just have to take that first initiative to go see a dermatologist and to get that relief because they deserve that,â she says. âThese are the trusted professionals... theyâve worked their whole entire lives to treat people for these causes. Itâs just incredible that we have these resources.â âOnce you do, itâs so easy,â Biles adds, insisting, âYou just have to make the appointment.â Stay updated with the latest Asian Games 2026 news , check the Asian Games medal tally and complete Asian Games schedule . title: âFeels a little crazyâ: Double Olympic winner Tatjana Smith comes out of retirement, eyes LA Olympics 2028 goal after âmissing the waterâ
text: Tatjana Smith (via Getty) Tatjana Smith has announced a surprise return to competitive swimming after initially retiring following the Paris Olympics 2024. The double Olympic champion is now targeting the 2028 Los Angeles Games, where she hopes to compete in the newly added 50m breaststroke event. Smith is South Africaâs most decorated Olympian. She won 200m breaststroke gold and 100m silver at Tokyo 2020 before adding 100m breaststroke gold and 200m silver at Paris 2024. However, her comeback is not guaranteed. Smith says LA 2028 is her goal, but she must first rebuild her race and qualify for the Games. Tatjana Smith targets new 50m breaststroke challenge Tatjana Smith initially walked away from swimming after the Paris Olympics. She had already achieved major success across two Olympic Games and was a former 200m breaststroke world record holder. However, retirement did not last as she expected. The South African swimmer said she eventually realised that she missed competing and being in the pool. That feeling helped convince her to begin another chapter in her career. The decision also comes with a completely different Olympic target. Smith is focusing on the 50m breaststroke, a new Olympic distance that gives her an opportunity to compete in an event without a long history of her own. âItâs definitely a new challenge, a new event, a new race, but also a new me,â she said. The change is significant for Smith. Her biggest Olympic achievements came in the 100m and 200m breaststroke events. At Tokyo 2020, she won the 200m breaststroke gold medal and took silver in the 100m. Three years later, she added another Olympic title in Paris. Smith won gold in the 100m breaststroke and finished with silver in the 200m. Those results made her one of the most successful swimmers in South African Olympic history. Now, she wants to create a different story in the shorter event. âFor the first time, I am choosing swimming and I am choosing the event and I am choosing a new event, that has no history but to try and write some new history. LA 2028 is the goal. It is not a promise. I still have to build a race, qualify and earn my place back on those blocksâ, she said in a video. title: A 42-year-old record, a truckerâs daughter: Vithya Ramraj breaks PT Ushaâs mark and rewrites history
text: Indiaâs Vithya Ramraj celebrates with the national flag after winning bronze in the womenâs 400m hurdles at the Asian Games 2026 in Aichi-Nagoya. Ramraj clocked a personal best of 54.75 seconds to break PT Ushaâs 42-year-old national record of 55.42 seconds, set at the 1984 Los Angeles Olympics. The image also features Usha from her competitive days, highlighting the record Ramraj finally surpassed. Vithya Ramraj had already made history by matching PT Usha's 42-year-old national record, and three years later, she finally broke it. The 27-year-old Indian hurdler clocked a personal best of 54.75 seconds to win bronze in the women's 400m hurdles at the Asian Games 2026 in Aichi-Nagoya, breaking the national record that had belonged to legendary Usha since August 1984. In 2023, at the Hangzhou Asian Games, Ramraj had clocked 55.42 seconds to claim bronze and equal Usha's mark set at the Los Angeles Olympics on August 8, 1984. That record had stood for 39 years at the time. Watch Vithya Ramraj targets Asian Games gold, eyes 53-54 seconds in 400m hurdles Asian Games Full Coverage | Medal Tally | Schedule Now, in Nagoya, Ramraj went one better, shaving 0.67 seconds off the old national record en route to her second individual Asian Games 2026 medal. Her compatriot Anu Raghavan finished fifth in 55.88 seconds, also recording a personal best. The 26-year-old was part of Indiaâs silver-medal winning mixed 4x400m relay team earlier in the Games, running the anchor leg and producing a strong finish to help India hold on to second place. The medal also adds to Ramraj's Asian Games record. She had won bronze in the women's 400m hurdles at the 2023 Hangzhou Games to go with to silver medals in the 4x400 relay and mixed events. A truckerâs daughter who refused to give up Vithya grew up in a modest family, with her father working as a truck driver. Her mother enrolled Vithya and her twin sister Nithya, a 110m hurdler, at the Sports Development Authority of Tamil Nadu hostel in Erode. Athletics was not a carefully planned choice. âAt a parent-teacher meeting, my PE teacher suggested sports for us. My mother chose athletics since it offered more visibility than team games. The sports hostel also helped, as my family couldnât afford the expenses,â Vithya had told Times of India in 2025. After school, Vithya pursued a BBA degree under the sports quota and joined the national camp at NIS Patiala in 2018. But progress was slow. She later moved to Chennai in 2022, while a Covid infection and appendicitis surgery disrupted her preparations for the Tokyo Olympic trials. âIn Patiala, I didnât get personal training, struggled with the food, and didnât know Hindi. While preparing for the Tokyo Olympic trials, I got Covid and later underwent appendicitis surgery. I had to leave camp and return home,â she had told Times of India. Her twin Nithya, who was training under coach Nehpal Singh Rathore, then helped bring Vithya into the setup. Until 2022, Vithya had primarily concentrated on the 400m flat, but Rathore encouraged her to pursue both events and set her sights on Ushaâs record. title: Tajinderpal Singh Toor misses third straight Asian Games gold, dedicates silver to 10-month-old daughter
text: Image credit: Instagram Tajinderpal Singh Toor came close to a third straight Asian Games gold in the menâs shot put but settled for silver in Nagoya. The 31-year-old threw 20.64 metres, finishing behind Iranâs Mohammadreza Tayebise, who took gold with 20.81 metres and broke Toorâs previous Games record. For the Indian champion, the medal carried a deeper meaning. He dedicated it to his 10-month-old daughter, calling her the lucky charm who changed his familyâs story after two difficult losses. A medal dedicated to his daughter Toor spoke about the personal weight behind the silver. âThis medal is for my daughter Rabab Kaur Toor. My wife lost two babies during her pregnancy, in 2022 and in 2024. Rabab has been the lucky mascot for me,â he told The Indian Express from Nagoya. 22 Sept 2026 | 14:56 Does your child tell you everything about school? What helps them open up? Rabab was born last November. Her arrival brought joy after the pain of two miscarriages that had left the coupleâs dream of becoming parents shattered. Holding the Tricolour and folding his hands in prayer once the final positions were confirmed, Toor made clear that the medal belonged to the little girl who had become his source of strength. A bittersweet day on the field Toorâs best throw of 20.64 metres was solid, yet it was not enough to defend the title he had won in Jakarta in 2018 and again in Hangzhou. In 2018 he set a Games record of 20.75 metres. That mark was bettered on Saturday by the Iranian athleteâs 20.81-metre effort. When it became clear he would finish second, Toor responded with quiet dignity. He posed for photographs with the national flag and acknowledged the result. The day was bittersweet, but it still placed him on the podium for a third consecutive Asian Games . Answering doubts after a difficult season Earlier this year Toor had finished only third at the Inter-State National Championships in Bhubaneswar, behind Karamveer Singh and Samardeep Gill. Questions about his form had begun to surface. âPeople had started talking after my performance at the Inter-State. This medal is an answer to all those who questioned my ability. Winning a third Asian Games medal is a special feeling,â said Toor, who hails from Khosa Pando village in Moga district. Karamveer, the other Indian in the final, placed tenth. On the biggest stage of the season, Toor delivered when it counted. Competing through a career of injuries Injuries have followed Toor throughout his career. Before the Commonwealth Games he suffered a Grade-One calf tear. An MRI confirmed the damage after the event. âPrior to CWG, I suffered a calf strain, and post the CWG, the MRI revealed that it was a Grade-One tear. I manage by adjusting technique. My coach MS Dhillon tells me never to stop,â he explained. The list is longer. A groin injury before the Tokyo Olympics, pain when he set the Asian Games record, a calf muscle tear at the Asian Championships in Bangkok, a knee problem before Hangzhou, and an ankle injury six months before Paris. âMy career and injuries go together,â he said. This year he has crossed 20 metres nine times and recorded one throw beyond 21 metres. His personal best remains 21.77 metres from 2023. He still believes more is possible. âI know I have a 22m throw in me.â For an athlete who has repeatedly returned from setbacks, the silver in Nagoya felt like another hard-earned step forward and one he was glad to share with his daughter. title: How Stephen Curry built his $350 million fortune? His $62.6M salary, $400M Li-Ning deal and lavish investments
text: Stephen Curry. Image via: Ezra Shaw /Getty Images Steph Curry has turned a remarkable NBA career into a vast business empire. The Golden State Warriors star is now estimated to have a net worth of $350 million , while his 2026-27 NBA salary stands at $62.6 million . His wealth extends far beyond basketball, with major endorsement deals, media ventures, investments and his own brand adding to his income. After more than a decade at the top of the sport, Curry has also secured another major contract that could take his career NBA earnings close to $650 million by 2029. Stephen Curry net worth and NBA salary Stephen Curry's current financial position reflects how much his value has grown since entering the NBA in 2009. The Warriors selected him seventh overall in the draft, and his first professional contract was modest compared with the deals he would later command. His breakthrough extension came in 2012, when Golden State gave him a four-year contract worth about $44 million. At the time, Curry was still dealing with concerns about recurring ankle problems. The contract soon became one of the most valuable bargains in NBA history. Curry developed into an MVP, won championships and changed the way teams approached three-point shooting while playing under that deal. His earning power changed dramatically in 2017. Curry signed a five-year, $201.2 million contract, becoming the first NBA player to agree to a deal worth more than $200 million. Four years later, he went even further. His four-year, $215 million extension made him the first player in league history to sign two contracts worth more than $200 million. Curry's latest extension arrived in September 2026. The two-year agreement is worth $116 million and begins with the 2027-28 season. It includes a player option for 2028-29. Based on those contracts, Curry's career NBA salary could reach approximately $648.7 million through the 2028-29 season if he exercises the option. Stephen Curry's $400 million Li-Ning deal NBA salary is only one part of Stephen Curry's financial story. His endorsement portfolio has become just as important to his overall wealth. Curry started his professional career with Nike before moving to Under Armour in 2013. His rise to superstardom helped turn that relationship into a much larger business opportunity, eventually leading to Curry Brand. That partnership later changed. Curry Brand became independent after the relationship between Curry and Under Armour ended in 2025, although Under Armour continued selling previously developed products during 2026. Curry then landed another huge deal. In June 2026, he signed a 10-year endorsement agreement with Li-Ning worth more than $400 million . The partnership covers more than basketball shoes. It includes apparel, lifestyle products, golf and plans to expand Curry Brand retail operations in China and the United States. The agreement is worth more than $40 million per year on average, giving Curry another major source of income outside his Warriors contract. Celebrity Net Worth estimates that Curry also earns around $30 million annually from endorsements , although the exact amount can vary from year to year. His commercial portfolio includes partnerships with companies such as Fanatics, Google, JPMorgan Chase, Panini, Rakuten and 2K Sports. Stephen Curry's business empire beyond basketball Curry has also built businesses that give him influence away from the court. His wider ventures operate under Thirty Ink, covering areas such as media, branding, investments and philanthropy. One of his best-known projects is Unanimous Media, which Curry founded with Erick Peyton in 2018. The company works across film, television, documentaries, publishing and podcasts. Its projects often focus on sports, family and faith. Curry has also explored entertainment in front of the camera. He played a fictionalised version of himself in the Peacock comedy "Mr. Throwback" and released the book "Shot Ready" in 2025. His business interests also include Gentleman's Cut bourbon and Underrated, a platform designed to give overlooked young athletes greater access to competition and development opportunities. That business approach has helped Curry build an identity that reaches well beyond his basketball statistics. His career has become a combination of sport, entertainment, branding and investment. Stephen Curry's career, championships and real estate Stephen Curry's wealth would not be possible without the basketball career that created his global profile. He has won four NBA championships , two regular-season MVP awards and the 2022 NBA Finals MVP. He was also the first unanimous MVP in NBA history after his historic 2015-16 campaign. That season remains one of the most memorable individual years in modern NBA history. Curry averaged 30.1 points per game, made 402 three-pointers and helped Golden State win 73 regular-season games. In 2021, he passed Ray Allen to become the NBA's career leader in made three-pointers. He later reached another historic milestone by becoming the first player to make 4,000 regular-season three-pointers in March 2025. Curry added an Olympic gold medal to his rÃ©sumÃ© at the 2024 Paris Games, helping Team USA win the men's basketball tournament. Join conversation View All Comments â Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful Â· TOI community guidelines His success has also shaped his property portfolio. Curry and his wife, Ayesha, have completed several major real estate transactions in California. Among their notable purchases was a $31 million Atherton estate bought in 2019. They later sold another Atherton property for $29.1 million in May 2026 after purchasing it for $30 million in 2020. The couple have also owned homes in Oakland, Orinda, Walnut Creek, Alamo and Menlo Park, along with a luxury condominium in San Francisco. Away from business and basketball, Curry and Ayesha have focused heavily on philanthropy. They founded the Eat. Learn. Play. Foundation, which supports children through programmes involving food, education and physical activity. Curry's financial rise therefore tells a larger story than a list of contracts. His NBA salary created the foundation, but endorsements, entrepreneurship, media and investments have helped turn one of basketball's greatest shooting careers into a much broader financial empire.
