title: '15 years ... I waited for long': Krishna Jayasankar set for her India moment at Asian Games
text: Krishna Jaisankar (Image credit: Agencies) Whenever Krishna Jayasankar gets some time, she opens her kit bag and looks at the badge on her T-shirt. It has one word written on it: INDIA. Every time she looks at it, her eyes get moist. But there is also a sense of confidence that builds within her. After waiting for 15 years, Krishna knows that when she finally wears the India jersey in Japan, it will mean much more than simply making her Asian Games debut. Watch 'I'm walking in as a medal contender, not a participant': Krishna Jaisankar on her Asian Games debut For the 23-year-old shot putter, the jersey will represent 15 years of ups and downs, missed opportunities, injuries and countless moments when she had to pick herself up and start again. âIt's a surreal feeling. I just can't wait to don that jersey in Japan. 15 years.... I waited for long and yes, I have earned it. I am very appreciative, like I'm very grateful for the opportunity and to be able to finally put Team India on my back,â Krishna told TimesofIndia.com in an exclusive interview. After missing out on selection several times, Krishna finally broke through and earned her place in the Indian team for the Asian Games 2026. Now, as she prepares to travel to Japan, the Indian shot putter wants to leave the old disappointments behind and write a new chapter - one that she hopes will end with a medal. Her message to herself when she reaches Japan is simple. âAll right, it's showtime,â Krishna said. A long road to the India jersey Krishna's journey has never been an easy one. There were moments when she wanted to give up. She left India at a young age, first moving to Jamaica and later to the United States, as she looked for opportunities to develop as an athlete. Then came the Commonwealth Games opportunity. Krishna was among the favourites to make it to the big event, but a hamstring injury disrupted her plans. She tore her hamstring just three weeks before the event. Yet, she returned to competition and managed to qualify for the Asian Games. She also became the national champion after 15 years. âI just think the fighter mentality that I have. Never to give up. Never to settle. Setbacks are meant for something. Setbacks are supposed to mould you, but not define you,â she said. Paris 2024 became a turning point The biggest setback came in 2024. Marred by injuries, Krishna missed the Paris Olympics. But the difficult phase also forced her to look closely at herself and rethink the way she was approaching her career. She began paying more attention to her nutrition, sleep and recovery. She also started spending more time reflecting and talking to herself. âIt was a very rough period for me,â she said. âI left my country, left my family, left my comfort zone. What does my opportunity cost? What am I getting back? I'm not making the team, I'm not competing. Why am I getting injured?â she said. That period eventually changed her approach towards her ultimate goal - representing India. Instead of looking too far ahead, Krishna decided to take things one step at a time. âIf you've got a dream, you've got to protect it. You have a dream, you've got to protect it,â Krishna said. From a basketball family to shot put Krishna grew up in a sporting family. Her parents, Prasanna and Jay Shankar, have been involved in basketball, and she closely watched the work they put into developing the sport. Her mother has also been a national selector for Indian basketball. But Krishna eventually chose athletics and found her own identity in shot put. âI think my inspiration was within my corners, which is my family. Whatever I am today it is because of their support. I wanted to choose a different sport and I did and I am really happy about it,â she said. âThanks to the Reliance Foundation, the Athletics Federation of India, the Sports Development Authority of Tamil Nadu, and everyone in Tamil Nadu. Everybody has supported me and believed in me,â the 23-year-old said. Chasing Asian Games glory Making her Team India debut at the Asian Games is a special moment for Krishna. But she does not want the excitement of finally making the team to overshadow her bigger target - winning a medal. Once she is in Japan, she wants to treat the competition like any other championship. âNow it's go time, there is no look back. I am looking forward, looking ahead in the future,â she said. âIt's going to be a show, man. It's going to be a show from all sectors of athletics. Let it be track, let it be field, we're going to put up a show. All we ask in return, support us. Keep us in your prayers,â Krishan said. Olympics - the ultimate dream For Krishna, the Asian Games is not the end goal. It is a start. Her bigger dream is the Los Angeles 2028 Olympics. She carries an Olympic chain with her even though she is yet to compete at the Games. For her, it is a reminder of where she wants to go. âI'm not an Olympian, but every single day I aspire to be one. I'm confident now I can say that that dream is no longer a dream. It's like, I'm converting it to be a reality,â she said. The chase for 18 metres Krishna won a gold medal at the National Federation Cup 2026 and, in the process, broke her own record of 17.09m. She won the top prize with a personal best throw of 17.35m. Now, Krishna has set herself the target of crossing 18 metres. She believes the Asian Games 2026 will be a great platform to achieve that feat while also challenging for the gold medal. âI am getting closer,â she said. âBut again, it's very important to believe in the process. No better place to do it than Japan. Let's have a PB in Japan. I know I am a medal contender,â she said. âSo, the mindset also is walking into the thing and be like, you know what, I'm walking in as a medal contender, not as a participant,â she said. Bodyshaming: Turning comments into strength Krishna has been muscular since childhood. Her appearance sometimes made her uncomfortable. She felt that she did not fit what she believed was society's traditional idea of how a woman should look. âI didn't even know the meaning of body shaming until, you know, somebody came and told me, hey, somebody's body shaming you,â she said. But over the years, Krishna learned to see her body differently. The same body that some people made fun of became the body that helped her break records and earn her place in Team India. âTo show the world, to show the society, that the body that you're making fun of and making me feel that I'm ashamed of is the body that's helping me break records, is the body that's helping me debut for Team India at the Asian Games,â she said. Her message to young girls is direct. Join conversation View All Comments â Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful Â· TOI community guidelines âBe confident in who you are. Do not change yourself for somebody. She also has another message: do not live for other people's approval. Do not seek validation from people because again, comparison is a thief of joy,â she said. Poll Vote & Share your view Which aspect of Krishna journey do you find most inspiring? Her long wait for recognition Her ability to overcome injuries Her confidence in her body Her dedication to the sport 3k+ users shared opinion today 5k+ users already voted today 3k+ users shared opinion today Share Opinion 'Dreams do come true' With 15 years of pain now behind her, Krishna is ready to write a new chapter in Japan. When she steps into the throwing circle with the shot in her hand, the 23-year-old will perhaps remember the 18-year-old version of herself who first dared to dream of representing India. Asked what she would say to the 18-year-old Krishna, the 23-year-old replied: âDreams do come trueâ. âKnow that your story is not just your journey. It's a story of so many untold stories. There are so many people that look up to you. If you have a dream, you bloody protect it,â Krishna signed off. title: Two gold at 13: Yu Zidiâs rise and Summer McIntosh rivalry dominate swimming talk, but youngest Asian Games record remains unclear
text: Yu Zidi (Reuters/AP Photo) At just 13, Yu Zidi is already swimming towards a rivalry that could define the next era of women's swimming. The Chinese teenager claimed her second gold medal at the Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games on Monday, winning the women's 200m individual medley in 2:06.10 â a time that took her to within 0.40 seconds of the world record held by Canadian Olympic champion Summer McIntosh. The result has only intensified the anticipation around a potential Yu-McIntosh showdown. The two could meet as early as next year's World Aquatics Championships in Budapest, before the spotlight turns to the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics, where Yu would still be only 15. McIntosh, who won three individual gold medals at the Paris Olympics in 2024, owns the world records in all three events Yu is targeting: 2:01.65 in the 200m butterfly, 2:05.70 in the 200m individual medley and 4:23.65 in the 400m individual medley. Watch TOISA Spotlight | Miraj Ahmed Khan on Olympic gold, setbacks, Rio 2016 and the fight that continues Yu closes in on McIntoshâs world record Yu's latest gold came less than 24 hours after she won the 200m butterfly in a Games-record 2:05.08. She will also compete in the 400m individual medley later this week. Her rapid rise has already taken her onto the biggest international stage. At the 2025 World Championships in Singapore, Yu competed at just 12 and finished fourth in all three individual events she entered. She also became the youngest-ever World Championships medallist by winning bronze as part of China's 4x200m freestyle relay team. Earlier this year, she added another eye-catching result by defeating American Regan Smith in the 200m butterfly at a meet in China. Smith had won silver in the event at the Paris Olympics. The comparisons with McIntosh are becoming increasingly difficult to ignore. Hong Kong's four-time Olympic medallist Siobhan Haughey said the emergence of swimmers like Yu reflects an exciting trend in the sport, pointing to McIntosh's own rise as a teenager. "When Summer first started she was also very young and swimming fast, so I think that's kind of the trend these days," Haughey said. Youngest Asiad gold medallist? Records don't have the answer Yu's achievements have naturally raised another question: is she the youngest athlete ever to win an Asian Games gold medal? For now, there is no definitive answer. Asian Games officials said records dating back to the inaugural edition in New Delhi in 1951 are incomplete, making it impossible to establish whether Yu is the youngest gold medallist in the history of the continental Games. She is not even the youngest competitor at Aichi-Nagoya. That distinction is believed to belong to 11-year-old Japanese esports competitor Yuki Kurihara. So while Yu is making history in the pool, the broader age record remains unresolved. Join conversation View All Comments â Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful Â· TOI community guidelines Chinaâs swimming machine keeps producing stars Yu's emergence also underlines China's extraordinary depth in Asian swimming. China won a record 28 swimming gold medals at the Hangzhou Asian Games in 2023, finishing well ahead of South Korea's six and Japan's five. The Chinese dominance has continued in Aichi-Nagoya, with the country winning five of the seven swimming golds on Monday after taking six of seven on Sunday. But Yu's story is bigger than China's medal tally. At an age when most swimmers are still developing towards senior international competition, she is already challenging the world's fastest and being discussed in the same breath as McIntosh. For now, McIntosh remains ahead on the stopwatch. But with Yu only 13, the gap is already shrinking â and the swimming world may be watching the beginning of a rivalry that could stretch all the way to Los Angeles. title: Bigger than the Paris Olympics: Asian Games 2026 kicks off with 11,000 athletes, 43 sports and some very different games
text: Glimpses from Asian Games 2026 opening ceremony. (Reuters Photos) The Asian Games are officially underway in Aichi-Nagoya, Japan, on Saturday and the numbers alone tell part of the story: this is a sporting event that is bigger than the Paris Olympics in athlete participation, while also offering a programme that looks markedly different from the world's biggest multi-sport spectacle. More than 11,000 athletes are expected to compete at the 20th Asian Games, compared with about 10,700 at the 2024 Paris Olympics. That does not make the Asian Games bigger than the Olympics in prestige or global reach. But by the sheer number of athletes taking part, the continental showpiece has once again crossed the Olympic mark. And the scale becomes even clearer when the programme is considered. Watch Asian Games: Sehdev Yadav reveals how SAI arranged rooms for Indian athletes A total of 43 sports featured at Aichi-Nagoya, with athletes from 45 countries and regions competing from September 19 to October 4. The Games also include an OCA Refugee Team. The official opening ceremony took place on Saturday, but competition had already been underway for more than a week in some disciplines. Basketball began on September 10, while football also started well before the ceremony, underlining one of the biggest differences between the Asian Games and the Olympics: the enormous programme forces several competitions to begin before the formal curtain-raiser. ALSO READ: How Indiaâs Asian Games medal story has changed over two decades 11,000+ athletes: Bigger than Paris, but not quite Hangzhou The most striking number in Aichi-Nagoya is the athlete count. The Paris Olympics featured about 10,700 athletes. The Asian Games have more than 11,000, making the continental event larger in terms of athlete participation. Organisers have not released a final official athlete total, but they have indicated that more than 11,000 athletes are registered. The number could ultimately approach the scale of the previous Asian Games in Hangzhou, China, where roughly 12,000 athletes competed in 2023. That puts Aichi-Nagoya in an unusual position. It is larger than the Olympics by athlete participation, yet it is also a very different event in terms of geography, sporting culture and the range of disciplines on offer. The Games involve 45 countries and regions, stretching from Afghanistan to Yemen, along with the OCA Refugee Team. Japan has the largest delegation, with 933 athletes. China is sending 815 athletes. Hong Kong, despite having a population of about 7.5 million, has around 580 athletes. China arrives as the dominant force from the previous edition. At Hangzhou, it won 201 gold medals, followed by Japan with 52 and South Korea with 42. India was next with 28 gold medals, while Uzbekistan won 22 and Taiwan 19. Members of India's contingent walk during the opening ceremony. (AP Photo) 43 sports: Olympic favourites meet Asian specialities The sheer number of sports is another reason the Asian Games can feel unlike the Olympics. There are plenty of familiar Olympic disciplines. Athletics, swimming and football remain central parts of the programme, alongside other established sports. But then there are sports that give the Asian Games a distinctly regional identity. Kabaddi , for instance, is a major Asian team sport combining speed, strength and physical contact. Sepaktakraw blends elements of volleyball and football, while kurash, an ancient form of wrestling originating in Uzbekistan, adds another traditional discipline to the programme. ALSO READ: Five little-known sports India will compete in at Asian Games 2026 The organisers have also made room for newer and less familiar events. Teqball, a sport that combines elements of table tennis and football, is making its Asian Games debut. Virtual taekwondo, padel and mixed martial arts are also part of the programme. Esports returns after making its debut at the Hangzhou Asian Games. That combination is one of the defining features of the continental event. The programme can move from athletics and swimming â sports at the heart of the Olympics â to kabaddi, sepaktakraw, kurash and teqball, all within the same Games. It is also one reason the schedule has become so demanding. Basketball began on September 10, more than a week before Saturday's opening ceremony. The men's basketball semifinals were played on Friday, a day before the Games were officially declared open. Football has also been underway for several days. The first gold medal of the Games is expected on Sunday, with the triathlon among the events likely to produce the first champion. Swimming will also provide one of the early highlights, with China's 100m freestyle world-record holder Pan Zhanle and 13-year-old sensation Yu Zidi among the names attracting attention. Italian cruise ship Costa Serena, which serves as a floating temporary athletes' village. (Reuters Photo) A very different athletes' village The scale of the Asian Games is not limited to the competition programme. A total of 17,000 athletes and officials are being accommodated across Japan. But unlike the Olympics, Aichi-Nagoya does not have a traditional dedicated athletes' village. Instead, accommodation has been spread across hotels, converted wooden containers and a cruise ship. The Costa Serena, an Italian cruise ship, is functioning as a floating athletes' village and can accommodate up to 5,000 athletes and officials. The arrangement is part of a broader effort to contain costs after the Tokyo Olympics, for which Japan officially spent $13 billion. A government audit suggested the actual figure could have been twice that amount. But the unusual accommodation arrangements have also become one of the biggest talking points before the Games. Athletes and officials have complained about cramped rooms, small beds and logistical problems. Some delegations have reported leaks in the converted wooden accommodation, while others have raised concerns about transportation and long journeys to training venues. South Korea said the containers at Garden Pier were too cramped for its basketball players. Delegations have also complained about registration delays, late buses and athletes being sent to incorrect venues. India's cricket authorities arranged separate hotel accommodation for the men's team because of the tight allocation of beds. The problems have added to the scrutiny surrounding the build-up, although the Olympic Council of Asia has described them as teething difficulties. Asian Games Teqball (AP Photo) A 16-day sporting festival with a distinctly Asian identity The Asian Games will run until October 4, bringing together more than 11,000 athletes across 43 sports and 45 participating countries and regions. Nagoya, Japan's third-largest metropolitan area after Tokyo and Osaka, is hosting the event. The metropolitan area has a population of about 9.5 million and is located roughly 350 kilometres south of Tokyo. The opening ceremony at Mizuho Park Athletic Stadium provided the official starting point after a buildup marked by organisational problems. Emperor Naruhito formally declared the Games open, with Empress Masako, IOC president Kirsty Coventry and OCA president Sheikh Joaan bin Hamad Al Thani among the dignitaries present. Join conversation View All Comments â Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful Â· TOI community guidelines The ceremony's theme was âHarmonic Heart Beatâ, with a heart-shaped stage forming the centrepiece. Japan's father-and-son hammer-throwing duo Shigenobu Murofushi and Koji Murofushi jointly lit the cauldron at the conclusion of the torch relay. But the real measure of the Games will come over the next 16 days. The Asian Games may not carry the same global prestige as the Olympics, but Aichi-Nagoya demonstrates why they remain a sporting giant in their own right. By participation, the Asian Games are already bigger than Paris. By character, they are something entirely different. Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

title: The peaks are higher, the floor is rising: How Indiaâs Asian Games medal story has changed over two decades
text: India at the Asian Games (AI generated representative image) âAbki baar, sau paarâ was the rallying cry when India arrived at the Hangzhou Asian Games in September 2023. By the time the Games ended, it had become more than a slogan. India had crossed the 100-medal barrier for the first time in its Asian Games history, eventually finishing with 106 medals â 28 gold, 38 silver and 41 bronze. The 100th medal came through the women's kabaddi team, which defeated Chinese Taipei in the gold-medal match. It was India's biggest-ever medal haul at the Asian Games. Watch Asian Games 2026: Triple jumper Praveen Chithravel shifts focus after CWG silver medal But as India prepares for Aichi-Nagoya 2026, the more important story is not that India finally reached 100. It is that 100 no longer looks like an isolated miracle when viewed against Indian sport's larger trajectory. Hangzhou came after four consecutive editions in which India had already crossed 50 medals. India is becoming increasingly consistent. At the Asian Games, 50-plus medals have become the norm. At the Olympics, India has produced multiple medals at five consecutive editions for the first time. India remains an under-achiever. But the direction of travel is increasingly difficult to ignore. From occasional highs to a new Asian Games floor The strongest evidence of India's sporting evolution is perhaps the simplest: 53 > 65 > 57 > 70 > 106. Those are India's medal tallies at the last five completed Asian Games â Doha 2006, Guangzhou 2010, Incheon 2014, Jakarta 2018 and Hangzhou 2022. Before this run, India had crossed the 50-medal mark only twice in the previous 14 editions. Both came at home. At the inaugural Asian Games in New Delhi in 1951, India won 51 medals, including 15 gold. When New Delhi hosted the Games again in 1982, India collected 57 medals, including 13 gold. It took another 24 years for India to cross 50 again. Doha 2006 changed that. India won 53 medals in Qatar, finally breaking the half-century barrier away from home. It was followed by 65 in Guangzhou, 57 in Incheon and 70 in Jakarta and Palembang. Then came Hangzhou. The five consecutive 50-plus medal campaigns represent something India had never previously achieved at the continental event. That is arguably more significant than the 106 itself. A record medal tally can be an extraordinary peak. Five consecutive campaigns above a particular benchmark point towards a structural change. India has therefore entered Aichi-Nagoya with a different kind of expectation. Another 106 may be difficult, particularly with a 499-athlete contingent compared with the 661 who travelled to Hangzhou. But the benchmark has moved. The question is no longer simply whether India can cross 50. It is whether a 50-medal campaign would now be considered underwhelming. Hangzhou did not just breach 100 â it moved India's ceiling The jump from Jakarta to Hangzhou was extraordinary. India went from 70 medals in 2018 to 106 in Hangzhou, an increase of 36 medals. But the gold-medal jump arguably tells an even more significant story. India won 16 gold medals in Jakarta. In Hangzhou, it won 28. That is a 75 per cent increase in gold medals in one edition. And India's Hangzhou medal haul (106) was twice its Doha tally (53) over a 17-year period. The 100-medal barrier, therefore, should not be viewed in isolation. India's Asian Games ceiling has moved. It would be unrealistic to treat 106 as an automatic target every time India enters an Asian Games. But if India can produce another 70-plus campaign in Aichi-Nagoya, it would create another significant benchmark â three consecutive editions above 70. That could eventually make 70-plus the next version of what 50-plus has become today. One ceiling becomes the next floor. The medal base is becoming broader There is another part of the Asian Games story that is easy to miss when the conversation is dominated by the overall tally. India is not merely winning more medals. Its medal-producing ecosystem is gradually becoming broader. Historically, athletics has been India's biggest Asian Games sport by a considerable distance, with 283 medals. Shooting follows with 80, wrestling with 65, boxing with 61 and lawn tennis with 34. Athletics remains the giant. But recent editions have shown that India's medal ambitions are increasingly supported by multiple disciplines. Hangzhou was an excellent example. Athletics produced 29 medals, shooting contributed 22 and archery added nine. More importantly, shooting produced seven gold medals, one more than athletics' six. That shows the modern Indian medal base is not entirely dependent on its biggest traditional discipline. Wrestling, boxing, squash, archery and tennis have repeatedly provided medal opportunities, while athletics and shooting continue to contribute. The Commonwealth Games in Glasgow in 2026 provided another encouraging indicator for boxing, with Indian boxers winning 10 medals, including seven gold â their best-ever gold-medal haul at the event. India's sporting rise is becoming less dependent on one discipline or one generation. That is what a broader sporting ecosystem looks like. The Olympics tell a quieter story of progress If the Asian Games provide the dramatic version of India's sporting evolution, the Olympics provide the subtler one. India has won only 41 medals across its entire Olympic history â 10 gold, 10 silver and 21 bronze. For a country of India's size and sporting ambitions, that remains underwhelming. But look at when those medals have arrived. From Beijing 2008 through Paris 2024, India won 24 of its 41 Olympic medals â 58.5 per cent of its entire Olympic medal haul in just five editions. Beijing 2008 produced three medals. London 2012 delivered six. Rio 2016 dropped to two. Tokyo 2020 produced a record seven. Paris 2024 ended with six. The numbers are not spectacular by the standards of sporting superpowers. But historically, they are significant. Before this five-edition run, India had achieved multiple-medal campaigns at only two Olympics â Paris 1900, when Norman Pritchard won two silver medals, and Helsinki 1952, when India won one gold and one bronze. Then came five consecutive Olympic editions with multiple Indian medals. That is the quieter revolution. And the country is no longer disappearing between Games. The consistency itself represents progress. Paris showed how close India remains to a bigger breakthrough The six-medal haul at Paris 2024 was disappointing because expectations had changed. After India's record-breaking Asian Games campaign a year earlier, there was genuine hope that the country could finally push into double figures at the Olympics. It did not happen. But Paris also showed why the ambition for 10 medals was not completely misplaced. India had several agonising near-misses. The archery mixed team finished fourth after losing its bronze-medal match. Lakshya Sen lost the badminton bronze-medal match. Shooter Arjun Babuta finished fourth in the men's 10m air rifle. Manu Bhaker, already a double medallist, missed out on a third medal after finishing fourth in the women's 25m pistol. India's skeet team lost its bronze-medal shoot-out, while weightlifter Mirabai Chanu finished fourth. Then came Vinesh Phogat's disqualification before her gold-medal bout after she was found 100 grams over the weight limit. Seven âwhat ifâ moments. That does not mean India should retrospectively count those as medals. But it demonstrates how narrow the margins can be at the Olympics. Four of those near-misses becoming medals would have taken India to 10. The more important takeaway is that India is beginning to produce enough finalists and medal contenders across different sports for the conversation to shift from âCan India win?â to âHow many can India convert?â That is a different challenge. And in many ways, it is a sign of progress. The real evolution: India's floor is rising The Asian Games and Olympics operate on completely different scales, but together they reveal a striking change in India's sporting story. The underlying pattern is comparable. India's old sporting story was one of sporadic success. Its emerging story is one of sustained presence. At the Asian Games, India has established a 50-medal floor. Hangzhou then pushed the ceiling beyond 100. At the Olympics, India has established something much more modest but historically important: five consecutive Games with multiple medals. That is why the central story of India's sporting evolution should not simply be âIndia is winning more medals.â It is that India is becoming increasingly consistent at winning medals. India is not there yet. The Olympic record remains underwhelming. But the direction is unmistakable. The floor is rising. Aichi-Nagoya is the next test India will enter Aichi-Nagoya 2026 carrying the weight of its greatest Asian Games campaign, but the objective should not simply be to reproduce Hangzhou's 106. A 499-athlete contingent is heading to Japan, compared with 661 in Hangzhou. That difference makes a direct comparison difficult. The more meaningful test is whether India can sustain the performance level that has emerged over the last two decades. Join conversation View All Comments â Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful Â· TOI community guidelines Can 50-plus remain the floor? Can 70-plus become the new expectation? Can more sports join the traditional medal pillars? Those are the questions that matter beyond the medal table. India may still be an under-achiever. But it is increasingly difficult to argue that the country is standing still. The medals are still not enough. The Olympic haul is still too modest. The Asian Games success still needs to be sustained. The conversion rate at the highest level still needs improvement. But the pattern has changed. From occasional Asian Games peaks to five consecutive 50-plus campaigns. From two historic multi-medal Olympics to five in a row. From a narrow collection of medal sports to a gradually expanding base. The peaks are getting higher. More importantly, the floor beneath them is rising. Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. title: Medals bring relief in Valarivan household
text: Saroja Valarivan (left), mother of Elavenil Valarivan, celebrates her win, in Ahmedabad on Sunday. Ahmedabad: A sense of palpable relief enveloped the Valarivan household in southern Ahmedabadâs Khokhra locality after ace shooter Elavenil Valarivan clinched silver medals in Aichi-Nagoya. Elavenil had returned empty-handed from the three major multi-sporting events, the 2018 Asian Games in Jakarta, 2020 Tokyo Olympics and the 2024 Paris Olympics, which she had participated in. Elavenilâs mother Saroja told TOI, âBecause of the last two shots, she missed the gold. A medal at the Asian Games was missing. In the 2018 edition in Jakarta, her rifle malfunctioned and she missed out the 2022 edition (held in 2023 because of Covid) in Hangzhou. This is the one medal she and we wanted her to win badly. We are relieved.â Despite the double podium finish, there was no big celebration in the Valarivan household. âHer father is happy and excited that she has finally won an Asian Games medal. There werenât huge celebrations on Sunday also. All family members watched the shooting event at their respective homes. We will plan a gathering after Elavenil comes back on Sept 26 after the conclusion of the 10m air rifle mixed team event,â said Saroja. Her medals mirror the achievement of Gagan Narang, whose Gun for Glory academy she trains at. Narang had won two silver medals in corresponding events in the menâs category at the 2010 Asian Games in Guangzhou. Asked about the significance of the 27-year-oldâs achievement, Narang told TOI, âFantastic. Iâm quite happy because I know what she has gone through to get to this particular medal. This silver is worth the price of gold actually with the kind of effort she has put in over the years.â He lavished praise on Elavenilâs evolution as a shooter. âShe is a completely different Ela from her early years, in terms of how she approaches the competition, how she understands the sport, its demands, her maturity and more of a smart worker than before,â said the former Olympic bronze medallist. Narang delved into how the Cuddalore-born, Ahmedabad-based shooter worked hard to put the distractions behind. âDisappointments are a part of the journey. We can either choose to get bogged down by them or stand up and take them head on and move ahead. Knowing and seeing Ela on the other side of the tunnel speaks volumes of who she is and how she has evolved over the years,â Narang stressed. He added, âWhen an athlete wins, they are showered with accolades, and when they donât, they fight a silent battle. Only the ones who believe in them stick by them. Even if Ela might have doubted her abilities, I and her team not even for a second were in doubt. We believed in her, kept our head down, put in the work and let the performance do the talking. âEla chose to put her blinders on to shut out the distractions and worked really hard.â And, the result was there to see at the Aichi Prefectural General Shooting Gallery. title: Who are Simone Bilesâ parents? The story of Ronald and Nellie and their bond with the gymnast
text: Who are Simone Bilesâ parents? The story of Ronald and Nellie and their bond with the gymnast Simone Bilesâ success in gymnastics has been tied to the support of her parents, Ronald and Nellie Biles. The couple adopted Simone and her younger sister, Adria, when Simone was six after she spent years in foster care. Ronald and Nellie gave her a stable home and encouraged her gymnastics talent from the beginning. They also became a constant presence at her competitions and supported her during difficult moments, including her Tokyo Olympics withdrawal. Years later, they remained by her side as she returned to competition and won medals at the Paris Olympics in 2024. Ronald and Nellie Biles adopted Simone when she was six Ronald and Nellie met in 1977 while Ronald was serving in the Air Force in San Antonio, Texas. Nellie was studying nursing at the time. Ronald was already a father to Simoneâs biological mother, Shannon. The couple married on Jan. 16, 1977, and later had two sons, Ronald Jr. and Adam. Simoneâs early childhood was difficult. Her biological mother struggled with drug and alcohol addiction and could not care for her four children. Simone and her siblings were placed in foster care. Simone spent three years in the foster care system and later spoke about being hungry and afraid during that period. Ronald and Nellie eventually adopted Simone and her sister Adria and moved them to Houston, Texas. Simone has said that this change gave her a second chance at life. She also made clear how important her adoptive parents became to her. Nellie once described the emotional change that happened after the adoption. She said that telling children you love and care for them is only words at first. For her, motherhood became real when she realized she would do anything for the children. Simone later said that her parents âsaved meâ and thanked them for supporting her from the beginning. She also described them as role models who showed her what a strong foundation of love and support looks like. Ronald and Nellie supported Simoneâs gymnastics career Simone first tried gymnastics when she was six after visiting a gym during a daycare field trip. Coaches noticed her ability and sent home a note encouraging her to take classes. Ronald and Nellie quickly signed her up. Nellie later recalled that Simone rarely wanted to miss practice. Even when Nellie suggested that she stay home because she was sick, Simone would insist on going. Simone also said her parents made sure she had what she needed to compete at her best. Ronald and Nellie became regular faces in the stands. Simone said her parents had never missed one of her competitions until the Tokyo Olympics, when COVID-19 restrictions prevented them from traveling to watch her. Their absence made the Tokyo experience harder for Simone. She withdrew from several events after experiencing the âtwistiesâ and focused on her mental and physical health. She later said that not having her parents there was one of the things that made the experience especially difficult. Join conversation View All Comments â Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful Â· TOI community guidelines The family returned to the stands for the 2024 Paris Olympics. Nellie said 17 family members traveled to support Simone. Ronald also became a lighthearted part of the Olympic coverage when he was seen using binoculars from the stands. Simone later called the moment âsoooo freaking cute.â Ronald and Nellie have also played a role beyond simply cheering from the stands. They own World Champions Centre in Spring, Texas, the gym where Simone trained. They opened the facility in 2014 so she could continue working with her longtime coach without having to move between gyms. Nellie has remained an important person in Simoneâs life away from gymnastics too. When Simone married NFL player Jonathan Owens in 2023, Nellie helped her plan the wedding. Simone said she looks to both of her parents as role models and values the love and support they have provided throughout her life. Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

title: Simone Biles questions Olympic gymnastics tie-break rules after Paris 2024 result as LA 2028 decision nears
text: Simone Biles questions Olympic gymnastics tie-break rules after Paris 2024 result as LA 2028 decision nears Simone Biles wants one simple change in Olympic gymnastics before the 2028 Los Angeles Games: if two athletes finish with the same score, both should receive the medal. Biles made the point after remembering her balance beam result at the Paris 2024 Olympics, where she and Suni Lee both scored 13.100 but were ranked fifth and sixth. With Biles still unsure about returning in 2028, the rule remains one part of gymnastics she would like to see changed. Simone Biles wants ties to mean shared Olympic medals During an interview with HELLO! on September 11, Biles was asked whether there was a gymnastics rule she would change. Her answer was direct: âIf itâs a tie, both people get the medal.â The comment connects to what happened in the balance beam final in Paris. Biles and Lee both finished with 13.100 points, but Biles was placed fifth because her execution score was higher. Biles had a 7.200 execution score, while Lee had 6.900. Both had the same difficulty score of 6.200. Under the rules used at Paris 2024, a tie in an apparatus final was first decided by the higher execution score. If that was also equal, the difficulty score was used. If the gymnasts were still level, they shared the same classification. The International Gymnastics Federation (FIG) listed those steps in its Paris 2024 rules. The system has changed over the years. Tied gymnasts once could receive the same medal, but the International Olympic Committee (IOC) introduced tie-break procedures for judged sports after the 1996 Atlanta Olympics, with gymnastics adopting a new system in 1997. One of the clearest examples came at the 2008 Beijing Olympics. Nastia Liukin and He Kexin both scored 16.725 on uneven bars, but He won gold after a detailed tie-break process based on judging deductions. The Washington Post later described the system as an âobscure tiebreaker.â Simone Bilesâ LA 2028 decision remains uncertain Bilesâ comments come while her own Olympic future is still open. The 29-year-old has not confirmed that she will compete at the 2028 Los Angeles Games. title: Who is Fariba Hashimi? Meet the Afghan cyclist who trained disguised as a man and won Asian Games silver after fleeing Taliban
text: Who is Fariba Hashimi? Meet the Afghan cyclist who trained disguised as a man wins Asian Games silver after fleeing Taliban. For Fariba Hashimi, becoming a top cyclist didnât start with dreams of gold medals or crossing epic finish lines; it started with figuring out how to ride a bike at all. Growing up in northern Afghanistan, just riding meant risking her safety. She and her sister, Yulduz, wanted to train, but for girls that meant disguises: baggy clothes, faces hidden behind layers of masks. Even then, just one trip down the road could easily end with people hurling insults, or worse: actual stones. The threats were constant. But Fariba wasnât easily discouraged. The sisters kept showing up, dodging harassment and occasional violent attacks. Once, a rickshaw driver drove straight at them. Sometimes, they used fake names just to enter small competitions because even their family didnât approve at first. Still, winning those secret races caught the attention of the Afghanistan Cycling Federation. Eventually, their father drove them to Kabul so they could try out for the national team. Then, everything changed. When the Taliban returned in 2021, life for ambitious women shrank overnight. Afghan girls and women lost school, lost work, lost access to public life itself. Eventually, Fariba and Yulduz had to flee their home, with help from Alessandra Cappellotto, an Italian world champion cyclist. Settling in Italy gave them safety, but their roots and dreams always pointed back toward Afghanistan. On September 22, 2026, standing on the podium in Aichi-Nagoya, Japan, Fariba wasnât just another cyclist with a medal. After years of hiding, sheâd earned silver in the Asian Games womenâs road race: the first Afghan woman to claim any Asian Games medal since 2002. It meant something far beyond winning a race. Fariba beat out dozens of competitors, coming in just behind Chinaâs Guo Li, with Hong Kongâs Leung Wing Yee in third. But for her, the result was personal, as well as political. She explained why so simply after the race: âThis silver medal can show a lot of resilience from Afghan women,â she said, as quoted by The Guardian. âI hope the next generation will come here and represent their country without any fear.â Her words echoed the journey of so many women who have had to hide their passions and identities in plain sight, hoping someday things might be different. Who is Fariba Hashimi? Fariba started cycling as a teenager in Faryab province, inspired by her older sister. Training meant long rides with the fear of being caught, but the sisters stuck together. They shared every harsh lesson the streets had to offer. Fariba once described to journalists how sheâd stack on two or three masks to keep people from recognizing her, just for a morning ride. In their earliest races, the girls used fake names because their family feared for their safety and reputation. But as their talent grew harder to ignore, things shifted. It wasnât just about their own determination. The feats they managed, like winning first and second in local races, caught the eye of sports officials. Eventually, their family got behind them, and that tiny bit of support made a huge difference. Today Fariba lives and trains in Italy, turning her early defiance into a professional cycling career. At the Asian Games, she powered through to second place, unaccompanied by any mechanic or professional support team. She had to fix and clean her bike herself, and even leaned on the kindness of Japanese competitors for a hand with maintenance. âI was the mechanic for myself. I was washing the bike myself. Thank you to the Japanese team. They were really, really nice to me, fixed my bike,â she said. Her gratitude was obvious. Anyone whoâs been forced to go it alone understands what it means to finally have someone in your corner, even if just for a day. From hiding her identity to the Olympics Cycling took Fariba beyond any limits set for Afghan women. Not only did she escape the immediate dangers back home, but she also made the leap to international competition, representing Afghanistan all the way to the Paris 2024 Olympics. There, the Hashimi sisters joined a handful of athletes embodying two realities at once: The risk of simply being a woman with dreams in Afghanistan, and the pride of carrying that flag before the world. Even at the Asian Games, Faribaâs victory didnât come easy. She lacked a proper support team and had to rely on herself for every practical detail and setback, making her silver medal as much an achievement in grit as athletic talent. She finished seventh in the womenâs individual time trial two days before her silver: an exhausting turnaround for any athlete, but she thrived on it. Why does her medal matter? Right now, Afghanistan is the only country on Earth where girls and women arenât allowed to attend secondary school or university. They canât work in most jobs, and sport is out of the question. Since 2021, opportunities for women have collapsed; UN Women and UNESCO both say the rollbacks are unmatched worldwide. All the while, Hashimiâs success stands as something stubborn and luminous: undeniable proof that Afghan women are made for more than what the Taliban decrees. The same government that forbids women from entering a gym now watches one carry the Afghan flag across an international finish line, visible and proud. âMillions of women, from many countries, have the same dream and they are standing with me,â Fariba said. That sense of shared hope, woven through her quiet determination, speaks louder than the medal around her neck. Whatâs next for Fariba Hashimi? Anyone thinking Fariba will stop at silver is missing the point. She and Yulduz are already eyeing the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics. Their journeyâs never been about just one finish line; itâs about showing Afghan women everywhere that the world is bigger than their cages. She hasnât forgotten the help sheâs had, or those she leaves behind. âThe next generation will come here and represent their country without any fear,â she says, back turned to the old world, eyes locked on the future. On that podium in Japan, Fariba held more than a medal; she held a message. For every girl whoâs forced to train in secret, whoâs told she isnât allowed to be strong, her ride is a signal: Keep going. The bicycle that once was hidden now carries the dreams of an entire nation, one that refuses to be invisible. You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. title: Why Pawan Sehrawat replaced Tajinderpal Singh Toor as India's Asian Games flag-bearer
text: Pawan Sehrawat Tajinderpal Singh Toor will not be able to lead the Indian contingent at the Asian Games opening ceremony after the celebrated shot-putter arrived without his ceremonial kit, forcing a late change in India's flag-bearers. Seasoned kabaddi player Pawan Sehrawat has been named as Toor's replacement and will now join shooting star Manu Bhaker in carrying the Indian flag at Saturday's opening ceremony. Watch 'We Love Smriti Mandhana!â Indian Fans in Japan on India vs Japan | Asian Games 2026 The 30-year-old Sehrawat was part of the Indian men's kabaddi team that won gold at the previous Asian Games. India's chef-de-mission Sahdev Yadav confirmed the change to PTI. Toor's absence is the result of a logistical issue involving the ceremonial kit. The athlete said he was informed that his kit would reach Nagoya airport only at 3pm, making it difficult for him to collect it and still reach the opening ceremony venue on time. "I am told that my ceremonial kit will reach at 3pm at the (Nagoya) airport. Reaching the opening ceremony venue after collecting my (ceremonial) kit from airport on time will be very difficult. So, I have told IOA (Indian Olympic Association) that I am not coming for opening ceremony," Toor told PTI. The athletics contingent has been stationed at the University of Tsukuba near Tokyo since September 13 for an acclimatisation camp. The team is scheduled to travel to Nagoya on September 21, two days before the athletics events begin. The athletes were not originally expected to participate in either the opening or closing ceremonies, which is why they did not have the ceremonial kits with them. "They will be leaving Nagoya on September 30, one day after the end of athletics competition and four days before the closing ceremony (on October 4)," a team official said. Toor confirmed that the ceremonial kits were not with the athletics contingent. "Nobody in athletics team has ceremonial kits with them," he revealed. The 75-member athletics contingent, however, has received its official competition kits. Multiple members of the group confirmed this to PTI. title: Father sold land, shop for Sonamâs rifle; she repaid in Asian Games silver
text: Sonam Maskar poses for a photo after clinching a silver medal in the Women's 10m Air Rifle Team event at the Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games 2026, in Nagoya on Sunday 10m rifle shooter Sonam with her father Uttam Maskar 10m rifle shooter Sonam with her father Uttam Maskar Sonam Maskar poses for a photo after clinching a silver medal in the Women's 10m Air Rifle Team event at the Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games 2026, in Nagoya on Sunday 10m rifle shooter Sonam with her father Uttam Maskar 10m rifle shooter Sonam with her father Uttam Maskar Sonam Maskar poses for a photo after clinching a silver medal in the Women's 10m Air Rifle Team event at the Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games 2026, in Nagoya on Sunday 1 2 3 Kolhapur : Shooter Sonam Maskar made India and her family proud on Sunday, winning team silver in the womenâs 10m air rifle event at the Asian Games in Aichi-Nagoya, Japan. The medal capped a remarkable journey for the 23-year-old, whose family backed her shooting dream even when money had almost completely dried up. In the individual event, Sonam finished sixth in the final, while teammate Elavenil Valarivan won silver. âI dedicate the award to my father and mother. Without their sacrifice, I wouldnât be here. The success has helped overcome all the hardships,â Sonam told ANI. Those hardships began during the Covid pandemic, when her father Uttam Maskar lost his Mahanand dairy distributorship. With no income and three children to support, he sold two vehicles and moved the family back to Varsha Nagar near Gargoti in Kolhapur district. But he refused to let Sonam give up shooting. âI sold a plot and a shop and raised money. My wife and I stayed with Sonam in Kolhapur and looked after her before she got selected at the Sports Authority of India facility,â Uttam said. âAt that time, I had no income. My other daughter was in the third year of architecture and my son had just completed Class X. With the money from selling the land and shop, I bought Sonam a weapon, kit and laptop costing around Rs 4.5 lakh in all,â he said. The familyâs fortunes have since improved. Uttam has regained his dairy franchise, while Sonam has completed her graduation and now works with the Railways. Interestingly, shooting was not Sonamâs first sporting love. Sonam and her siblings were fond of chess from childhood. When she joined Tolani College in Mumbai for junior college, however, chess was not available. She opted for rifle shooting instead. âShe found shooting very interesting and soon started winning medals. That is how her journey began,â Uttam said. Sonam later competed at the state and national levels and earned a place in Indiaâs junior team. She represented the country in ISSF championships in 2023 and 2024 before adding the Asian Games team silver to her growing list of achievements. A key chapter in that journey unfolded in Kolhapur. Sonam joined Vedh Academy at 19 and trained there between 2021 and 2023 under Shiv Chhatrapati Award-winning coach Radhica Havaldar and her shooter husband Rohit Havaldar. âSonam has the in-built calmness and focus required to become a successful shooter. She used to train for four hours a day at the academy. She would spend another hour or two working on her physical strength,â Rohit Havaldar said. Sonam now joins Kolhapurâs rich shooting tradition. The city has nurtured several shooters who went on to shine internationally, including Tejaswini Sawant, who brought the first gold for India in World Championship, and 2024 Paris Olympics bronze medallist Swapnil Kusale. title: 'Haar nahi maanunga': Sujeet Kalkal's Asian Games 2026 gold mission on the road to LA Olympics
text: For Sujeet, the Asian Games is more than just another tournament. It is a fresh start for the wrestler from Haryanaâs Bhiwani district. NEW DELHI: The last time Sujeet Kalkal came close to an Olympic dream, he never even got the chance to step on the mat. Now, as he prepares for his maiden Asian Games in Aichi-Nagoya, Japan, the 23-year-old wrestler is looking at the continental event as the first major marker of a new Olympic journey - one that he hopes will eventually take him to Los Angeles in 2028. âAsaan nahi tha, bhaisaab. Fir se start kiya hai, haar nahi maanunga. Olympics to sapna hai, poora karna hai bass [It wasnât easy. Iâve started again, and I wonât give up. The Olympics is a dream, and I have to fulfil it, thatâs all],â Sujeet told TimesofIndia.com ahead of the Asian Games. There is reason for that confidence. Sujeet enters Aichi-Nagoya having established himself among the leading wrestlers in the 65kg category. He won the Asian Championships in Bishkek earlier this year and has continued to build his credentials in 2026. He also won the 65kg selection trials for the Senior World Championships in Lucknow last week, beating Anuj Kumar 8-3 in the final. The Asian Games, however, will present a different test. Sujeet's 65kg category features some of the biggest names in Asian wrestling, including Japan's Olympic champion Kotaro Kiyooka. Sujeet's competition starts from October 2, when the men's freestyle 65kg, 86kg and 125kg categories will be contested. For Sujeet, the Asian Games is more than just another tournament. It is a fresh start for the wrestler from Imlota village in Haryanaâs Bhiwani district. âI was very happy to qualify [for the Asian Games] . It is a fresh start, and I will not disappoint. Behind this success is the hard work of my father, my coach and my entire team. I am in good form. I will come back with the gold medal,â Sujeet said. âThe 65kg category is a very challenging and competitive weight category. The worldâs best wrestlers always compete in this category. But I have complete faith in my hard work and preparation. My entire focus is only on gold, brother. I have worked very hard,â he added. It will also be a chance to measure how far he has travelled since April 2024, when a three-day ordeal at Dubai International Airport ended his first Olympic campaign before it had even begun. Three days at Dubai Airport It was April 2024. Sujeet was at Dubai International Airport, waiting to continue his journey to Bishkek, Kyrgyzstan, where he was scheduled to compete in the Asian Olympic Qualifying Tournament. But record rainfall had caused floods in Dubai and badly disrupted air travel. Sujeet was stranded at the airport. He could see water everywhere and could only pray that the situation would improve so he could travel to Bishkek, where the qualifiers were scheduled to take place. Sujeet could only watch the time, calculate the days and hours on his fingers, and then sit back. His connecting flight was delayed and eventually remained stranded at the airport for three days. A flight was finally arranged, but by the time he reached Kyrgyzstan and then the venue, it was one and a half hours after the weigh-in had been completed. The Wrestling Federation of India and officials tried their best to find a way to get Sujeet into the competition. But the United World Wrestling rules left them with no option. The opportunity was gone. âI felt very bad. I have no words. It was four years of hard work, and it all ended in that one moment. I was in good form, and everything was over in a moment. I cried alone too, but I had faith in God. I explained things to myself and returned to India,â Sujeet said. Father's words gave him strength Sujeet returned to India devastated. At home, his father Dayanand was waiting for him. Dayanand, a former Greco-Roman wrestler, knew what his son was going through. Sujeet immediately hugged his father. He became emotional and had his father's shoulder to cry on. His father hugged him and told him: âKoi nahi beta, fir se mehnat karenge hum, Olympics khelna haiâ. Those words stayed with Sujeet. âI didn't give up' Starting again was not easy, but Sujeet was adamant. He won gold at the United World Wrestling Ranking Series in Budapest in the menâs 65kg division at the start of 2025. He added two more gold medals to his tally in Zagreb and at the Tirana Grand Prix. He then won a gold medal at the World U23 Championships in 2025 in Novi Sad, Serbia, followed by another gold at the Asian U23 Championships in Vung Tau, Vietnam. He didn't stop there. Sujeet became Asian Champion after winning gold in Bishkek, Kyrgyzstan. With that gold medal finish, he also rose to the No. 1 ranking in the world. Now, he is set for his first Asian Games. A medal in Aichi-Nagoya would take him another step closer to his next big target - the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics. âI didn't give up. I have worked very hard. I have to go a long way. If I had competed in Paris, I would have been 21. I am 23 now. I will be 25 when the Los Angeles Olympics comes around. Age makes a big difference. But I don't want to step back. My mindset is still the same â to win a medal for the country,â he said. Join conversation View All Comments â Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful Â· TOI community guidelines 'Haanikarak baapu' For Sujeet, wrestling was never just a sport. His father Dayanand, a former national wrestling champion who also represented India at the World Championships, introduced him to the sport at a very young age. Sujeet was just five when he was pushed into the 'akhaada'. Dayanand could not go to the Olympics to represent India. Now, he wants his son to fulfil that unfulfilled dream. âPapa is very strict," he says. "Wo dangal mein haanikarak baapu they na, wo waise hi kuch hain (laughs). He told me, âSon, you have to become a wrestler. A wrestlerâs son should be a wrestler.â I have learnt a lot from him since childhood. He is both my guru and my father. Whatever I am today is because of him,â he said. âHis dream is to see me at the Olympics and see me win a medal. I will definitely fulfil this dream of my father,â Sujeet signed off. title: âWe should not waste our energyâ: Manu Bhaker urges Indian athletes to look beyond Asian Games chaos
text: Manu Bhaker (AFP Photo) NEW DELHI: Shooting ace Manu Bhaker has urged her fellow Indian athletes to put the organisational issues surrounding the Asian Games behind them and focus on competition, saying the continental showpiece represents a âonce in a lifetime opportunity and experienceâ. The build-up to the Games in Japan has been marred by complaints from athletes and officials of several participating countries, including India, over cramped accommodation, organisational mismanagement and long travel times between hotels and training venues. Watch Asian Games: Sehdev Yadav reveals how SAI arranged rooms for Indian athletes With criticism mounting over the arrangements, Bhaker called on the Indian contingent not to allow the problems to distract them from their performances. âTo all my fellow athletes from India, we will have some issues. I saw a couple of issues circulated in social media and people telling me these are the issues,â Bhaker said in a video message posted by the Indian Olympic Association. âRegardless of whatever the issues we have, this is probably a once in a lifetime opportunity and experience. We have to make sure that we enjoy the time rather than complaining,â she added. âWe should not waste our energyâ Bhaker, a double Olympic medallist, said Indian athletes had worked too hard to reach the Asian Games to allow the organisational difficulties to consume their attention. âWe have prepared the best we can and so we must try to perform the best we can. We have worked so hard to be here and we should not waste our energy in pointing out that this is not right and that is not right. Medal may come or not, that is another story, but we must give our best.â The 24-year-old has been given another significant responsibility at the Games after being named one of India's two flag bearers for Saturday's opening ceremony. Bhaker created history at the Paris Olympics in 2024 when she became the first athlete from Independent India to win two medals at a single edition of the Olympic Games. She won bronze in the women's individual 10m air pistol and mixed team 10m air pistol events. Manu Bhaker to lead India's contingent as flag bearer The Asian Games will also carry a strong personal significance for Bhaker, who is competing at the continental event for the third time. âWhen I came to know of this (being chosen as one of the flagbearers), I had flashbacks of my earlier days. When I started, I never thought I would reach this far one day. It's definitely feeling proud and honoured,â she said. âI was just 16 years old when I competed in the Asian Games in 2018. This is my third Asian Games. I was in Palembang (Indonesia) in 2018 and so could not attend the ceremony.â Bhaker recalled that her late coach Jaspal Rana had allowed her to attend opening ceremonies of multi-sport events only when she was a flag bearer, given the tight competition schedule for shooters. Since our matches usually start just a day after the opening ceremony, it becomes hectic for us. âSo in opening ceremonies, I am either a flagbearer or I watch the ceremony on television.â Earlier on Saturday, seasoned kabaddi player Pawan Sehrawat replaced shot-putter Tajinderpal Singh Toor as the other Indian flag bearer after Toor was unable to attend the ceremony because he did not have the required ceremonial kit in his luggage. And, you know, when I started, I never thought that this was where I could reach one day in my sport. So, it is definitely a very heartwarming feeling. I feel really proud, really honoured, and really, really happy to be chosen as the flag bearer for my country. title: 'Maybe 32': Anju Bobby George hopeful of more athletics medals despite Neeraj Chopra miss at Asian Games
text: Neeraj Chopra NEW DELHI: The absence of Neeraj Chopra may have taken away Indian athleticsâ biggest individual name, but former long jumper Anju Bobby George believes it need not take away from the athletics contingentâs medal ambitions at the Asian Games. The 2003 Paris World Championships bronze medallist expects Indiaâs track and field contingent to cross the 30-medal mark. India won 29 athletics medals â six gold, 14 silver and nine bronze â at the 2022 Asian Games in Hangzhou, its best-ever medal haul in the sport at the continental showpiece. âNeeraj is a big name in athletics, with multiple world-level medals. It is very unfortunate that he is not in our team this time because of an ankle injury. Yes, thatâs a setback,â Anju told TOI in an exclusive interview. âBut definitely we have many other athletes who are performing well. This time, we are expecting more than last time â more than 30, maybe 32.â Watch Devajit Saikia on Ajit Agarkar's future, IPL window & BCCIâs big AGM decisions For Anju, the defining feature of the current athletics squad is its breadth. Rather than relying on one or two medal contenders, there are podium possibilities across disciplines, particularly the jumps, middle and long-distance events and relays. âThis is the beauty of our athletics contingent this time. If you take any event, we are aiming for medals,â she said. The womenâs long jump could be one of the most intriguing contests for India in Aichi-Nagoya, with Ancy Sojan and Shaili Singh both entering as serious medal hopes. Ancy, in June this year, jumped 6.88m in Bhubaneswar to break Anjuâs 22-year-old national record of 6.83m. âRecords are always meant to be broken because that is the path, thatâs the growth,â she said. âOtherwise, after I got the World Championships medal, nobody else wouldâve done such wonderful achievements for Indian athletics. Ancy is now seasoned, sheâs fixed and sheâs performing. Shaili is also jumping above 6.80m, but she is yet to set her approach and rhythm and is committing fouls. Otherwise, both jumpers are equally good. Join conversation View All Comments â Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful Â· TOI community guidelines We are expecting gold and silver. Either Ancy or Shaili will win gold.â In menâs long jump, Murali Sreeshankar provides another compelling comeback story. The 27-year-old, who missed the Paris Olympics after suffering a patellar tendon rupture in 2024, has returned to top level and produced an 8.38m season-best in June â the second-best jump of his career behind his 8.41m national record. âHe is such a tremendous athlete. He was nowhere last year because of the injury. We wonder how he came back, how he conquered again. After injuries, especially in jumps and that too in the take-off leg, coming back is such a big, big thing. He did that with his mental strength,â Anju said. title: Asian Games 2026: India's full schedule on September 19, Saturday; Quimcy Dsouza in Teqball semifinal before opening ceremony
text: Quimcy Dsouza. (Photo/Agencies) The Asian Games 2026 will officially begin on Saturday, with the opening ceremony scheduled to start at 2:30pm IST in Nagoya. However, a few competitions, including women's cricket, soft tennis and teqball, have already got underway ahead of the ceremony. India's schedule for Saturday (September 19): Teqball 6:30am IST: Women's singles semifinal â Quimcy Dsouza vs Sumaya (Indonesia) Opening Ceremony 2:30pm IST onwards: Asian Games 2026 opening ceremony Quimcy Dsouza reaches Teqball semis; mixed doubles pair eyes bronze India's Quimcy Joaquim Dsouza moved within one win of creating history after reaching the women's singles semifinals in teqball at the Asian Games in Nagoya on Friday. Making her Asian Games debut, Quimcy upset top seed Yuina Sakamoto of Japan 2-1 (10-12, 12-11, 13-11) in her first Group A match. She followed that up with a 2-0 (12-9, 12-7) win over Cambodia's Koemyean DY in her second group match, finishing on top of Group A and booking a place in the semifinals. By topping the group, Quimcy received a bye in the quarterfinals. The 24-year-old will face Indonesia's Sumaya in Saturday's semifinal. A win will guarantee India its first-ever medal in Teqball, one of the six sports making its Asian Games debut. Even if she loses in the semifinals, Quimcy will still have a chance to win bronze on Sunday. In the mixed doubles event, Quimcy and Mohammed Anas Imran Beg were beaten 0-2 (7-12, 10-12) by Vietnam's Hoang Minh Tan Nguyen and Gia Nghi Trinh in the quarterfinals. However, the Indian pair remain in contention for a bronze medal after winning their repechage match. Teqball is one of six sports making its Asian Games debut in Aichi-Nagoya, alongside Mixed Martial Arts (MMA), Padel, Surfing, BMX Freestyle and Virtual Taekwondo. The sport combines elements of football and table tennis. It was invented in Hungary in 2014 by Gabor Borsanyi, Gyorgy Gattyan and Viktor Huszar, while the first official Teqball World Championships were held in Budapest in 2017. In Teqball, players use every part of the body except their hands and arms to rally a standard size-five football across a curved table divided by a transparent plexiglass net. The ceremony is scheduled for Saturday, and a 158-strong Indian contingent will take part in it. "Manu Bhaker will be one of the flag-bearers," India's chef-de-Mission Sahdev Yadav said. title: Champions return, 314 debutants arrive: Inside Indiaâs 500-plus Asian Games campaign
text: India eye record medals at Asian Games 2026 NEW DELHI: Hoping to build on the historic campaign three years back at Hangzhou, India begins its campaign at the Asian Games in Aichi-Nagoya with a 500-plus athlete contingent, aiming to better the 106-medal tally racked up at the last Games. While the build-up to the Games has been marred by mismanagement, an accommodation crisis and the threat of a typhoon looming large over the Japanese prefecture, for the athletes, once the Games begin, it will be, as the adage goes, âgame mode onâ. The 500-plus athlete Indian contingent comprises a sizeable group of returning champions and experienced campaigners. 314 of those athletes are preparing for their first appearance at the continental event. Watch Animesh Kujur targets Asian Games medal after breakthrough season Interestingly, women athletes make up 46.7% of the contingent. At 15, Vaibhav Sooryavanshi is the youngest member. Equestrian rider Shruti Vora, 55, is the oldest. Vaibhav Sooryavanshi will be the youngest to play for India at Asian Games (TOI Graphics) India will compete in 256 events across 36 of the 43 sports at Aichi-Nagoya, with the Games beginning on September 19 and running until October 4. Avinash Sable, returning from a year-long injury, will try to defend his men's 3000m steeplechase title, while Tajinderpal Singh Toor returns in the men's shot put. Parul Chaudhary will be another athlete trying to defend her women's 5000m crown, while India's men's 4x400m relay team will also go into the Games as defending champions. In badminton, Satwiksairaj Rankireddy and Chirag Shetty will aim to defend their men's doubles title. Their gold in Hangzhou was India's first Asian Games title in the event. Indian compound archers swept all five gold medals in the discipline at Hangzhou, and returning champion Jyothi Surekha Vennam will be the fulcrum around whom India's archery campaign will revolve. Then there are athletes whose Asian Games story is still waiting for a first chapter. India's record-breaking numbers in the last Asian Games (TOI Graphics) Mirabai Chanu âs missing Asian Games medal Mirabai Chanu has won a world title, Olympic silver and Commonwealth Games gold. The Asian Games medal remains missing from her collection. The 32-year-old will lead India's four-member weightlifting team in Aichi-Nagoya, with Gyaneshwari Yadav, Seram Nirupama Devi and Harjinder Kaur completing the squad. Chanu missed the 2018 Asian Games because of injury and did not compete at Hangzhou. Now, after a career that has already included a world championship title, an Olympic medal and multiple Commonwealth Games titles, the Asian Games is the major multi-sport medal still absent from her cabinet. Anahat arrives as a world junior champion Anahat Singh is another young Indian athlete arriving in Japan with a title already behind her. The 18-year-old is a World Junior Squash Champion and has made the transition from junior squash to the senior international circuit at a young age. She is part of India's eight-member squash team in Aichi-Nagoya. Joshana Chinappa, Tanvi Khanna and Shameena Riaz are the other members of the women's squad, while Abhay Singh, Velavan Senthilkumar, Veer Chotrani and Suraj Kumar Chand make up the men's team. Squash was among India's gold-medal sports at Hangzhou. Manu Bhaker, Aishwary Pratap and a large shooting group Shooting will once again be one of the major sports to follow, with 27 events on India's programme. The contingent had bagged 22 medals at Hangzhou, including seven golds. Manu Bhaker returns in the women's squad alongside the in-form Esha Singh, Rahi Sarnobat, Elavenil Valarivan, Ashi Chouksey, Suruchi Singh and Tilottama Sen. India's Asian Games contingent (TOI Graphics) The men's group includes Aishwary Pratap Singh Tomar, Rudrankksh Patil and Anish Bhanwala. There will also be a sizable shotgun shooters' bunch, with the veteran Mairaj Ahmed Khan leading the pack alongside Kynan Chenai, Shapath Bharadwaj and Ahvar Rizvi. Neeru Dhanda, Manisha Keer, Maheshwari Chauhan and Parinaaz Dhaliwal are also part of the shotgun group. Neeraj Chopra, meanwhile, will not be in Japan. The javelin thrower, who defended his Asian Games title in Hangzhou, is missing the 2026 Games after an ankle ligament injury during training. Athletics remains the biggest group Athletics has the largest athlete representation, with 78 competitors, and also has the biggest programme with 43 events. They had bagged a total of 29 medals, including six golds, at Hangzhou, and the expectation will be to go many a medal better this time around. Alongside Sable, Toor and Parul are names such as Gulveer Singh, Animesh Kujur, Harita Bhadra, Jyothi Yarraji, Murali Sreeshankar, Praveen Chithravel and Tejaswin Shankar. India's Asian Games event split (TOI Graphics) Hockey: defending champions and a womenâs team on the rise The men's hockey team goes into Aichi-Nagoya as the defending Asian Games champion, but its recent World Cup campaign has left a different question hanging over the side. India won gold in Hangzhou in 2023, beating Japan 5-1 in the final, and the title also secured direct qualification for the Paris Olympics. The team now has another Olympic berth at stake in Japan, with the Asian Games gold medallist earning direct qualification for Los Angeles 2028. The women's team comes to Japan with a more encouraging recent result. India finished fifth at the 2026 Women's Hockey World Cup, their best finish at the tournament in 52 years. The campaign included a 2-2 draw against China, the 2024 Olympic silver medallists, a result that carried particular weight after India's 4-0 defeat to the same opposition in the Hangzhou Asian Games semifinal. The women's team has not won the Asian Games since 1982, and gold in Aichi-Nagoya would also bring direct qualification for the 2028 Olympics. Salima Tete will captain the side, with Savita Punia, Lalremsiami, Navneet Kaur, Deepika and Nikki Pradhan among the experienced players in the squad. Cricket brings another set of familiar names India's men's T20 team is led by Shreyas Iyer and includes Abhishek Sharma, Sanju Samson, Ishan Kishan, Shivam Dube, Tilak Varma, Axar Patel, Washington Sundar, Jasprit Bumrah and Arshdeep Singh. Sooryavanshi is also part of the squad. Harmanpreet Kaur leads the women's side, with Smriti Mandhana, Shafali Verma, Deepti Sharma, Richa Ghosh and Renuka Thakur among the selected players. India won both the men's and women's T20 gold medals at Hangzhou. There will also be Indian participation in four esports events - eFootball, Puyo Puyo Champions, League of Legends and Pokemon Unite. Haryana leads the state-wise numbers Haryana has the largest representation with 96 athletes. India's athletes at 2026 Asiad by states (TOI Graphics) Maharashtra follows with 49, Tamil Nadu 37, Punjab 35, Manipur 34, Uttar Pradesh 32 and Delhi 30. Join conversation View All Comments â Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful Â· TOI community guidelines Karnataka, Kerala and Madhya Pradesh have 24 athletes each. The representation stretches across the country, with athletes also coming from Andaman & Nicobar Islands, Arunachal Pradesh, Jammu & Kashmir, Mizoram, Nagaland, Puducherry, Tripura, Sikkim, Ladakh and Lakshadweep. The support structure behind the contingent is spread across several programmes. National Coaching Camps account for 134 athletes, followed by TOPS Development with 78 and TOPS Core with 77. Khelo India has 65 athletes, TAGG 48 and National Centres of Excellence 25. The support behind the athletes (TOI Graphics) Aichi-Nagoya therefore brings together a group that already knows the Asian Games podium and another that has never experienced it. Mirabai Chanu still has one major medal to add. Anahat Singh arrives as a world junior champion. Manu Bhaker and Aishwary Pratap lead another large shooting group, while Sable, Toor, Parul, Jyothi and Satwik-Chirag return as defending champions. And around them are 314 first-timers, spread across 256 events in 36 sports. Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.
