title: India wants more Olympic medals but 'doesn't participate in half the sports'; PM Modi speaks out 'bitter truth'
text: Prime Minister Narendra Modi NEW DELHI: Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Thursday said India cannot expect a significant rise in its Olympic medal tally unless it starts competing in many sports where it currently has little or no representation, including surfing and sport climbing. Addressing athletes, students and volunteers virtually during the Khelo India Dialogue ahead of National Sports Day on August 29, PM Modi said India's sports vision is not just about winning medals but also about making sports a part of nation-building. Sports minister Mansukh Mandaviya joined the event virtually from IIT Gandhinagar. Prime Minister Modi pointed out that India still does not compete in many Olympic sports. "In the Olympics, there are so many different sports... Indian teams don't even participate in half of them, which means that we are not competing for a major chunk of the medal tally," Modi said, calling it a "bitter truth". He said this has been the situation for many years. "And this has been going on for decades. In 2012, we competed in only 13 sports. We were not even there in over 20 events and not many in the country even knew about some of these competitions. "Other countries win medals in those sports, and we don't even participate. To increase our medals, we have to improve in these sports," he pointed out. India participated in 16 of the 32 sports at the 2024 Paris Olympics. PM Modi specifically mentioned surfing and sport climbing, two sports that are part of the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics but have never seen an Indian competitor. Join conversation View All Comments â Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful Â· TOI community guidelines "For example surfing and sport climbing...We have such a vast coastline, we have such a vast hilly region where there could be a natural affinity for sports like these. from water sports to winter sports, we have the required demography as well as geography," he asserted. He said India has the natural conditions to develop athletes in these sports. "Despite this, we are not seen in these sports anywhere in the world. That's why we have to find opportunities of growing these sports in different regions. To increase our medal tally, we will have to master these sports as well," he added. title: Novak Djokovic injuries: How every painful setback tested the tennis star, yet he rose each time to fight his way back
text: Novak Djokovic injuries: How every painful setback tested the tennis star, yet he rose each time to fight his way back â¢;Novak Djokovicâs career has had almost everything a tennis player can face physically, from breathing problems and heat illness to serious elbow, shoulder, abdominal, hamstring and knee injuries. Some forced him to stop matches, while others came during Grand Slam runs. Yet Djokovic kept finding ways back. Even in 2026, after another difficult physical battle at the US Open, he is still competing at the highest level. Novak Djokovicâs major injuries and how he fought through them â¢ 2005 French Open: Djokovic retired against Guillermo Coria with a lower-back injury. â¢ 2006 French Open: He stopped against Rafael Nadal because of a back and thigh problem. â¢ 2007 Wimbledon: A badly infected blister on his left toe, along with back and overall physical problems, forced him to retire against Nadal in the semifinals. Djokovic later said he did not want to make the injury worse. â¢ 2009 Australian Open: Djokovic retired against Andy Roddick after struggling with heat illness, cramps and soreness in extreme conditions. â¢ 2010â11 health struggles: Djokovic had repeated breathing and energy problems during matches. He later changed his diet after identifying a sensitivity to gluten, which he credited with helping him feel stronger and more comfortable on court. â¢ 2016â18 right elbow injury: The elbow problem became a major setback and ended his 2017 season after Wimbledon. He had surgery in January 2018. Months later, he won Wimbledon and the US Open and finished the year as world No. 1. â¢ 2019 US Open: A left shoulder injury forced Djokovic to retire against Stan Wawrinka while trailing 6-4, 7-5, 2-1. â¢ 2021 Australian Open: Djokovic suffered an abdominal muscle tear during his match with Taylor Fritz but continued the tournament and won the title. â¢ 2023 Australian Open: He arrived with a left hamstring injury and needed heavy strapping and medical treatment during early rounds. He still defeated Stefanos Tsitsipas in the final to win his 10th Australian Open title. â¢ 2024 French Open: Djokovic tore the meniscus in his right knee during his fourth-round win over Francisco CerÃºndolo. He withdrew from the tournament and had surgery. Just over eight weeks later, he won Olympic gold in Paris after beating Carlos Alcaraz. â¢ 2025: A continuing shoulder injury eventually forced Djokovic to withdraw from the ATP Finals after he had won the Athens title. â¢ 2026 US Open: Djokovic faced another physical test against Mariano Navone. He dealt with vomiting, cramps, back and shoulder pain during a four-hour, 36-minute first-round match before losing in five sets. Novak Djokovicâs recent injuries show the same fight The 2026 US Open loss was very different from some of Djokovicâs famous injury comebacks because this time he could not find a way through. Still, the match showed why his physical struggles have become such an important part of his story. He had already dealt with health problems during the season, yet continued to compete. That attitude was clear after his 2024 knee surgery too. Djokovic did not simply return to tennis; he pushed himself back into Grand Slam and Olympic competition. He reached the Wimbledon final and then won Olympic gold only weeks after the operation. Join conversation View All Comments â Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful Â· TOI community guidelines His career has therefore been shaped not only by the injuries themselves, but by what he did after each one. Some setbacks forced him away from the court, some tested him during matches, and some required surgery. Each time, Djokovic found another reason to continue. title: Israel heads to Paris Olympics as Palestinian delegation calls for exclusion
text: Reuters Photo NEW DELHI: The Israeli Olympic team departed for Paris on Monday amidst calls from the Palestinian delegation to prohibit their participation in the upcoming Summer Games. The Palestinian contingent's request comes as a response to the ongoing conflict in Gaza. As the Olympic Games are set to commence on Friday, the event is overshadowed by increased security concerns and growing global condemnation of the escalating death toll and humanitarian crisis in Gaza. In a letter addressed to Thomas Bach, the head of the International Olympic Committee (IOC), the Palestine Olympic Committee demanded Israel's exclusion from the Games. The letter "emphasized that Palestinian athletes, particularly those in Gaza, are denied safe passage and have suffered significantly due to ongoing conflict". The Palestinian delegation argues that the bombings in Gaza constitute a violation of the Olympic truce. The Palestinian Olympic Committee has reported that around 400 Palestinian athletes have lost their lives, and the demolition of sports infrastructure has further worsened the situation for athletes who are already facing significant limitations, stating "approximately 400 Palestinian athletes have been killed, and the destruction of sports facilities exacerbates the plight of athletes who are already under severe restrictions". The committee's statement also made reference to the recent ruling by the United Nations' highest court, which determined that Israel's occupation of Palestinian territories is unlawful. Prior to departing for France, Yael Arad, the President of the Israel Olympic Committee, expressed that the participation of the team's 88 athletes in the Games was a "victory". "Our first victory is that we are here and going, and that we didn't give up and have been competing in hundreds of competitions since October 7," Arad told journalists at Ben Gurion airport. "It's no secret that these Olympic Games are a little more difficult for all of us. But we have full confidence in the organisation of security," Arad added. Speaking at the same conference, judoka Inbar Lanir acknowledged that Israeli athletes have become mired in controversy over the war, but added they were "used to" it. "My part is to connect everyone by sports. It's above all politics and wars and hate. So, I'm feeling safe and I'm excited to represent my country." Thomas Portes, a French lawmaker, ignited a political controversy over the weekend when he declared that Israeli athletes were "not welcome" and urged for "mobilisation" surrounding the Olympics during a demonstration supporting Palestinians. However, Stephane Sejourne, the French Foreign Minister, affirmed on Monday that Israeli athletes were indeed "welcome in France". Israel Katz, the Israeli Foreign Minister, expressed his gratitude to his French counterpart in a post on X, saying, "for his welcome message to the Israeli delegation at the Paris 2024 Olympic Games, and for his assurance regarding the safety of our athletes". Several pro-Palestinian protesters and activists in France and the United States, along with Palestinian sports clubs and the Washington-based Council on American-Islamic Relations, had joined a call for the IOC to restrict Israel's official participation in the 2024 Summer Games due to the ongoing conflict in Gaza. In March, Pierre-Olivier Beckers-Vieujant, the head of the IOC coordination committee for Paris 2024, stated that it was "out of the question to imagine" imposing sanctions on Israel over the war in Gaza, similar to the measures taken against Russia and its Olympic Committee in response to the invasion of Ukraine. The Olympic Games in Paris are scheduled to take place from July 26 to August 11. Numerous Israeli athletes are vying for podium finishes at the upcoming event. Among them is Avishag Semberg, a taekwondo competitor who clinched a bronze medal at the 2020 Olympics. Another strong contender is gymnast Artem Dolgopyat, who made history by winning Israel's inaugural gymnastics gold in 2020. Lanir, a reigning world champion in her division, is also expected to make a strong showing. Meanwhile, a contingent of eight Palestinian athletes will also be participating in the Paris Games, showcasing their skills and representing their nation on the global stage.

title: Simone Biles seeks more Olympic gymnastics glory as athletics kicks off in Paris
text: Simone Biles (Photo by Patrick Smith/Getty Images) NEW DELHI: Simone Biles , the renowned US gymnast, is set to make history once again at the Olympic Games in Paris. On Thursday, she will compete for the all-around title, aiming to become the first woman to regain this prestigious crown after her well-documented withdrawal in Tokyo due to the "Twisties". As the sixth full day of competition unfolds, a total of 16 gold medals will be awarded across various sports. Paris is bracing for extreme weather conditions, with storm warnings in place for the early hours of Thursday morning. Biles, who recently claimed her eighth Olympic medal and fifth gold with the US team, solidifying her status as the most decorated US Olympic gymnast, is determined to showcase her skills in style. She plans to unveil a new skill on the uneven bars, which would be the sixth unique skill named after her. However, Biles will face fierce competition from her teammate, Sunisa Lee, the reigning Olympic all-around champion. Lee's comeback story is equally compelling, as she was diagnosed with two undisclosed kidney conditions in early 2023 but declared herself "in remission" in April, feeling stronger than ever. Another top contender is Brazil's Rebeca Andrade, who expressed her honor to compete alongside Biles. "She's a reference, a role model for the whole world, gymnastics and athletes alike to see how happy she is to compete. That's what's sport is all about," said Andrade. The athletics events commence with the men's and women's 20km walk races. Massimo Stano from Italy aims to secure consecutive gold medals in the men's event after his victory in Tokyo. However, he faces tough rivals in Perseus Karlstrom from Sweden, the current world number one, and Koki Ikeda from Japan. In the women's race, Antonella Palmisano, also from Italy, defends her Olympic title. The iconic Eiffel Tower serves as the backdrop for these races. The swimming schedule remains packed, featuring the women's 200m butterfly final. Summer McIntosh, a 17-year-old Canadian sensation and rising star of the Games, competes in this event. Already crowned the 400m medley champion and securing silver in the 400m freestyle, McIntosh encounters a formidable field, including the defending champion, Zhang Yufei from China. Tatjana Smith from South Africa takes center stage in the women's 200m breaststroke, striving to achieve a feat last accomplished by her compatriot Penny Heyns at the Atlanta 1996 Games - winning both the 100m and 200m titles. Smith, who set a world record of 2:18.95 when claiming gold in Tokyo, enters the race in exceptional form after securing the 100m title on Monday. Additional gold medals are at stake in various disciplines, including kayak canoeing, fencing, judo, rowing, sailing, and shooting. The golf competition begins, featuring eight of the world's top 10 players, such as two-time major champion Collin Morikawa and the world's top-ranked player, Scottie Scheffler. The unpredictable Parisian weather, which has fluctuated from heavy rainfall during the opening ceremony to a heatwave just days later, may once again play a significant role. Paris and its surrounding areas are currently under an orange alert, the second-highest level, with forecasts of heavy rain, hail, and winds reaching up to 90 kilometers per hour. The weather has already impacted the archery competition, leading to the postponement of the final session on Wednesday.

title: Paris Olympics 2024: Google Doodle celebrates skateboarding
text: NEW DELHI: Google on Saturday celebrated Skateboarding events scheduled to be held during the Paris Olympics 2024 at Place de La Concorde by releasing a special Doodle featuring a group of birds skateboarding on a rooftop. The Google doodle highlights the men's skateboarding events , which consist of two rounds. The men's street prelims are scheduled for the afternoon, followed by the final round in the evening. The 2024 Paris Olympics kicked off on July 26 and will continue till August 11. Skateboarding, along with breaking, surfing, and sports climbing, is one of the four new sports that have been introduced to the Olympic program, joining the 28 traditional Olympic sports. The Paris Olympics 2024, which marks the 33rd edition of the event, will see athletes from over 200 countries gathering at the French capital to compete in 329 events across 32 sports disciplines.

title: Paris Olympics 2024: Bajrang Lal Takhar sets modest target for Balraj Panwar
text: Bajrang Lal Takhar Bajrang Lal Takhar is returning to the Olympics after a gap of 16 years, this time as a coach. The Arjuna awardee and Padma Shri is in Paris to guide Balraj Panwar , the countryâs lone rower at the Games, in single scull. âIt is a proud moment for me that I have got a chance (to be at the Olympics) as a coach, and I am at a loss for words. Itâs difficult to explain my feelings,â he said. âDefinitely happy and excited, but it is different as a player and a coach. I have to get the best out of my boy, that is my biggest target. I got to learn by competing in the Olympics, now I am getting to learn as a coach. If we can focus on our performance and implement the lessons, it will be good for us not only in this event but also for (Indian) rowing in the future.â Earlier this month, Panwar and Takhar along with assistant coach Gurdarshan Singh and sparring partner Salman Khan underwent a two-week camp in Gravelines before the core members moved to Paris last Sunday. The lightweight double scull duo of Arvind Singh and Arjun Lal Jat had given Indian rowing its best-ever finish at the Olympics with their 12th place finish in Tokyo. In single scull, in which India failed to qualify in 2020, Dattu Bhokanalâs 13th position in 2016 Rio stands out as the best-ever so far. Takhar himself was 21st in 2008 Beijing followed by Sawarn Singh Virk at 16th in 2012 London. The coach suggested it would be more appropriate to set Dattuâs performance as benchmark than that of Arjun-Arvind combinationâs. âThe two are different events. I will look at how Dattu (Bhokanal) did. He finished 13th and that is the challenge for me,â Takhar said. âWe are looking to reach the semifinals.â Panwar sealed his berth for Paris by finishing third in the Asian Qualification event in Chungju, South Korea, in April.

title: Paris Olympics 2024: New Zealand eye repeat of World Cup win in Olympic opener vs India
text: Image credit: Hockey India The last time New Zealand faced off against the Indian menâs hockey team was in the crossover stage of the World Cup last year. In front of a packed Kalinga Stadium in Bhubaneswar, the hosts took a 2-0 lead early in the second quarter, but the Black Sticks played out of their skin to make it 3-3 at the end of regulation time and eventually grabbed the win via penalty shoot-outs to break the hearts of the Indian fans. It was a massive blow to the hosts but New Zealand were ecstatic and they will be looking to repeat the feat at the Olympics on Saturday when the two teams play their opening game at Stade Yves-du-Manoir in Colombes near Paris. Speaking ahead of the game, Sean Findlay, who won the player of the match award in Bhubaneswar, expectedly sounded quite excited about the upcoming encounter. âItâs a cool opportunity for both India and New Zealand. Obviously doing well in the first match will prepare us well for the rest of the group matches heading towards the quarterfinals,â said Findlay from Paris earlier this week. âFrom previous experiences, we know they will be very tight and they can go both ways. But we are hoping to get the job done and grab all the three points.â Asked whether their win during the World Cup will have any bearing on Saturdayâs encounter, Fundlay said, âWe know India will come out and try to get their revenge. They will try to get one better on us after we knocked them out of the World Cup. As far as the actual game is concerned, it will be high tempo and New Zealand will have to put out a complete team performance. And a couple of individuals will have to step up and play crucial parts in big moments.â Hopefully, they will be able to do that because New Zealand coach Nicol would surely like to grab a win against his former South Africa teammate and current India coach Craig Fulton. Speaking ahead of the encounter, Nicol said from Paris, âItâs exciting to face off against India in the first match of the Olympics. They are the bronze medallists from Tokyo Olympics. There should be a great atmosphere and a great start to the tournament. We also had a classic encounter at the World Cup, and we havenât played since.â And helping him out will be Gregg Clarke, who was part of Indiaâs support staff during the World Cup and Tokyo Olympics and is also well acquainted with both Nicol and Fulton, having played with them for South Africa. âWe didnât bring him into the squad just because of the India match but he obviously trained a lot of these players and has a lot of knowledge on who will be playing on Saturday. Itâs of course very valuable for us and hopefully itâs the 1% that we need to hopefully earn the win,â Nicol added. Well, itâs hard to say whether his wish will come true or not on Saturday but whatâs certain is it will be quite a memorable affair.

title: Paris Olympics 2024: Athletes training in Spala to depart for Paris on July 29
text: Reuters Photo NEW DELHI: Three Russians â two coaches and one masseur â attached with the Indian Olympics contingent are yet to receive their Olympic Identity and Accreditation Cards (OIACs), as they are yet to submit their mandatory undertaking to IOC which says that Russian and Belarusian athletes, coaches, govt and state officials can be allowed to compete, invited or accredited for the Games âonly if they do not actively support the war or do not work for either countryâs military or national security apparatusesâ. Most of the cases involved liking or sharing posts on social media in support of the war. Those athletes from Russia and Belarus who have been allowed to compete in Paris are participating with -out a national title, flag or anthem and are referred as âIndividual Neutral Athletes (AIN)â after giving the undertaking that they do not support the war. While Sibileva has been coaching Paris-bound race walkers Akshdeep Singh, Vikash Singh and Paramjeet Singh Bisht, Kapustin has been training triple jumper Abdulla Aboobacker. Emira, who wasnât originally part of sup -port staff, was also scheduled to travel with the athletics team. A majority of the 29-member Indian athletics contingent has been training in Spala since the beginning of this month and will be de -parting for Paris from the Polish city on July 29. In the case of race walkers and Aboobacker, they will be reaching Paris either on Sunday or Monday but without the Russian coaches . The race walkers and Aboobacker were supposed to travel to Spala for the pre-Olympic training camp along with other contingent members, but they couldnât do so after the Polish govt specifically asked the Russian coaches to give an undertaking in writing that they do not sup -port the war and have no active role to play in it. When Sibileva and Kapus -tin refused to give such an undertaking fearing backlash from the Russian govt, Polish govt refused them visas. The Athletics Federation of India deemed it futile to send the race walkers and Aboobacker to Spala without their foreign coaches. They stayed put at the Sports Authority of Indiaâs (SAI) Bengaluru centre and continued their training for Paris. They will be joining the other contingent members directly in Paris from India. For the Paris Games, when the Games OC asked for such an undertaking from them as mandated by the IOC, the Indian Olympic Association (IOA) wrote to the AFI seeking the same for the processing of their accreditations. Itâs not clear f the Russians will get the visa for France or not, but their wards are already bracing for the fact that they might have to be without their coaches during the most important assignments of their lives.

title: Exclusive - 'I want to win a medal this time': Manika Batra on her Paris Olympics aspirations
text: Manika Batra (Getty Images) NEW DELHI: Indian table tennis teams, both menâs and womenâs, recently scripted history by booking their tickets to this yearâs Paris Olympics . It will be the first time India will compete in the table tennis team events at the Olympics. Earlier, both the Indian teams failed to secure direct qualifications to the Paris Games, after losing their respective pre-quarterfinals matches at the World Table Tennis Championships in Busan, South Korea. The prestigious tournament offered Olympic quotas to the quarter-finalists. It could have been âso close, yet so far awayâ for the Indian teams, but they finally made the cut through their world rankings. The Indian womenâs team qualified through their latest rankings of 13, while the menâs team makes it as 15th ranked team. After the historic qualification to the Summer Games, India's top-ranked table tennis player Manika Batra delved into their qualification journey, challenges, preparations ahead of the Olympics, aspirations, dreams, and much more during an exclusive chat with TimesofIndia.com. Excerpts: How was the journey to qualifying for the Paris Olympics? The experience of the World Championships this year was satisfying. Everything was very good in the way we all played and the team's spirit. The team spirit played an important role. Sreeja, Ayhika, Diya, Archana â we were supporting and cheering for whoever was out there on the court. We displayed our abilities well this time, playing like fighters against every team, be it China or Hungary. Yes, we had this national camp before the World Championships. The camp helped us a lot individually, and staying with the team improved our synergy. We are happy that we eventually qualified for the Olympics in the women's team for the first time. So we will prepare really well for the big event. (Getty Images) Were there any major challenges you encountered en route to qualifying for the Olympics? There were challenges, some good challenges, I would say. All the matches were very close encounters, against China and Hungary; the one against Spain was an important one. We were 0-2 down, but the way we won the match 3-2 from that point was vital for us. Planning how to make the comeback was a huge challenge for us at that time. Then Ayhika won her third match, I won my match, and then Sreeja won the last one. That was a challenging match for us. Apart from that, there were not many challenges as we all were so focused on giving our 100 per cent in this team tournament. How do you prepare physically for such a high-stakes competition like the Olympics? We do have limited time left before the Olympics. I will do my best to improve every aspect of my game, be it my table skills or the physical side of the game. I will also focus on my recovery as I want to go fresh into the Olympics. The women's team will plan together how to train collectively. That would ultimately help us during the team matches. Right now, I will be focusing on singles with my coach Aman Balgu. (Getty Images) I would like to train in India for singles because I have a different style. But for the team training, we need to be together. We are yet to plan whether to train in India or outside India because we have to be together. We will plan that accordingly. What are the goals that you have set for yourself both team wise and individually? I want to win a medal this time. I will just focus on putting in the effort without thinking too much about the results. I don't know what the results will be. But it is my aim to win a medal, and I will go with that goal only, nothing less.

title: Paris Olympics: After Korean coach's accreditation fiasco, 'tainted' physio's presence sparks row in Indian archery contingent
text: Baek Woong Ki (left) (Getty Images file photo) NEW DELHI: A day after Korean chief coach Baek Woong Ki was forced out of India's archery contingent due to a lack of Olympic accreditation, controversy erupted regarding the inclusion of 'tainted' physio Arvind Yadav at his expense. Baek Woong Ki and Dronacharya award-winning High Performance Director Sanjeeva Singh were excluded from the support staff, with allegations surfacing against Yadav's misconduct from the previous year. A top official from the Archery Association of India (AAI) disclosed that Yadav, facing accusations of making an 'inappropriate approach' to a Canadian teenager during the Youth World Championships in Limerick, Ireland, in November last year, was instead included in the contingent. Despite the allegations, India secured an impressive medal haul of six gold, one silver, and four bronze at the event. "As per the complaint from the World Archery competition manager Thomas Aubert, Yadav had made an inappropriate approach to a Canadian teenager on social media," the official told PTI. "The Canadian coach reported this to the WA, who in turn raised the complaint with AAI. Federation called an ethics committee meeting and dismissed the matter saying the 'inappropriate approach' to the teenaged Canadian archer was a 'normal hi, hello'," he revealed. Yadav denied the allegations vehemently. He claimed that the accusations were part of a conspiracy to tarnish his reputation. "It's a conspiracy to malign me. Nothing of this sort has happened. Why didn't AAI take action against me then? Also, the archers could have objected to my appointment," Yadav said. The AAI source claimed that Yadav is very close to the body's secretary general Virendra Sachdeva. "Whenever there is a top competition he makes such a back-door entry. He was there in Rio Olympics too. He didn't accompany the team during the Asian Games last year." "This time also he came three months prior to join the national camp and was given an accreditation. The AAI could have easily cut off his name and allowed the Korean chief coach who is specifically contracted for the Olympics," the AAI official added. AAI president Arjun Munda declined to discuss the accusations against Yadav. He stressed that the selection of the support staff is based on the archers' preferences, emphasizing that the federation does not impose staff members on the team. "Why are you raking this up? Let's not talk about it. Let's not create another controversy now," Munda told PTI when asked about Yadav's inclusion and the incident last year. Munda insisted that it's the archers who "wanted him" to be a part of the support staff. "This is somehow a tricky decision which depends on the players' comfort and whom they want in the team and the federation gives priority to that. AAI doesn't interfere in this, we don't want to force someone in the team," said Munda. AAI blames IOA for Woong Ki accreditation fiasco The AAI official, who raised questions on Yadav's inclusion, also pointed out that the IOA-approved 13-member medical team for Olympics, which is headed by acclaimed sports injury expert Dr Dinshaw Pardiwala, should have been enough for the archers. "The team has physiotherapists, nutritionists, psychologists, even a sleep therapist this time. Why does the federation needs their own physio and psychologist (Gayatri Vartak) who has joined only a few months back?" the official questioned. "They could have struck off those two names and easily included Baek and Singh, who has accompanied the Indian team in all the junior and senior events in this Olympics cycle," he said. "Singh is an expert in archery and someone who set up the Centre of Excellence in Sonipat at the cost of Rs 100-crore. He also brought in the current AAI sponsors NTPC," he added. In search of their maiden medal in the Olympics, the Indian archery team has spent 10 days at their base camp in Compeigne, which is 80km north of Paris. The AAI blamed the Indian Olympic Association for rejecting their "repeated requests" to accommodate Singh and Woong Ki, despite the fact that the IOA had clearly specified it "won't allow more than four officials" for the six-member contingent. India have Sonam Singh Bhutia (from Army Sports Institute) as the men's coach and Padma Shri Poornima Mahato as women's coach, who is from Tata Archery Academy since two of their archers in the team. All the three male archers are from ASI. "IOA set a yardstick and despite all our requests they didn't accept one more accreditation. "I spoke to PT Usha personally requesting her to include... The IOA should have fought for it. It is beyond my logic why they are not allowing one official in AAI whereas many officials are accompanying in other federations," Munda added. Former AAI functionary Anil Kamineni said IOA follows a quota system and there was no way another coach could be accommodated. "This is how it is and we should now focus on doing well in the Olympics. Our archers have been doing well and let's hope for the best," Kamineni said. Woong Ki left for India on Saturday and made it clear that he would not stay beyond August 30, when his contract ends. Stay updated with the latest IPL Live Score Score, IPL news on Times of India . title: 'I really want to say sorry': Boxer Lovlina Borgohain's emotional message after Paris Olympics exit
text: NEW DELHI: Tokyo 2020 bronze medalist Lovlina Borgohain was eliminated from the Paris Olympics after a defeat to Chinaâs Li Qian in the women's 75kg quarterfinal at the North Paris Arena. Lovlinaâs 1-4 split decision loss marked the end of India's boxing campaign in Paris, with no medals secured. Following her exit, Lovlina, who was one of India's biggest hopes for a medal in Paris, shared an emotional message on social media. âI sincerely apologize to the entire nation for not bringing home a medal this time, especially to the people of Assam who always support me,â Lovlina wrote. âI will work harder and come back stronger. This isnât the end; Iâm looking for a fresh start. I also want to thank all the coaches, support staff, SAI, Assam Government, BFI, Reliance Sports Foundation, IOS Sports, and all my sponsors for their unwavering support and encouragement,â she added. The 26-year-oldâs defeat concluded Indiaâs boxing efforts at the Olympics, following Nishant Devâs earlier elimination from the menâs 71kg quarterfinals in a closely contested match. The six-member boxing team, comprising four women and two men, represented India at the Games, with four members exiting in the preliminary rounds.
author: TOI Sports Desk

title: Former India goalkeeper Jude Menezes hopes to take Japan women's hockey team into the knockouts
text: Jude Menezes Kolkata: Playing for India, Jude Menezes made it to the Olympics only once. It was Sydney in 2000 where the Indian menâs hockey team failed to make it to the knockouts and finished seventh. He did compete at the World Cup two years later but never took part in the Olympics as a player again. Twice after that, he did go to the Olympics but as part of the support staff of the New Zealand womenâs hockey team. Even then success eluded him as in 2016, they finished fourth and three years back in Tokyo, the team lost to the Netherlands in the quarterfinal and finished eighth. Now, Menezes has an even more challenging task at hand as the coach of the Japanese womenâs hockey team. After taking over the team post Tokyo Olympics he guided them to a couple of titles but the going hasnât been easy. Despite the odds though he was able to guide them to the Paris Olympics and it was a huge achievement for the former India goalkeeper. Since then, the team has again struggled but Menezes is rather hopeful of making it to the knockouts. âWe are taking one match at a time initially. We are in a tough pool where we got four teams ranked above us but it doesnât matter. What matters is the performance on the day. And we need to win at least two games to be among the top-four teams and make it to the knockouts,â said Menezes ahead of Japanâs opener against Germany on Sunday. To make sure they are at their best in Paris, Japan played a couple of matches against the Netherlands in Zwolle, Netherlands, and Menezes believes it was one of the preparations that they could have got. âItâs very critical because they are the best team in the world. The pace that they play at is a great learning for us because we usually donât get the opportunity to play against them. So just giving this exposure to my players was very beneficial because every other team that we play in the Olympics will be lesser than the Dutch,â he added. Besides the matches in Zwolle, they also played a few warm-up games in Paris but he believes the team hasnât reached its full potential yet and that they can perform even better. âIt's satisfying to see the steady progress. We are still learning, still growing and itâs good to see that we are heading in the right direction. So, the Olympics will be a good test to see where we are,â added the Mumbai-born coach. âBut I am never satisfied. I am always looking to be better. To a certain extent maybe I am satisfied but I do believe we can do a lot better. So, the quest for improving and the quest for excellence is always ongoing.â Well, they certainly will have to be much better than what they have been so far to make it to the knockouts because, besides Germany, they will be facing off against China, France, Belgium, and the Netherlands in the other group matches. Not only did they finish fifth in the Nations Cup in June, but they also lost all their matches during a tri-nation Test series in Australia where China was the other competing nation. But Menezes does have the coaching acumen to turn things around and hopefully, he will be able to do that over the next couple of weeks.
author: TOI Sports Desk

title: Paris Olympics: Simone Biles proud of showing her strength, 'coming out on top'
text: Simone Biles (Photo by Naomi Baker/Getty Images) NEW DELHI: Simone Biles departs from Paris feeling a sense of accomplishment and pride in her achievements. As a three-time Olympian, she continues to demonstrate her unparalleled prowess in gymnastics while maintaining her poise and elegance. During the Olympic Games, Biles, at the age of 27, secured gold medals in the team, all-around, and vault events. Additionally, she earned a silver medal in the floor exercise competition. In an interview with Reuters on Tuesday, the decorated athlete, who now boasts a total of 11 Olympic medals, shared that she is still absorbing the experiences of the past few weeks. Nevertheless, she expressed satisfaction in her unwavering resolve and the outcomes she achieved. â(I am) just showing my strength through and through and just coming out on top each and every time so Iâm just really proud of that,â she said. Biles, a four-time Olympic gold medalist and bronze winner at the Rio Games in 2016, has undergone significant personal growth since her teenage triumph. Despite facing challenges during the Tokyo Games in 2021, where she withdrew due to a mental block known as the "twisties", Biles has emerged as a resilient and self-aware athlete. When reflecting on her current self, Biles confidently stated: "A hard worker, dedicated, strong, beautiful, smart." These words encapsulate the qualities she has cultivated over the years, showcasing her determination and personal development. Beyond her individual achievements, Biles has also taken on the role of a supportive teammate. Sunisa Lee, one of her fellow gymnasts, has praised Biles for her ability to boost confidence and provide guidance behind the scenes, highlighting her leadership skills and positive influence within the team. "Having (my teammates) there to lean on was absolutely amazing and I wouldn't have made it through without them," Lee told Reuters.

title: ArcelorMittal showcases low-carbon steel tie-up with Paris Olympics 2024
text: Paris Olympics (X Photo) NEW DELHI: ArcelorMittal , the steel giant led by Indian businessman Lakshmi Mittal , is highlighting the different aspects of its low-carbon steel collaboration with the upcoming Olympics and Paralympics in Paris. The company, based in Luxembourg, announced recently that its recycled and renewably-produced XCarb steel is being used in the construction of the Torches that have been traveling around the globe, as well as the Olympic Rings adorning the famous Eiffel Tower and the Agitos symbol of the Paralympics on top of the Arc de Triomphe in Paris. The Paris Olympics 2024 is also breaking new ground by reusing the Torches, marking the first time this has been done. This initiative has significantly reduced the carbon footprint associated with the production of the Torches, as only 2,000 were needed compared to the 12,000 required in previous years. The move towards sustainability and eco-friendly practices is a key focus of the upcoming Olympic and Paralympic Games in the French capital. "We think the Games are about sport, but they transcend sport," Ian Louden, the Head of Brand for ArcelorMittal, told reporters in Paris. "They go over and above sport itself, trying at least to bring together the world on a platform of equality and peace and shared belief. For example, for the very first time in Paris 2024, there are equal numbers of male and female athletes. As a leading global industrial company, we think this is exactly the kind of event in society that we should support," he said. ArcelorMittal, a prominent steel manufacturing company, has once again partnered with the Olympic Games, this time for the upcoming Paris 2024 event. The collaboration builds upon their previous involvement in the London 2012 Olympic Games , which resulted in the creation of the iconic ArcelorMittal Orbit designed by renowned British Indian artist Anish Kapoor. For the Paris Games, set to commence on July 26 and conclude on August 11, ArcelorMittal will be providing the essential steel and manufacturing expertise for two significant elements. The first is the Olympic Torch, which has been designed by French artist Mathieu Lehanneur. The second involves the Spectaculars, comprising the Olympic Rings and the Agitos, a project overseen by engineer Professor Pierre Engel. "This is the work of a big team, from the production of the steel in Chateauneuf in Burgundy to the lifting of the rings involving about 200 people," said Professor Engel. "We had to face several challenges and the first one was to decide the position, then imagine innovative lighting and, of course, the safety of a project involving such iconic landmarks of Paris," he said. Engel and his team worked at pace over the course of 18 months with a retired Army man in charge of keeping the timelines to military precision. "We could not risk any drifting timelines associated with the construction industry with this project, with the date of the Games a definitive finishing line," noted Engel. Measuring 29 metres wide by 15 metres high, and positioned approximately 84 metres off the ground, in between the first and second floors of the Eiffel Tower, the Rings appear in their coloured form of red, blue, green, yellow and black â depicting the five continents of the world. At night, they are lit up in white "because you cannot light black", explains Engel. The Agitos, meanwhile, depicted in red, blue and green, are lit up in colour 24/7. "Being an official partner of the Paris 2024 Olympic and Paralympic Games and supplier of the Torch gives ArcelorMittal an incredible opportunity to showcase the beauty, flexibility and potential of steel," said CEO Aditya Mittal. ArcelorMittal's XCarb products are manufactured using the electric arc furnace process, incorporating a high proportion of scrap steel and relying solely on renewable energy sources. As a result, the carbon footprint of these products can be as minimal as roughly 300kg of CO2 per tonne of completed steel. The 2024 Olympic project, carried out entirely within France, involved repurposing scrap steel from discarded vehicles and household appliances. The "Spectaculars" are anticipated to have a lifespan extending well past the Olympic Games. The city's Mayor has expressed a desire to maintain their presence atop the landmarks at least until the end of the year, with the expectation that they will find a second life in the subsequent set of Games hosted by France. As the grand opening ceremony approaches on July 26, Paris is actively engaged in preparations and embellishments. The Torch will traverse the River Seine, ultimately reaching the Olympic Cauldron situated at an undisclosed location within the French capital, the details of which remain closely guarded. "This global event, the most famous and engaging sports event in the world, resonates with the values that drive our group and all our employees around the world: the desire to constantly raise the bar; inclusion and diversity; and the quest for net zero, illustrated by the Paris 2024 ambition to limit its CO2 footprint," added ArcelorMittal Chairman Lakshmi Mittal.

title: Iran slams Israel participation in Paris Olympics
text: (Getty Images) NEW DELHI: Iran condemned the reception and protection of Israeli athletes at the upcoming Olympic Games in Paris, calling for their exclusion due to Israel's actions in the Gaza war. The Israeli delegation arrived in France on Monday under tight security, amidst global criticism over the high civilian casualties and humanitarian crisis in Gaza. "Announcing the reception and protection of the apartheid terrorist Zionist regime's delegation means giving legitimacy to the child killers," Iran's foreign ministry said in a post on X. "They do not deserve to be present at the Paris Olympics because of the war against the innocent people of Gaza," it added, calling on organisers to ban Israel. The conflict in Gaza erupted following the October 7 attacks on Israel by Hamas, a militant group backed by Iran. The attacks resulted in the deaths of 1,197 people in Israel, most of them civilians, according to an AFP tally based on Israeli official figures. In response, Israel launched an offensive in Gaza, leading to the deaths of at least 39,090 people, mostly civilians, based on data from Gaza's health ministry. Iran, which does not recognize Israel, enforces a strict policy prohibiting any contact between Iranian and Israeli athletes. Since the 1979 Islamic revolution, Iran has aligned its foreign policy strongly in support of the Palestinian cause. Back in February, Iran's football federation requested FIFA to suspend Israel's football association because of the ongoing conflict in Gaza. Additionally, Iranian weightlifter Mostafa Rajaei received a lifetime ban last August for shaking hands with an Israeli competitor at an event in Poland, according to state media. In 2021, Iran's supreme leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei advised athletes, "not to shake hands with a representative of the (Israeli) criminal regime to obtain a medal." This directive underscores Iran's deep-seated opposition to any form of engagement with Israeli representatives.

title: Paris Olympics 2024: Medals feature Eiffel tower iron pieces in unique design
text: Olympic medals (AP Photo) NEW DELHI: The Paris 2024 Olympic and Paralympic medals will feature a unique design that incorporates a piece of the Eiffel Tower. Each gold, silver, and bronze medal will have a hexagonal, polished chunk of iron taken from the iconic landmark embedded in its centre. This marks the first time in Olympic history that a host city has included pieces of a famous monument in the medals. The iron pieces, weighing 18 grams each, were obtained from girders and other parts that were replaced during renovations of the Eiffel Tower. They were stripped of paint, polished, and varnished before being stamped with Paris 2024 and the Olympics games logo. The hexagonal shape of the iron pieces represents France, often referred to as "L'Hexagone" due to its geographical shape. The medals, designed by Paris jewellery house Chaumet , feature disks of recycled gold, silver, or bronze surrounding the iron pieces. These disks are crinkled to reflect light and make the medals shine. The ancient Greek goddess of victory, Nike, is depicted on the other side of the Olympic medals, along with a small representation of the Eiffel Tower. The Paralympic medals show a view of the tower from underneath, with Paris 2024 written in Braille and notches on the edges to distinguish between gold, silver, and bronze. The Paris Mint is producing 5,084 medals in total, with the gold medals weighing 529 grams and containing 6 grams of gold plating over silver. The silver medals weigh 525 grams, while the bronze medals weigh 455 grams and are made of a copper, tin, and zinc alloy. Each medal measures 85 millimeters across and 9.2 millimeters thick. They will be presented in a dark-blue box from Chaumet, along with a certificate from the Eiffel Tower Operating Co. verifying the authenticity of the iron pieces. title: Paris Olympics 2024: Through sun and rain, there will always be Paris
text: Reuters Photo PARIS: The boats from Fridayâs opening ceremony all stowed away, the Olympics have well and truly begun. The constant drizzle over the city, its gloomy skies, raincoats and umbrellas â parapluies, in these parts â and the mawkish expressions of the Parisians, is just a distraction. Donât fall for it. Soon the skies will clear, the sun will shine through, bring with it that breeze, returning the city to old ways of its famous summer. Be distracted by that. But until then, Italy and Brazil are battling it out on the volleyball court, a high-octane clash that could remind an old-timer of the 1980s and â90s football matches of the sporting heavyweights. Inside the Paris Expo Porte de Versailles, the venue for the volleyball tournament, in a sign of the changed times, spectators are happier waving their cellphones with the torches on than hollering at each other as the Italians prevail 3-1. Later in the evening, Rafa Nadal , the adopted son of Paris, and the sportâs heir apparent, Carlos Alcaraz will line-up together for Spain on the clay of Roland Garros. It is an early-day marquee event, a big-ticket, the opposition doesnât matter, even if it happens to be Argentina (thereâs very little of the football parallel at play here). But how weird it must feel to perform at a venue that bears a statue of you at the entrance â an installation in steel capturing a furious backhand return at full tilt â what else is left to do, to prove? But then this is Nadal, this is his âhomeâ, the Paris Olympics is his final appearance and while there are contenders banging on the door, his doubles partner here, no less, no one can evict him from his Parisian apartment. Talking of home, and of statues, the Spaniard, with the sneer-smile but impeccable manners, was at hand to take over the torch from Zinedine Zidane , that other human installation France has erected, in an opening ceremony symbolism that spoke volumes. The French, with their avant garde thought and fearlessness to express, may just have attempted the most outrageous pageantry with their aqua-tableau over the Seine Friday. That they had gotten away with it, may have irked the English-speaking press no end, who in their self-appointed roles as the worldâs judges of anything and everything, were decreeing that even after they had walked on water, the French had still come up short. And that, the opening ceremony of the 2012 London Olympics â even if no one remembers how it went â remains the bar that is yet to be surpassed. Talk about being stranded on an island. But in an opening ceremony meant to showcase sporting excellence, hope and glory â much of it bankrolled by global corporate wealth â when you pre -sent Dionysus, the Greek god of wine and ecstasy, telling us not to take ourselves too seriously, or nudging us to reflect on the absurdities we spawn by that, the rest of the world will carp in a reluctant, grudging acceptance of cultural superiority. When you have the moral courage to depict inclusiveness, gender equality and the freedom to choose with suggestions of a threesome â the much-malinged menage a trois in these parts â the conservatives will be shocked, their sensibilities shaken, but you neednât explain yourself. It was in this strange cultural mÃ©lange â there were more global stars that Paris invited to be part of their theatre than others can ever even begin to think of â that the calming reassuring presence of Zidane may have soothed the nerves of the easily outraged. Not that the mostly-unspeaking, famously apolitical Frenchman returns us to conservatism, but it is his universal appeal that unites us all despite usually being out of reach, of touching distance. Imagine what unique aura Zidane must possess then, that 26 years after his face was plastered on the faÃ§ade of the Arc de Triomphe after a thankful nation chanted his name â the son of an Algerian immigrant â for delivering France their first World Cup in 1998, on Friday, of all of Franceâs great Olympians, his presence has stayed with us much after the last boat came in.

title: Paris 2024 headquarters searched as part of corruption investigations
text: Reuters Photo PARIS: The headquarters of the Paris 2024 Olympics organising committee and those of its infrastructure partner were being searched by police on Tuesday as part of investigations into alleged embezzlement of public funds and favouritism, prosecutors said. The national financial prosecutor's office (PNF) said the Paris 2024 headquarters were raided amid a preliminary investigation launched in 2017 into contracts made by the Summer Games' organising committee. The headquarters of SOLIDEO, the public body responsible for delivering Olympic and Paralympic infrastructure, were also being searched amid a preliminary investigation dating back to 2022, following an audit by the French Anti-Corruption Agency, the PNF added. "A search is currently under way at the headquarters of the Organising Committee," Paris 2024 said in a statement. "Paris 2024 is cooperating fully with the investigators to facilitate their inquiries." Paris 2024 did not give any further details and made no further comment after the prosecutors' statement. The Paris 2024 Olympics, which organising committee president Tony Estanguet has vowed will be "beyond reproach", will be held from July 26-Aug. 11 with the Paralympic Games taking place from Aug. 28-Sept. 6. The searches coincided with the start of a two-day International Olympic Committee Executive Board on Tuesday to discuss a number of issues, including progress of Paris 2024 Games preparations. "We are aware that there has been a search by police of the Paris 2024 headquarters today," an IOC spokesperson said. "We have been informed by Paris 2024 that they are cooperating fully with the authorities in this matter." The total budget of the Games has soared to 8.8 billion euros ($9.62 billion) from an initial assessment of 6.6 billion in 2017. The infrastructure alone is expected to cost 4 billion euros from an original estimate of 3.2 billion. The cost is limited as most of the events will be held in existing facilities. The cost of security, which according to France's supreme audit institution would reach at least 400 million euros, has not been included in the overall budget. It is not the first time that Olympics organisers have been the subject of an investigation. Japanese prosecutors earlier this year indicting six companies including advertising giant Dentsu Group and seven individuals over suspected rigging of bids worth $320 million for the Tokyo 2020 Olympics and Paralympics. The indictments followed months of investigations into alleged corruption in the planning and sponsorship of the Tokyo Games, held in 2021 after a COVID-19 postponement. title: Brilliant Faith Kipyegon wins third straight Olympic women's 1,500m gold
text: NEW DELHI: Faith Kipyegon of Kenya etched her name in the annals of Olympic history on Saturday, becoming the first woman to secure three successive gold medals in the 1,500m event. The 30-year-old athlete, who previously triumphed in 2016 and 2020, delivered a strategic tour de force at the Stade de France, clinching victory in a new Olympic record time of 3min 51.29sec. Jessica Hull of Australia claimed the silver medal with a time of 3:52.56, while Georgia Bell of Great Britain secured the bronze in 3:52.61. Kipyegon's extraordinary feat solidifies her position as one of the greatest female middle-distance runners of all time. The reigning world champion's Olympic journey was not without its challenges, as she faced disqualification after initially placing second in the women's 5,000m on Monday, only to be later reinstated. "After what I went through over the 5,000m, I didn't sleep until yesterday," Kipyegon said after Saturday's win. "I want to thank all the people that supported me -- my coach, my management, my fans for telling me 'You've got this over the 1,500, You're going to make it.' "Making history is what I was aiming for and I really thank god for this." Kipyegon added she had promised her daughter she would deliver 1,500m gold after missing out in the 5,000m. "I told my daughter, 'I'm going to make you proud in the 1,500m,'" she said. "It was anybody's race. So for me to make history. Unbelievable. I'm crazy or something. I'm really really happy."

title: Mirabai Chanu sets marker for Paris Olympics
text: NEW DELHI: Injury-hit Mirabai Chanu is all set to push the weight envelope at the Paris Olympics next month. Admitting that she has reached â85 percentâ of her performance after recovering from hip tendonitis that she suffered during her fourth-place finish at the Hangzhou Asian Games, the Tokyo Olympics silver medallist has set herself a target of lifting a record 90kg in snatch and somewhere closer to 120kg in clean and jerk in Paris to become the first Indian weightlifter to win two Summer Games medals. âThe injury is fine now. I have recovered from that but I am going slow in my training. I am lifting 80-85 percent in repetitions and not going for 100 percent till the Olympics. My best in snatch is 88kg and 119kg in clean and jerk. In Paris, Iâll target 90kg-plus in snatch and also somewhere closer to my best in clean & jerk. Right now, I am going gradually and lifting 70-80kgs in snatch and 100-110kgs in clean & jerk. I will try to give my best performance in Paris but canât predict the colour of the medal,â said Mirabai, who will be competing in her preferred womenâs 49kg class. In weightlifting , India will have sole representation in Mirabai with no other lifters qualifying for the Games. The 30-year-old Manipuri weightlifter insisted that her success at the Games will depend on how well she manages to keep herself injury free. By her own admission, Paris will pose an arduous challenge as the âcompetition is going to be very toughâ. âI learnt a lot after the injuryâ¦how to keep myself safe because injuries can happen anytime. We need to follow the instructions of the coaches, adopt the right technique, rest and exercise properly, and how to build your muscles. I have started to understand my body and you canât push it beyond a certain limit. Injuries can happen anytime. It was a difficult phase and there were self-doubts. I am happy to make a comeback,â said Mirabai, who returned to competition after a six-month long injury layoff following her participation at the Phuket World Cup in April where she lifted a total of 184kgs (81kg in snatch and 103kg in clean & jerk). To have success in Paris, Mirabai will have to target a total lift of 200kg-plus to stand a chance to win her second Olympics medal. âPressure will be there. The competition is going to be very tough. Iâll try to give my best,â added the former world champion. title: Paris Olympics 2024: Everything you need to know about Torch Lighting Ceremony today
text: The cauldron lighting ceremony which is set to kickstart the Paris Olympics 2024, will commence today in Trocadero, Paris. Source: AFP via Getty Images The Paris Olympics 2024 is set to commence with the highly anticipated cauldron lighting ceremony today. This event marks the official start of the Games, symbolizing unity and the spirit of competition. The cauldron lighting ceremony is a grand spectacle that includes various performances, speeches, and a parade of nations. The final torchbearer, whose identity is often kept secret until the last moment, will carry the flame to the cauldron. This moment is the climax of the torch relay and signifies the unity and competitive spirit of the Games. The ceremony will be attended by dignitaries, athletes , and spectators, and will be broadcast live, allowing viewers worldwide to witness this historic moment. The rich and fascinating history of the torch lighting ceremony The tradition of lighting the Olympic flame dates back to the ancient Olympic Games in Olympia , Greece. In ancient Greece, the Olympic flame was kept burning through the duration of the ancient Olympics at the altar of Hestia, goddess of the Hearth. The flame symbolized the fire stolen from the Greek god Zeus by Prometheus and as tribute flames were lit every four years to honour Zeus and his wife Hera at the Olympic games. The modern Olympic flame was first introduced at the 1928 Amsterdam Games, but the torch relay began in 1936 at the Berlin Olympics. This was orchestrated by Carl Diem, the organizer of the Games, and was used as a propaganda tool by the Nazi regime. The flame is lit using a parabolic mirror to focus the sunâs rays, ensuring it is ignited naturally. This ritual connects the ancient and modern Games, preserving the heritage and significance of the Olympics. The torch relay is a significant part of the Olympic tradition, symbolizing peace, unity, and friendship. Once lit in Olympia, the flame embarks on a journey across the host country, carried by thousands of torchbearers. Each torchbearer represents a link in the chain of unity, passing the flame from one to another. The relay covers various landmarks and cities, engaging communities and spreading the Olympic spirit. Tennis player Naomi Osaka was the final torchbearer at the 2020 Tokyo Olympics. Source: Getty Images The cauldron lighting ceremony is the climax of the torch relay and the official start of the Olympic Games. Over the years, many notable individuals have had the honor of lighting the cauldron. Muhammad Ali , the legendary boxer battling Parkinson's at the time, lit the cauldron at the 1996 Atlanta Olympics, creating an unforgettable and emotional moment. Cathy Freeman, an Australian sprinter, lit the cauldron at the 2000 Sydney Olympics and more recently, Naomi Osaka, a tennis star, lit the cauldron at the 2020 Tokyo Olympics, representing hope and resilience. Significance of the ceremony The cauldron lighting ceremony holds deep symbolic meaning. It represents the continuity of the Olympic Games, linking the ancient traditions with the modern era. The flame embodies the values of peace, friendship, and unity, which are central to the Olympic movement. The ceremony also acts as a reminder of the global nature of the Games, bringing together athletes from around the world to compete in a spirit of mutual respect and excellence. What time is the 2024 lighting ceremony? Date: Friday, July 26 Location: Trocadero , Paris Time: 11 PM IST or 7:30 PM CEST (Paris Time) Cauldron lighting time: 2:30 am IST or 11:00 pm CEST (Paris Time) Former US skier Lindsey Vonn carries the Olympic torch in the Olympic village during the torch relay ahead of the Summer Olympic Games Paris 2024. Source: Getty Images The 2024 torch relay began in Olympia, Greece, on April 16, 2024. The flame traveled through Greece before being handed over to the Paris 2024 organizing committee in Athens on April 26. The flame then crossed the Mediterranean Sea and arrived in Marseille, France, on May 8, 2024, passing through the hands of 10,000 torchbearers from various cities and overseas French territories for two months before arriving in Paris. The final leg of the relay will see the flame carried along the Seine River, culminating in the cauldron lighting ceremony at the Trocadero. The event will be broadcast live, allowing viewers worldwide to witness this historic moment. Where to watch it? You can watch the Paris Olympics 2024 cauldron lighting ceremony live in India on the Sports18 1 SD and Sports18 1 HD TV channels. Additionally, live streaming will be available for free on Jio Cinema. The ceremony is scheduled to start at 11:00 PM IST today. Paris set for its first Olympics in 100 years

title: Paris Olympics: Breakdancing, Surfing, and more new sports to watch
text: NEW DELHI: The Paris Olympics in 2024 is set to introduce ground breaking changes that will redefine the Games. The opening ceremony will take place along the Seine River, where athletes will be paraded on boats to a large crowd of spectators, marking a significant departure from the traditional stadium setting. Moreover, the Paris Olympics is poised to be the most gender-inclusive edition in its 128-year history, with an equal number of male and female athletes participating across 329 events in 32 sports. The Games will also feature the introduction of new sports and the continuation of events that debuted at the 2020 Tokyo Olympics, while some sports have been discontinued to maintain universal appeal. New events in Paris Olympics 2024 Breakdancing Paris Olympics 2024: Breakdancing, also known as breaking, is a new addition to the Paris Olympics. Originating in the Bronx in the 1970s, this urban dance form has gained mainstream acceptance as a sport. Its popularity among young people was evident during the 2018 Youth Olympics in Buenos Aires, where over a million viewers watched the competition online. The IOC included breakdancing to stay relevant and appeal to a new generation. At the Paris Olympics, there will be male and female divisions, each featuring 16 dancers (B-Boys and B-Girls). Contestants will engage in one-on-one battles lasting around a minute, judged on creativity, performance, personality, technique, variety, and musicality. Events will be held at Place de la Concorde, transformed into an outdoor sporting venue. Improvisation is crucial, as dancers must create routines on the spot, adapting to the DJ's music. As French B-Girl Carlota Dudek explained to France 24 English, "When you go to get up on stage, you don't know what music is going to play or the DJ, so it's partly improv. It's really intuitive. You have to adapt to the moment." Kayak Cross Paris Olympics 2024 Kayak cross, also known as extreme slalom, will debut at the 2024 Olympics. Unlike traditional slalom, this event features four rowers racing head-to-head on an artificial white-water course. Its fast-paced, action-packed nature makes it an ideal spectator sport, with races lasting less than a minute. Debuting at the 2015 International Canoe Federation's World Cup, kayak cross quickly gained popularity. Kimerbly Woods, a UK Olympic canoeist, emphasises the competitive nature of kayak cross. In an explanation video, she pointed out that audiences "can expect a lot of carnage â¦ a lot of battles, a lot of bruises, a lot of tactics, a lot of surprises in the moment." The Olympic event will have both female and male competitions, starting with individual time trials followed by thrilling head-to-head races where boat contact is allowed, adding excitement and unpredictability. Kiteboarding Paris Olympics 2024 Kiteboarding, also referred to as kitesurfing, is an exhilarating sport that will make its Olympic debut at the Paris 2024 Games. It will be one of the ten sailing events featured in the competition. The kiteboarding competition will follow the Formula Kite format, with 20 male and 20 female athletes participating. Competitors will use approved kites and compete in wind conditions ranging from five to 40 knots. Two athletes to keep an eye on are Daniela Moroz from the United States and Maximilian Maeder from Singapore. Moroz currently holds the top spot in the Formula Kite women's rankings, while Maeder leads the men's category. In addition to mixed kiteboarding, sailing at the Paris 2024 Olympics will introduce two other new mixed events, including the mixed 470 class. New Sports that are returning from Tokyo Olympics Skateboarding Paris Olympics 2024 Skateboarding, which debuted in the 2020 Olympics, will return to the Paris Games with 88 participants, 8 more than in Tokyo. The competition will feature male and female street and park events. Skaters will have multiple 45-second runs to perform various tricks, with judges scoring each run from 0 to 100. The street event also includes a trick segment, where skateboarders get five chances to showcase individual tricks. Both events will be judged on the difficulty and variety of tricks performed. Skateboarding (Reuters Photo) Commenting on skateboarding's inclusion in the Olympics, renowned US skateboarder Tony Hawk expressed to Olympic.com that the sport had "finally come of age" and that it is becoming more inclusive, with "people of all genders [and backgrounds] â¦ all enjoying it together." Also see: Paris Olympics: India's top 10 medal contenders Surfing Paris Olympics 2024 Surfing, which debuted at Tokyo 2020, returns to the Paris Games with 48 participants, equally split between male and female athletes. This year's competition will be held in Teahupo'o, Tahiti, marking the furthest Olympic venue from the host city. Teahupo'o, known for the Tahiti Pro world championship, attracts top surfers like Gabriel Medina and Kelly Slater. Competitors will be judged by five experts on the complexity and variety of tricks, speed, flow, and power. Surfers will embrace the challenge to achieve the highest scores possible.. Teahupo'o is known for its massive waves, which can be daunting even for experienced surfers. "The first time I surfed Teahupo'o was my senior year," pro US surfer, Caroline Marks, said in an Olympic.com interview. "I felt like I was thrown in the deep end of the pool and I had no idea how to swim." Sport climbing Paris Olympics 2024 Sport climbing debuted in the 2020 Olympics to attract younger audiences. While climbers were excited, many were unhappy with the combined event format, which included speed climbing, bouldering, and lead climbing. Bouldering and lead climbing require endurance, with bouldering involving a four-meter wall scaled in four minutes without a rope, and lead climbing a 15-meter wall scaled in six minutes with one attempt. Speed climbing, focusing on speed, was considered incompatible with the other two. In response, the IOC will separate bouldering and lead climbing from speed climbing at the Paris Games. The number of events will double, and participants will increase from 40 in 2020 to 68. Tom O'Halloran, an Australian athlete who participated in the Tokyo 2020 Olympics, described the format as "a pretty brutal format." In an interview with Yahoo Sports, he likened the situation to having track athletes who are familiar with only one discipline having "to suddenly do the shot put, the 100 metres and the 1500 or something."

title: Security fears stalk 2024 Paris Olympic organisers
text: PARIS: Two years out from Paris hosting the Summer Olympics there is widespread concern over security, exacerbated by the dreadful spectacle of the chaotic scenes at the Champions League final at the Stade de France. Police tear-gassing frustrated Liverpool fans, including children and the disabled, was not the fault of the supporters but, according to a damning fact-finding mission by two French senators, the fault of the organisers. "These dysfunctions were at every level, not only during the implementation but also during advance preparations," said the co-chair of the enquiry Laurent Lafon. The debacle set alarm bells ringing with next year's Rugby World Cup being hosted in France but most of all for those dealing with security issues around the Olympics. "Hopefully this serves as a wake-up call for everybody," a security source told AFP. The nervousness surrounding security at the Olympics led French Interior Minister Gerald Darmanin to set a clear roadmap for new Paris police chief Laurent Nunez, who has replaced Didier Lallement. "You will be the prefect of police in charge of the Olympics and the entire police prefecture must be geared towards that," Darmanin said during Nunez's inauguration ceremony. A government source told AFP the disastrous sequence of events at the Champions League final would "stick to them like a plaster up to the Olympic Games". With 13 million visitors expected and 15,000 athletes competing, the level of anxiety over the massive security operation at the Olympics was already high. For months the biggest security headache for the organising committee has been the Opening Ceremony on the Seine on July 26. On paper, the ceremony promises to be stunning, with the teams on around 180 boats travelling down the Seine, through the heart of the City of Light. On the banks, an estimated 600,000 spectators will take in the spectacle, half a million of them free of charge. Spectacular indeed, not least for the global television audience, but a massive security headache. "We are not ready at all," said the government source. "If a drone drops grenades onto the crowds below we do not know how we will neutralise them." Fears over a drone attack is nothing new. There have been worries in the past that events such as marches might be targeted. "It is the magnitude of the crowds spread out over six kilometres of the banks of the Seine which is the problem," the source added. That is accentuated by a dispute between the organising committee and the police. The former wants to see spectators lining the entirety of the route, whilst the latter want everyone attending issued with a ticket and placed in enclosures along the river. "This is a clash of two contrasting philosophies," a source from Paris-2024 told AFP. The biggest problem for the police in providing security for the ceremony is a lack of available officers. According to a police source, it would require "nearly 7,000 officers" which in the height of summer is all but impossible. The deficit in numbers cannot be filled by private security guards as they have fallen short of hiring the 24,000 it is believed are needed for the Games. "We do not have the numbers," Bernard Thibault, a member of the organising committee told AFP in mid-April. The shortage of private security staff is a throwback to London in 2012 and Tokyo last year when both host cities were forced to fall back on the military. In both cases, operations ran smoothly. "It is plain and simple," a highly-placed police source told AFP. "The 24,000 agents required for the Games do not exist, and never will. "The army will be called on to do the job." The authorities have also prioritised preventing cyber-attacks -- the Olympics has been a high profile target for years. According to a source close to the organisers, several hundred cyber-investigators from the French Interior Ministry will be keeping an eye on potential attacks. An Olympic intelligence centre has also been set up, as promised in the 2018 Olympic Law, to combat any risk of an attack. Despite these measures the highly-placed police source believes there needs to be a greater sense of urgency. "Clearly for the moment there are still holes in the racquet. So we better get our skates on."

title: Who is Michelle Kroppen? Deepika Kumariâs archery opponent at Paris Olympics
text: Michelle Kroppen (AFP Photo) NEW DELHI: World No. 13 recurve archer Michelle Kroppen from Germany is set to face off against former World No. 1 archer Deepika Kumari from India in the Round of 16 at the Paris Olympics 2024 on Saturday, August 3. Kroppen recently secured a silver medal in the mixed team event, despite a 0-6 loss to South Korea in the final. In the ranking round, Kroppen finished seventh with a season-best score of 670, while Deepika Kumari placed 23rd with a score of 658. However, Kroppen's career-best throw stands at 680, compared to Deepika's 686. Notably, Michelle Kroppen played a crucial role in the German women's team's bronze medal victory at the Tokyo Olympics in 2021. She has also earned numerous medals for the women's team, mixed team, and individually at various international competitions, including the World Championships, European Games, and European Championships. Currently, Michelle Kroppen holds the World No. 13 ranking in the World Archery rankings for recurve women, with her career-best ranking being World No. 5, achieved in June 2019. In the ongoing Paris Olympics 2024 , Michell Kroppen and her partner Florian Unruh recently settled for the silver medal after a 0-6 loss to South Korea in the mixed team gold medal match. Germany secured three women's quotas for the Paris Olympics 2024 through the 2023 World Archery Championships. The highly anticipated Round of 16 match between Michelle Kroppen and Deepika Kumari is scheduled for Saturday, August 3, at 1:52 PM IST at the Paris Olympics 2024. title: Paris Olympics 2024: Sharon van Rouwendaal wins Olympic 10k marathon swimming gold
text: Sharon van Rouwendaal (AP Photo) NEW DELHI: Sharon van Rouwendaal , the Dutch swimmer, secured the gold medal in the women's 10k marathon swimming event at the Paris Olympics on Thursday with a late surge. Van Rouwendaal finished with a time of "2hr 03min 34.2sec", while Moesha Johnson from Australia claimed the silver medal, 5.5 seconds behind, and Ginevra Taddeucci of Italy took the bronze. The competition was held on the River Seine, with the iconic Eiffel Tower serving as a backdrop, after the water pollution levels were deemed safe enough for the event to proceed. Van Rouwendaal, who had previously won gold in Rio in 2016 and silver in Tokyo, made her decisive move past Johnson near the Pont des Invalides bridge, overtaking her around a pilon. The Dutch swimmer, who also held the world champion title from Budapest in 2022, maintained her lead until the finish line, leaving no chance for her competitors to catch up. Johnson, who had been leading the race from the halfway point, suffered a devastating defeat as she and the other two top swimmers had broken away from the rest of the field during the final lap. Although the decision to hold the race on the river created a spectacular visual experience, it had posed challenges for the organizers. The triathlon event had been significantly disrupted by poor bacterial readings in the water last week, leading to the cancellation of all swim training sessions and the postponement of the men's individual race by 24 hours until Wednesday. Similarly, training for the 10k race had also been called off due to the water pollution levels.
